en: In the first chapter, titled *Mānasollāsa*,
we ever pay homage to Gaṇeśvara, whose mantra has perfected the attainment of desired fruits,
and who sweeps away obstacles like cotton with the wind from his flapping ears.
A certain pure Sarasvatī, a companion to consciousness, blazes forth alone;
by her, even the light within those who are awakened is made manifest.
I bow to Maheśvara, the seed of the Bhagavatā, whose form is the Liṅga;
though unmanifest, he is fully manifest within whom all that is moving and unmoving resides.

Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Hara! Protect me, protect me! You are the conqueror of the universe for the sake of Viṣṇu’s manifestation; you are Hari, Narahari—salutations be to you! O God, grant me the state that is imperishable and beyond falling.
I bow to the God who bears the sound of the Vedas,
who always dwells within the interior of the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu, which possesses the grace of humming bees.
We pay homage to that Śakra, the deity even of the gods,
who with his thousand eyes beholds the affairs of the universe.
Worship that one who, having constantly swallowed the veil of darkness here, vomits forth universal light with his hundreds of rays,
and who has made the protection of the universe his sole purpose.
I bow to Āditya, who performs wondrous sports.
Salutation to that flower-bowed god of unexhausted power, by whose will the Sthāṇu was born bearing his beloved as half of his own body.
I pay homage every day to Vālmīki, the author of the first poem,
from whom this meritorious speech, tasting like nectar, has proceeded;
[and likewise] to the illustrious King Someśvara, the ornament of the Cālukya dynasty.
This treatise, which brings joy to the mind, benefits all the world,
instructs one in all matters, and serves as a book on worldly conduct,
has been composed with great effort by King Soma for diligent study.
Here, first, the twenty causes for the acquisition of a kingdom are told;
thereafter, the twenty causes for the stability of the acquired kingdom.
For a sovereign whose kingdom is stable,
there are twenty enjoyments that produce pleasure, and likewise, there are twenty diversions.
The twenty sports leading to a happy rebirth are proclaimed;
there, I shall first state their summary in brief:
one must avoid falsehood and avoid malice toward others.
The avoidance of those who should not be approached, the avoidance of what should not be eaten,
the avoidance of malice, the avoidance of association with the fallen,
the avoidance of anger, and the avoidance of self-praise.
Generosity, captivating speech, the performance of sacrifices and works of public utility, devotion to all the deities, the offering of libations to cows and Brahmins,
and likewise the performance of libations for the ancestors and for guests— these must be practiced.
Worship, service to one's gurus, austerity, and bathing at sacred fords.
The nourishment of the poor, the helpless, the afflicted, and kinsmen, as well as the protection of those who have come for refuge— these twenty [qualities] lead to the attainment of sovereignty.
Now, regarding the twenty causes for the stability of a kingdom that has been attained:
the seven constituent elements, as well as the three powers and the six measures of policy.
Furthermore, there are four means; thus twenty [elements] are proclaimed:
the sovereign, the minister, the ally, the treasury, the realm, the fort, and the army.
The constituent elements of sovereignty are the subjects, the guilds of the citizens, as well as peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge.
There are six qualities; three powers—born of majesty, energy, and counsel;
and the fourfold means: sowing dissension, punishment, conciliation, and bribery.
Now, twenty types of royal enjoyments are described in order:
those of the house, the bath, and the pair of sandals.
The enjoyment of betel, ointments, garments, and garlands;
the use of ornaments and seats; and likewise the use of fly-whisks and the royal throne.
And the enjoyment by his sons of food, water, foot-massage, vehicles, umbrellas,
and beds.
For incense and for women, there are twenty distinct enjoyments;
thus, twenty enjoyments have been described as diversions.
Now I shall describe the pastimes of weapons and treatises, the sports of elephants and horses,
the diversions of wrestling, and the amusements involving cocks.
The diversion of quails, rams, and buffaloes,
the diversion of pigeons,
and the diversion of dogs.

The diversion of hawks, fish, and deer; the diversion of song and instrumental music; the diversion of dance and of storytelling; and the diversion of wonders—for the sake of delighting in diversions, these twenty have been proclaimed.
Now, twenty pleasure-giving pastimes are described in sequence:
on a mountain, in a pleasure garden, on a swing, and with water-sprinkling.
Was it perhaps play upon a grassy meadow, in the sand,
in moonlight, in a field of grain, in a gathering of wine-drinkers, or even in the telling of riddles?

The play of the fourfold army and the inexhaustible [treasury], the play with cowries and the lord of serpents, and the play with the *phañjikā* in the darkness— these are appropriate for the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).
There are twenty distinct types of play: swinging, amorous play, and other forms of play.
"One hundred chapters and five sections"—
thus has the seed of the *Mānasollāsa* been briefly stated;
now I shall describe it at length with its hundreds of branches, like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*).
Whatever sin one commits by speaking falsely in a legal testimony out of desire, greed, fear, or anger— that is proclaimed to be untruth.
When one utters a statement in the presence of a deity preceded by an oath,
and then violates it out of delusion, that is proclaimed to be untruth.
"It leads away from heaven, brings ill repute, is loathed by the world, and is utterly sinful; therefore, one should avoid it entirely.
Thus [it is said].
Chapter One: On the Avoidance of Untruth.
Whatever beating, cutting, affliction, various forms of killing,
or binding one inflicts upon others is called malice toward others.
Slander, speaking ill of others, giving verbal abuse, threatening, and exposing one's vital secrets— whatever one performs that constitutes malice toward another is called *paradroha* (malice).
[This includes coveting] houses, wives, cattle, fields, land, grain, wealth, and so forth.
That foolish-minded person who commits injury against others is called a "hater of others" (paradroha).
Since injury inflicted by another is exceedingly difficult for oneself to endure,
one should therefore avoid the terrible act of hating others, which leads to hell.
Thus ends the second chapter, "On the Avoidance of Malice Toward Others."
A girl in her menses, one who has fallen from her status,
a female ascetic, one born of a noble caste, another's wife, one who is helpless, a mother-in-law, a sister, and a daughter.
In that regard, the wives of one's teacher and Brahmins, the wives of sons, friends, and kings,
and the wives of servants and kinsmen are women who must not be approached.
"Going to those who should not be approached is declared to be the supreme destroyer of the lifespan of men; it brings fear in the next world. Therefore, one should avoid it. Thus [it is said].
Chapter 3: On the Seduction of Unapproachable Women.
Garlic, leeks,
onions, village cocks, domestic pigs, and mushrooms are not to be eaten.
The pigeons, parrots, hawks, swans, owls, cranes, cuckoos, mynas, vultures, and dogs have been fully enumerated.
Sacrificial animals are censured, with the exception of goats and the like;
furthermore, worms, insects, and moths are not to be eaten by us.
The lizard, the durdara, the snake, the mongoose, the domestic owl, the crocodile, and the porpoise have been proclaimed [as the guardians].
The three kinds of liquor— those made from molasses, honey, and flour— are declared inedible and should not be drunk.

One should avoid all types of liquor, including *maireya*, as well as any drinkable substance; and one should also avoid the milk of a cow that has not yet had its calf, or that which is within ten days of calving.
The milk of a beloved cow that has recently calved, or the milk of a she-goat or a she-camel by a bull, is unfit to be drunk.
For it is proclaimed that one falls into hell by eating what is forbidden to eat and drinking what is forbidden to drink,
especially upon seeing the prosperity, beauty, or valor of another.
Magnanimity, skill in the arts, virtuous conduct, good fortune, and the perfection of qualities.
He who is intolerant goes to the abode of Yama and incurs reproach in this world; therefore, one should not be intolerant.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on the Avoidance of Envy.
Additional verses concerning those wearing sectarian marks who are defiled by mortal sins:
One becomes fallen through association with those who violate the Dharma, such as Caṇḍālas and those of the lowest castes.
Therefore, by associating with the fallen, a man falls into the Raurava hell and incurs dishonor in this world; for that reason, one should avoid him.
Thus it is said.
Chapter Six: On Avoiding Association with the Outcaste.
Anger destroys wisdom, as well as oneself, one's family, and wealth;
through anger, the destruction of dharma occurs; therefore, one should utterly avoid it.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, "On the Avoidance of Anger."
He who praises himself out of delusion is dead even while living;
he goes to torment in the next world. Therefore, one should avoid that.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Avoidance of Self-Praise.

Gifts that destroy great sins and yield great meritorious fruits should be given to a learned Vedic scholar who is poor, endowed with good character and conduct, knowledgeable in the Purāṇas and Vedas, and a householder.
Great gifts should be given for the satisfaction of Mahādeva:
silver, gold, and jewels; garments, beds, and seats;
as well as elephants, horses, buffaloes, cows, and oxen capable of bearing the yoke.
A house, a village, as well as land, a female slave, a maiden, ornaments,
food and drink, sesame and medicinal herbs, and the supreme gift of fearlessness to one who is afraid.

Whatever is desired by someone in this world, whatever happiness they have in their own home—all that should be given to the learned man by one who desires that very thing to be inexhaustible. Thus ends the ninth chapter, on Giving.
Truth should be spoken; that which is pleasant should be spoken; that which is beneficial but unpleasant should not be spoken.
Nor should that which is pleasant but false be spoken—this is the eternal dharma.
One should speak what is beneficial, one should speak in moderation, and one should speak what is pleasant and meaningful.
He who always speaks thus is honored by the wise in this world;
he is honored by the wise on earth and honored by the gods in heaven—
he who always speaks what is agreeable is a wise man in both worlds.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on Pleasant Speech.
The sacrifice to men, the sacrifice to Brahman, and thereafter the sacrifice to the gods,
the sacrifice to beings, and the sacrifice to the ancestors— these are the five sacrifices.
One should cause the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, culminating in the Aśvamedha, to be performed.

One should perform [the sacrifice] during the autumn and spring seasons according to the prescribed rule; for a sacrifice lacking food burns the kingdom, one devoid of mantras destroys the officiating priests,
and a sacrifice without gifts kills the patron and the teacher.

One should perform ten thousand, one hundred thousand, or ten million fire-offerings for the sake of pacification, and one should have them performed by the foremost of Brahmins with the desire for auspiciousness.
A well may be without a door, or it may have a single door; a pond has many doors, while a lotus-pond is long in shape and is called a *dīrghikā*.
A pond (taḍāga) is defined as one whose water is enclosed by a dam;
the excavation of these [reservoirs] should be performed by divers with their faces turned downwards.
He should establish fire-sanctuaries, water-stations, shelters,
and groves.
The three constellations of the east, Viśākhā, Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī, and Maghā, as well as Āśleṣā and Mūla, are the downward-facing asterisms.
The digging of wells and the like, as well as the excavation of hidden treasures, the construction of tanks, and the propitiation of deities,
as well as gambling and calculation— these should always be performed when the faces [of the planets] are downward-turned.

Thus, the man who performs acts of public utility (*pūrta*) and sacrifice (*iṣṭa*) according to the prescribed rules attains supreme perfection, which brings auspiciousness in both worlds— namely, the maintenance of sacred fires, the establishment of water-stations (*prapā*), the performance of sacrificial sessions (*sattra*), and the cooking of food for the needy.
One should establish an assembly hall and a monastic residence, as well as dilapidated temples,
according to the principles of Viśvakarman and in accordance with the treatise of Maya.
By means of the measurements determined according to the procedure proclaimed by Matsya and in accordance with the *Piṅgalāmata*, [one attains] the four aims of human life.
The lord of the earth should devoutly cause temples and monasteries to be built,
according to the measurement of nine tālas and in accordance with the prescribed injunctions.
First, the wise man should have images made according to the previously described method;
they should be complete in all their limbs, slightly plump, and pleasing to the eye.
Equipped with the aforementioned weapons and the arms as described,
[one should strike] on its back, on the region of the shoulder, at the nape of the neck, or on the crown of the head.
Alternatively,
having placed a long stalk produced from the *madana* tree, resembling a *kāsa* flower,
one should then smear the image with consecrated [substances].
Having ground clay, soot, and chaff, along with cotton, a hundred times over;
One should apply a small amount of finely ground, powdered salt to the wound.
One should grind everything together with clay on a very smooth stone slab;
having rubbed that three times, one should smear it all over.
The first application should be clear, dried in the shade;
after two days have passed, the second [application] should then be made again.
When that has dried, a third thick coating is desired; leaving out the opening of the stalk, one should smear everything with clay and dry it with effort using appropriate methods, being wise.
First, a wise man should weigh a piece of beeswax that has not adhered to the image;
he should then have it fashioned from tin, copper, silver, or gold.
One should prepare copper, which is eight times the weight of that [silver], as well as the substance known as rīti (bronze).
Silver should be twelve times [the weight] and gold sixteen times more;
one should envelop the desired substance,
such as gold and so forth, with clay.
One should dry the crucible, shaped like a coconut, as before;
then, having heated it in the fire, one should extract the wax from the image.
Afterwards, one should heat the crucible with the residual fire of embers;
then brass and copper will attain the state of liquid by means of nine charcoal pieces.
Surely, when cast into heated coals, silver would turn into liquid.
Gold attains the state of mercury when it has been heated five times after making a hole at the top of the crucible with an iron rod.
Having held it firmly with tongs,
one should take up the heated crucible and place a burning wick upon the tip of a heated needle.
Having carefully bent the crucible held with tongs,
one should pour the liquid into the mouth of the tube in an unbroken stream.
Having filled the area up to the edge of the Nālaka forest, one should then cease;
for the sake of cooling the heat, one should extinguish the fire situated near it once the image has attained coolness.
One who is skilled and light-handed should, by its very nature, break open the burnt clay.
Then that image made of material substance becomes just like one fashioned by Madana himself, manifest and adorned with all its major and minor limbs.
Wherever one perceives anything excessive, one should pacify it through various means;
one should not cut off the stalk, but rather subsequently bring it to a state of brilliance.
By this method, having properly maintained the image and having installed it according to the rules on an auspicious lunar day, the king should worship it every day.
Or Viṣṇu, or Gaṇeśa, or Durgā, or Sarasvatī,
or the Sun in the form of a discus, or Śiva.
One should worship the one in the form of the *liṅga* with a spirit of devotion and a mind purified by faith,
using leaves, flowers, auspicious fragrances, and food offerings.

The man who thus performs the rites of fulfillment (pūrta) and sacrifice (iṣṭa) according to the prescribed rule with incense and lamps attains supreme perfection, which brings auspiciousness to both worlds.
Thus ends the chapter on Sacrificial Rites and Charitable Works.
One should prepare the arghya, the pādya with auspicious waters, the madhuparka,
as well as the ācamana and the bath, each accompanied by its respective substances.
Having bowed with devotion according to the eight-limbed [prostration] and having offered praise, by means of mantras, meditations, recitations, fire-offerings, mudrās, and various forms of worship.
In this manner, a man with a joyful mind should dismiss [the deity] after having worshipped his chosen god.
Through such worship, he attains a great kingdom; of this there is no doubt.
[He should avoid] both censure and hatred toward other gods as well.
Upon seeing a deity or a temple, one should avoid [neglecting it], pay homage, and not overstep [the bounds of respect].
Thus, he who has taken recourse to a faithful disposition and attained equanimity obtains excellent prosperity through the grace of all the gods.
Thus ends the chapter on devotion to all deities without exception.

One desiring merit should always give morsels of food to cows until they are satisfied; by this gift of one's own and others' food, as well as by pleasant speech and respectful honor toward the best of the twice-born, Viṣṇu is pleased.
One should satisfy them with one's whole being; by that, one attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter on the Satiating of Cows and Brahmins.
One should perform the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) under that [deceased's] name with sesame seeds mixed with water; likewise,
one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) produced from cow’s milk together with sugar,
as well as various foods, sanctified meats, clarified butter, and honey.
And with various other delightful cooked foods prepared by others,
one should devoutly feed the foremost of the twice-born on behalf of the ancestors;
with a mind purified by faith, one should perform the śrāddha rite without sloth.
Thus, whoever performs the śrāddha ceremony and gratifies the ancestral deities shall experience an increase in progeny; his kingdom shall flourish and his life-span shall be great.
Possessing his desires, he attains whatever he wishes for in his mind.
But by performing [this] unintentionally, one shall attain supreme Nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the chapter on the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa), the fourteenth.
The wise know him to be a guest who has arrived from another land, whose family and name are unknown, who is afflicted by hunger, and whose feet are covered in dust;
he who does not honor such a guest when he has arrived is a fool.
Having taken away all of his merits, the guest departs swiftly;
therefore, a wise person should honor the guest with devotion using their whole being.
When the guest is honored, Viṣṇu is honored—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, on the honoring of guests.
The progenitor, the one who initiates [the sacred thread], the one who imparts knowledge,
the sustainer, and the protector from fear— these five are remembered as gurus. Among them,
the teacher (ācārya) is superior to the sub-teacher (upādhyāya), and the father is superior even to the teacher.
The mother is even more worthy of honor than the father; she is distinguished by her superior gravity.
One should act for the benefit of those who are venerable through their mental, verbal, and physical deeds;
their command must not be transgressed, and one should always practice service toward them.
Thus, for one who serves the teacher with devotion, having bowed down, being composed, grateful, and firm in resolve, the fruit of merit is great.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, on Service to the Teacher.

Through arduous penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, through various meritorious vows, by subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, or likewise on leaves, flowers, and unhusked grain; by those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, those who subsist on smoke, and those who abstain from food entirely.
By enduring cold and heat, by the desire for the welfare of all beings,
by celibacy, austerity, restraint of the senses,
recitation, meditation, silence, breath-control, and meditative absorption;
One who, being self-restrained, performs the emaciation of the body through these austerities, obtains every desire— even that which is difficult to attain; of this there is no doubt,
whether it be far off, difficult to propitiate, or situated in a state of extreme difficulty.
All that is to be accomplished through austerity, for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on Austerity.
The Jāhnavī, the best of rivers; the auspicious Yamunā and Narmadā; the holy Tāpī with its surging waves; the Gautamī, which destroys sins;
and the delightful Devapādodbhavā, which flows through the lap of Śrīśaila.
The Tuṅgabhadrā is ever auspicious, destroying sin by the mere sight of her;
there, the world-renowned Vañjarā, Bhīmarathyā, Kṛṣṇā, Veṇyā, and Bṛhannadī, who removes all impurity, have come together.
These and other rivers, oceans, lakes, ponds, natural pools, and mountain springs,
as well as sacred lotus-pools and the merit-bestowing Śuklatīrtha that grants happiness— [all these were seen].
The holy site of Prabhāsa is renowned, as is Kedāra, which destroys afflictions; Prayāga is the king of holy sites, bestowing desired objects;
and there is the priceless Arghya-tīrtha, frequented by hosts of gods.
Vārāṇasī is greatly meritorious, frequented by Mahādeva,
endowed with great power, and the destroyer of great sins;
Sarasvatī removes evil through three baths, while Yamunā does so through five.
By merely bathing in the Jāhnavī, or even by the sight of the Narmadā,
one who bathes in these holy tīrthas is liberated from sin;
he obtains his heart's desire and rejoices like Mahendra himself.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on bathing at sacred fords (tīrthasnāna).
He who utters the piteous words "Give me," driven by desire and having fallen into a state of wretchedness due to poverty, is proclaimed to be a *dīna* (the miserable).
With a heart softened by compassion and free from desire for his own interests, the king should grant whatever wealth or other things are desired to that indigent person for the sake of dharma.
One who is bereft of mother and father, deprived of friends and kinsmen,
and parted from his masters and relatives is designated as "without a protector" (anātha).
Those who are afflicted must be protected with effort through medical treatments, mantras, rituals, and other such means.
One should provide for their search by means of food, drink, beds, and seats.
Physicians who were learned in the science of weapons and treatises, skilled through diligent practice,
possessing the discernment to analyze and resolve, holding ambrosia in their hands, and speaking with kindness.
Having provided various medicines individually,
and having appointed attendants who were free from laziness and knowledgeable in dharma;
In fever, in hemorrhagic disease, in cough, in dyspnea, in consumption,
in vomiting, in alcoholism, in the abdominal enlargements, and in disorders of the small and large intestines;
In cases of dysuria, urinary disorders (prameha), abscesses, abdominal tumors (gulma), and piles; in anemia, edema, erysipelas, black moles, vitiligo, and diseases of the skin.
In cases of vāta-śoṇita (blood disorders) as well as other diseases,
one should administer the appropriate treatment in accordance with the medical scriptures.
Having understood the primary cause of diseases and their true nature clearly through their symptoms,
according to place and time, and in accordance with the principles of suitability and constitution;
That phlegm (sāma), having destroyed the digestive fire situated in the stomach over a long period and having obstructed the movement of the abdominal fire,
casts it outside.
Thus emerged the fire, which, having taken recourse to the body and causing it to burn, is called "fever" (jvara) by those who know it; it is the lord of all diseases.
Medicine that is properly digested destroys the morbid humor (doṣa) located in the digestive tract (koṣṭha).
If unripened, it does not produce any quality; it is like nectar [only when ripe].
Since medicine does not take effect in one afflicted by fever without the digestive fire,
one should therefore not administer medicine, but rather employ fasting.
The wise declare that fasting— consisting of the avoidance of food that is chewed, eaten, sucked, licked, or drunk—
is the cause of lightness of the body.
Having considered the fault of the doshas, the strength, the season, the constitution, and likewise the cause,
fasting should be practiced until the body becomes purified.
For one night, three nights, or even five nights;
for seven nights, nine nights, or ten nights plus one.
The time for administering fasting has been determined according to the nature of the doshas;
thereafter, the medicine that destroys the disease of fever should be given.
Eating once a day, as well as drinking gruel or thin rice-scum with lukewarm water—
fasting is thus remembered as being of various kinds according to the provocation of the humors (doṣas).
When one who has undergone fasting regains health, hunger, thirst, alertness,
relish for food, clarity of mind, vigor, digestion, and lightness of body are the signs [of recovery].
The physician should properly treat the patient who has become free from fever through fasting, light and wholesome food, and moderate eating for as long as seven days.
Even when leaping has been properly performed and the signs of successful leaping are observed,
if the fever is not released, one should treat the patient with gruels (peyā).
Having ascertained which of the humors— wind, bile, or phlegm— is predominant by its symptoms,
one should prepare a gruel with substances that pacify that specific humor and administer it.
One should recognize Vata when pain is predominant, and Pitta when there is burning heat;
one should know Kapha when there is numbness, but in a mixed case, one should recognize the combination of humors.
When the three doshas are aggravated and equal, a sannipāta occurs;
the patient becomes difficult to treat, so one should attend to him with great effort.
A gruel prepared with bilva, balā, pṛthakparṇī, ginger, coriander, and blue lotus should be administered;
it destroys fever caused by vāta and pitta.
In cases of pain in the abdomen, bladder, and head, an excellent physician should administer a warm gruel prepared with *kṣudrā* and *gokṣura* to one afflicted by diseases caused by *vāta*.
*Gokṣura*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *guhā*, and also *atiguhā* [are used for this purpose].
A gruel prepared with these [herbs] removes the afflictions of dyspnea, cough, and fever.
A gruel prepared with the roots of śrīparṇī, bilva, ṭeṭūka, tarkārī, and likewise pāṭalā,
along with barley, removes the affliction caused by phlegm.
Even gruel prepared with fried rice, combined with long pepper (pippalī) and emblic myrobalan (āmalaka),
and drunk with ghee, is a purgative for obstructed feces.
[164] Long pepper (māgadhī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), raisins (mṛdvīkā), and the medicinal herbs of the āmalaka— these [with sugar] form a cooling drink.
Once prepared, it should be drunk; it relieves colic and constipation in the stomach.
A gruel prepared with *vyāghrī*, jujube (*badara*), *vṛkṣāmla*, *pāṭalā*, *bilva*, and *gokṣura*, taken with sugar,
destroys thirst and bestows pleasant perspiration and sleep.
In summer when kapha and pitta are predominant, when kapha is situated in the region of the navel,
and in cases of thirst, vomiting, burning sensation, and intoxication accompanied by alcohol— always [administer it].
When blood has flowed upwards, a liquid gruel (peyā) is not at all recommended;
rather, one should take fruit juices that subdue fever, or Vāruṇa wine which destroys worms.
When it has been digested, one should drink [the medicine] mixed with sugar and honey;
when hungry, one should satisfy oneself with gruel or boiled rice with fried grains.
Water boiled with grains such as mung beans and the like is called *yūṣa* (soup);
*yūṣa* that is without fat or salt is designated as *daka*.
One should know that broth combined with salt and fat is "salty" (lāvaṇika);
one may prepare it with six ingredients, or with those two [salt and fat], or with the juices of mung beans or rice.
Having understood the origin of the disorder, one should protect the strength with great effort;
one should digest the morbid humor (doṣa) by means of fasting, medicinal gruels, nectars, and meat soups.
When the maturation of the humors has occurred after more than seven nights,
one should gradually eliminate the remaining humors with digestive decoctions.
The bitter taste should be administered as it removes bile; the pungent taste destroys phlegm;
and this astringent taste also removes bile and phlegm, yet it is not the best of tastes.
In acute fever (navajvara), the astringent decoction obstructs the waste products (mala) and may lead to irregularity of the fever;
it may also produce nausea, loss of appetite, and hiccups.
When the fever has become mild, when the body has attained lightness,
and when the morbid humors have been mobilized, the experts prescribe that medicine be administered after three nights.
A decoction of mustā, parpaṭaka, and śuṇṭhī; or parpaṭaka with śuṇṭhī;
or even yavāparpaṭaka should be administered as a destroyer of fever.
Pāṭhā, uśīra, and vālaka, whether prepared as a decoction (kaṣāya) or taken cold when digested,
destroy thirst, bad breath, bad taste in the mouth, and indigestion.
The leaves of *paṭola*, *kaṭukā*, and the seeds of *kuṭaja*—
this decoction, when boiled, is a destroyer of continuous fever (*santata-jvara*).
A decoction prepared with pāṭhā, paṭola, kaṭukā, sārivā,
and mustā destroys even the most agonizing fevers.
A decoction prepared from raisins, the three myrobalans, neem, patola, guduchi,
and vatsaka destroys fever that arises on the following day.
A decoction prepared with ginger, guḍūcī, bhūnimba,
and sandalwood quickly destroys fever occurring on the third day.
A decoction of *guḍūcī*, *āmalaka*, and *mustā*, combined with honey,
quickly wards off fever occurring on the fourth day.
A decoction made from mūrvā, nimba, paṭola, ativiṣa, dhanvayavāsaka,
śuṇṭhī, mustā, amṛtā, and yāsa removes fever caused by vāta.
A decoction of amṛtā, pippalīmūla, nāgara, indrayava, ambuda,
and the laghu-pañcamūla should be used in fever born of pitta.
A decoction made from kaṭukā, parpaṭa, mustā, bhūnimba, and durālabhā,
along with vatsaka, destroys fever arising from phlegm (kapha).
There is another fever arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), in which pitta is considered to be predominant;
it produces a burning sensation (dāha) either in the skin or in the internal cavity (koṣṭha), and this occurs either before or after the onset of other symptoms.
Similarly, there is a cold [fever] caused by vāta and kapha, which is difficult to overcome and preceded by a burning sensation;
in that case, when the fever begins with coldness, the kapha is first liquefied and then dried up by pitta.
When [the fever] has become calm and cool, there occurs belching with sourness, intoxication, and thirst;
however, in cases of burning sensation and the like, these symptoms reappear along with drowsiness, perspiration, vomiting, and exhaustion.
A decoction prepared from paṭola, kaṭukā, mustā, prāṇadā, and madhuka—
taken in combinations of three, four, or five ingredients— is used for cold-fever and irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
For the destruction of cold [fevers], incense and ointments should be prepared with kāyasthā, nākulī, tiktā, vayasthā, agaru, cauraka, sahadevī, and vacā.
Oil cooked with these very same drugs, ground together and combined with salt,
alkali, and sour liquids, destroys coldness when used for massage.
For cold-fever (śītajvara), the application of śilājatu oil is the supreme remedy;
likewise, an errhine (nasya) consisting of asafoetida and rock salt, combined with aged ghee, is effective.
A powder of dhātrī rubbed with ghee, or amlavetasa with water, applied as a paste, removes burning;
likewise, the froth produced from the leaves of the badarī tree does so.
An application of Kāleya, badara, Anantā, yaṣṭī, candana, and kañjika, mixed with ghee, as a head-paste removes thirst, burning sensations, and fever.
When one is freed from a fever caused by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), a severe swelling occurs at the root of the ear; because of this, only a few are ever liberated.
The purification of the mercury must be performed repeatedly with *nīrajābī* [a specific medicinal preparation];
it should be carried out with such effort that the mercury does not undergo calcination (*pāka*).
One should cook ghee with either bitter or sweet [herbs];
when prepared in this manner, the sweet ghee should be administered for disorders of vāta and pitta.
Pitta, aggravated by substances that are alkaline, sour, or salty, as well as by physical exertion and excessive exposure to the sun, vitiates the blood.

Then, from the nose, mouth, and ears, as well as from the passages of the anus and urethra, that which is known as *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) flows forth; thus it is declared by the best of physicians.

Raktapitta that is characterized by a single doṣa, is recent, occurs in the upward direction, is strong, and is free from complications is easily curable; if it flows downward, it is said to be palliable.

When blood-bile (raktapitta) has spread downward and upward, involves all three humors, and is accompanied by many complications, it is incurable; such cases should be abandoned by the best of physicians.
One should administer one karṣa of a linctus prepared from śyāmā and trivṛt with their decoction and paste, combined with sugar, for a patient suffering from hemorrhaging.
This bolus (modaka) prepared with long pepper (pippalī), the three myrobalans (triphalā), black creeper (śyāmā), sugar (śarkarā), trivṛt, and honey,
conquers blood disorders arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
The Vata, provoked by substances that increase Vata and having displaced the Kapha,
brings about a cough in the chest that is afflicted by diseases of the heart and the flanks.
One should cook ghee with sixty palas of the juices of both Amṛtā and Kaṇṭakārī until one-fourth remains; this ghee conquers cough.
One should drink the powder of kṛmighna, auṣadha, rāsnā, māgadhī, hiṅgu,
saindhava, kṣāra, and bhārṅgī along with a measured quantity of clarified butter (ājya).
This is recommended for cough produced by wind combined with phlegm,
as well as for hiccup, impaired digestion, and asthma.
From chronic cough, dyspnea arises; from dyspnea, the vital air (marut) becomes aggravated.
From the aggravation of that wind, as well as from anemia, fever, and disease, [dyspnea occurs].
One should drink the powder of karcūra, the root of puṣkara, and likewise the fruit of āmalakī,
with clarified butter or with meat broth, in cases of dyspnea.
From the suppression of natural urges, as well as from the depletion of ojas, unctuousness, and semen—
even from deficient physical exercise— one suffers from the ailments of dyspnea, cough, and fever.
Vata, when excessively aggravated, excites kapha and pitta;
entering the joints of the body, it brings about the disease of wasting (kṣaya).
Rāsnā, sesame, and blācūrṇa, along with ghee, yaṣṭikā, and utpala, when licked,
will remove emaciation and destroy weak digestion.
Through the consumption of unwholesome food, the bodily air (māruta) becomes excessively aggravated;
the udāna wind then causes vomiting accompanied by pain in the navel and the back.
A decoction made from Jambū, Cūta, Balā, Uśīra, Vaṭa-shuṅga, and Avaroha,
when drunk together with honey, destroys vomiting.
Honey mixed with powdered harītakī, or jujube fruit mixed with honey,
or an emetic using emetic substances, shall destroy chronic vomiting.
From deficient, improper, or excessive drinking, intoxication quickly arises;
thereafter, vomiting, delusion, dizziness, lethargy, and incoherent speech occur.
This intoxication (madātyaya) arises within five days or seven nights;
if it persists beyond that, it is proclaimed as a different disease.
In cases of alcoholism accompanied by nausea, burning sensations, and cardiac pain,
the expert in clinical application should administer emetics using appropriate emetic substances.
In cases of thirst, grape juice mixed with honey should be given;
or water with the tubers of white lotus (utpala), or even water alone.
An application made to the face with ciñcā, pomegranate, vṛkṣāmla, kola,
and amlavetasa destroys thirst arising from intoxicating liquor.
Cooling measures should be employed in cases of delusion, burning sensations, and confusion;
likewise, a thick covering is beneficial for headache and numbness.
In cases of alcoholism characterized by excessive sleep and delirium,
one should administer meat broth prepared from goat, partridge, quail, antelope, and rabbit.
One should eat roasted flour cakes and drink sweet syrups;
or, ghee drunk by itself is an excellent remedy for intoxication (madātyaya).
The wise have described as "hemorrhoids" (arśas) the sprouts that arise from the folds of the rectum and anus, caused by the retention of feces.
An ointment prepared with Śṛṅgī, Harītakī, Kuṣṭha, and Bhallātaka fruits,
combined with Tuttha, destroys hemorrhoids.
An ointment should be applied using the roots of śigru, the seeds of nimba, the leaves of aśvattha,
bilva, the root of pīlu, and asafoetida (rāmaṭha).
Those who know the truth have declared that powdered *pathyā* mixed with salt and stirred with buttermilk, when drunk, cures hemorrhoids; likewise, they prescribe *guḍapathyā*.
From excessive drinking of water, the disease of diarrhea (atisāra) arises intensely;
it is said to be of three types: undigested (āma), digested (pakva), and with blood (sarakta).
In that [condition], long pepper, ginger, and musta, as well as yughaṇavallabhā,
are employed as a powder, a bolus, or a decoction for the purpose of digestive processing (pācana).
In cases of chronic diarrhea (pakvātisāra), one should administer jambū leaves, dhātakī, cumin, mango seeds, and the bark of the mahāvṛkṣa;
likewise, [a decoction] boiled with bilva, aragvadha, gokaṇṭa, pañcāṅgula, and barley [should be given]. ||232||
Pathyā (harītakī) that has been steamed and mixed with honey is the remedy for chronic diarrhea.
Viṣā, kuṭaja seeds, mustā, vālaka, and bilvaka—
the decoction of these quickly destroys even severe bloody diarrhea.
In a man who does not eat wholesome food when bouts of diarrhea have arisen,
*grahaṇī* occurs, which repeatedly causes both constipation and diarrhea.
A decoction of ginger (śuṇṭhī), ativiṣā, and mustā, when drunk, destroys that [fever];
this same preparation, when combined with guḍūcī, is called Caturbhadra.
Dīpyaka and maṇimantha, well-ground with water and administered,
quickly destroy even the most difficult cases of grahaṇī.
Dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) is of three types, arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha.
That caused by vāta produces pain in the penis, the groin, and the bladder.
In the case of Pitta, it causes a painful discharge that is yellow, accompanied by a burning sensation, or hot and mixed with blood;
in the case of Kapha, it causes a discharge characterized by heaviness.
Uruvūka, balā, bilva, the two types of pañcamūla,
barley, punarnavā, the root of bhīru, kulattha, and likewise badara.
Matsyākṣa and matsyabheda—all these were prepared in equal proportions;
with their decoction, along with medicinal pastes (kalka), and combined with ghee and oil.
A trident [poison] is destroyed when drunk with a mixture of the fat of a boar and a bear,
along with the five salts.
Śatāvarī, gokṣuraka, kaseru, and vidārī;
and the five roots of kuśa, kāśa, kuśālī, and śara.
The decoction of that [plant], mixed with sugar, cooled, and combined with honey, destroys dysuria caused by pitta; indeed, all cooling treatments [are beneficial].
In cases of dysuria caused by kapha, one should administer small cardamom mixed with wine and the juice of emblic myrobalan,
and also induce emesis.
Food and drink that is sweet, cold, unctuous, sour, heavy,
and slimy cause prameha through the vitiation of kapha.
A decoction prepared from viśālā, triphalā, mustā, dārvī, and dāru,
when mixed with a paste of niśā, wards off urinary disorders (meha).
Triphalā, citraka, dārvī, and kaliṅga, mixed with honey and boiled in water,
destroy urinary disorders (meha) instantly when drunk.
Or one should drink the juice of the śrīphala fruit combined with honey,
or even the fresh juice of guḍūcī mixed with honey.
When blood is provoked by the consumption of food that is dry, stale, non-warm, parched, and burning,
it produces swelling and that indeed becomes an abscess (vidradhi).
One should cook castor oil with eranda, vidārī, vṛścika, and punarnavā; by applying an ointment made from these, one may conquer abscesses (vidradhi).
One should promote healing with niśā, dārvī, payasyā, and yaṣṭīmadhu mixed with milk;
for wounds arising from kapha, one should use the sprouts, bark, and fruits of the milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣa).
The physician should destroy the abscess with preparations consisting of decoctions, pastes, and so forth;
or he may thoroughly treat one who is excessively emaciated by diarrhea, fever, and vomiting.
One who is hungry employs cold water for the sake of food and drink;
and having eaten, he quickly performs actions that agitate the body.
In him, a gulma arises caused by the agitation of vāta;
[the remedy consists of] pungent-smelling viḍa salt, ginger, puṣkaramūla, and the three salts.
The powder of asafoetida and leadwort,
along with long pepper, cumin, bishop’s weed, coriander, and the five pungent spices (pañcakola), destroys abdominal tumors (gulma).
Having added a paste made from pomegranate, jujube, and radish to ghee mixed with curd, milk, and meat broth;
Taking three parts of water, one should cook it to destroy abdominal tumors (gulma),
which arise from the persistence of indigestion due to impure food and drink.
From the obstruction of feces, a disease arises in the abdomen from within the digestive fire;
[this is cured by] powdered Māgadhī (long pepper) processed twenty-one times with the milk of the *snuk* plant.
When drunk with warm water, it destroys abdominal diseases;
[the dose is] three palas of ginger and six fruits of the ten roots (daśamūla).
One āḍhaka of oil, one prastha of ghee, and combined with one droṇa of whey,
one should cook everything over a gentle fire until only the ghee and oil remain.
One should employ it in such a measure as to conquer all abdominal diseases without exception;
for when the powerful Vāyu quickly pervades the entire body with Pitta, [this remedy must be used].
Entering between the skin and the flesh, it would cause pallor of the skin.
Take one pala each of *citraka* and *śṛṅgavera*.
One should take half a pala of long pepper (pippalī) and two palas of coriander (dhānyaka);
one should also take a kuḍava of pomegranate (dāḍima) and grind them together with water.
One should cook twenty palas of ghee with one āḍhaka of water;
it is used for anemia, heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and disorders of Vāta.
This formulation is prescribed for diseases of the *balāsa* and spleen;
one afflicted by diarrhea should quickly consume salt and sour substances.
In him, a swelling arises that is difficult to cure and spreads throughout the entire body.
[The remedy consists of] viṣā, śuṇṭhī, devadāru, kṛmighna, indrayava, and uṣaṇa.
One should cause the patient suffering from swelling to drink this decoction for the alleviation of the swelling,
prepared with castor root, ativiṣā, rāsnā, devadāru, and mahauṣadha (ginger).
Guggulu should be administered together with all the [other] ingredients for all parts of the body, as it is for men;
for blood that has become excessively provoked by sharp, burning foods.
A spreading ulcer causes what is called *visarpa* (erysipelas);
[for its treatment], *mustā*, *ariṣṭa*, and *paṭola* should be ground with cold water.
On the following day, one should wash the erysipelas with that plaster;
[the paste consists of] fresh banyan shoots mixed with the inner core of plantain.
Mixed with lotus-root knots, these applied as a plaster destroy erysipelas;
[likewise, they counteract] the effects of incompatible food and drink, the disparagement of virtuous people, and the harm caused by killing.
Leprosy and vitiligo arise from cruel actions performed in previous lives;
one should consume the fruit of the *dhātrī* and the leaves of the *nimba* ground together.
One should apply a paste of *kāsamarda* root and *kuṣṭha* with the juice of *dantaśaṭha*;
likewise, *guḍūcī*, nimba leaves, *paṭola*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*.
Equal parts of triphalā, karañja, vāsā, and rāsnā—
ghee properly cooked with their decoction and paste [is thus prepared].
This, when drunk with the alkali of the rājavṛkṣa tree combined with the pūtikīṭa insect, destroys all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) before long.
This plaster quickly destroys vitiligo and restores the skin to an even color;
however, when used in excess, it causes Vāyu to deplete the bodily tissues (dhātus).
When provoked, it causes difficult diseases preceded by sharp pain;
however, these are cured by drinking the decoction of *kokilākṣaka* while subsisting on its leaves.
And for one who has bathed with that water, rheumatism (vātavyādhi) is destroyed.
[The ingredients are] ginger, rāsnā, citraka, devadāru, and sahācara.
One should drink the decoction of these mixed with oil to alleviate diseases caused by Vāta;
blood becomes aggravated by food that is pungent and excessively burning.
Impelled by the wind due to exposure to the sun, salt, sourness, travel, and the practice of physical exercise,
that [phlegm] moves through the nasal passages.
From all the pores of his skin, that disease of wind-blood (vāta-śoṇita) [was expelled] by means of the juice,
decoction, paste, or powder of Amṛtā.
Sugar-cane juice, grapes, fermented barley water (sauvīra), whey, wine, and the water of grain-husks quickly destroy even long-standing vātaśoṇita (gout).
When a disease characterized by an excess of blood arises and the blood spreads throughout the entire body, sprinkling with water mixed with sugar and honey is recommended.
Venesection should be performed following oleation and sudation,
after firmly compressing the limbs with various types of bandages.
One should pierce the vein with a straight incision using a small axe (kuṭhārī) with a grain-shaped head (vrīhivaktra),
located at the edge of the eye on the forehead, or on the nose, or on the surface of the tongue.
At the wrist, at the joint of the arm, and two finger-breadths above the ankle,
one should remove the local [fever] with horn-tips or with lotuses strung together.
One should incise glandular swellings with sharp instruments cooled by cold applications and extract them;
having incised a large calculus with instruments, one should remove it from the body.
Having inserted a finger into the middle of the rectum,
the wise physician should skillfully rotate the middle finger to bring the stone toward the vicinity of the bladder.
Having recognized it as swollen, one should cut it with a sharp instrument with lightness of hand;
one should then boil horse gram (kulattha), calcite (aśmabheda), and gokṣura in water.
A wise person should have that decoction drunk; by it, one may also remove urinary calculi.
In this same manner, [it should be used] for other diseases, wherever a particular humor (doṣa) is predominant.
A wise physician should administer medical treatment for that disorder.
Thus ends the section on medicine.
He states the synonyms for the medicinal herbs: *yavāsa* is *durālābhā*;
*kaṭukā* is *tiktā*;
*sārivā* is *sugandhī*.
Dhanvayavāsa, yaśasvin, durālabhā;
the small *pañcamūla* (consisting of the two types of *bṛhatī*, *śāliparṇī*, *pṛṣṭhiparṇī*, and *gokṣura*);
*kāyasthā*, *kākamācī*, *nākulī*, *lāṅgulikā*, and *vayasthā* (dhātrī).
Coraka is granthiparṇī; śilā is manaḥśilā; kālayā is dārvī; anantā is durālabhā; śyāmā is kṛṣṇā; trivṛt is the red trivṛt; auṣadha is śuṇṭhī;
and vaṭaśuṅga is an unopened leaf-bud.
Vṛkṣāmla is *tintiḍīka*; kola is *badara*; śṛṅgī is *karkaṭakaśṛṅgī*;
pītula is *gotru* in Karṇāṭa; eraṇḍa and urūvuka are both *pañcāṅgula*;
viṣā is *ativiṣā*; maṇimantham is *saindhava*; and bilva is *śrīparṇī*.
*Kāśmaryā* is *tarkārī*; *ṭakkalī* is *ṭuṇṭuka*, known as *ḍuḍulu* in Karṇāṭa;
this is the great *pañcamūla*. *Abhīrukā* is *śatāvarī*. *Vṛścika* is [known] as *velāḍaka* in Karṇāṭa.
*Saindhava*, *sauvarcala*, *viḍa*, *kāca*, and *samudra* [are the salts]. *Payasyā* is *dugdhī*.
Rāmaṭha is asafoetida; ūṣaṇa is black pepper; mahauṣadha is dry ginger; vāsā is āṭarūṣaka. Thus ends the glossary of medicinal herbs. ||300||
Those born from the paternal side, those born from the maternal side,
and those who are related by blood— these are proclaimed to be one's kinsmen.
One should speak sweetly to kinsmen, offer them appropriate seats,
and share with them gold, garments, and ornaments.
Wage-earners, servants, female slaves, male slaves, and laborers,
as well as those who assist with counsel or the sword, are proclaimed to be "servants" (bhṛtya).
One who desires the welfare of both worlds must properly protect these [dependents], as well as provide for their maintenance and nourishment, and practice giving and honoring them.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter on the nourishment of the poor, the helpless, the afflicted, kinsmen, and servants.
One who has fled from tigers, lions, elephants, thieves, or even enemies,
and comes for refuge out of fear, is called a "seeker of refuge" (śaraṇāgata).
One should protect one who has come for refuge, even at the cost of one's life or wealth;
such a person attains great fame and is honored by all people.
Rituals performed according to injunctions and the protection of a terrified being were weighed on a scale;
therein, the saving of life was found to be superior.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, on the Protection of Those Who Have Come for Refuge.
This instruction on the means for those born of royal lineage to attain sovereignty was perfectly composed by King Someśvara,
who is like Sarasvatī incarnate and whose fame is like the moon, for the delight of his subjects.
And for the increase and further growth of even the greatest floods of merit.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Causes and Means for Attaining Sovereignty," in the *Mānasollāsa*, the *Abhilaṣitārthacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Someśvaradeva, known as Bhūlokamalla, the ornament of the Cālukya dynasty and the crest-jewel of the lineage of the Great Emperor Śryāśraya.
The second chapter:
Twenty causes for the attainment of a kingdom have been described here;
now, with a view toward its stabilization, I shall state the reasons.
Truthfulness, courage, noble lineage, virtuous conduct, youth, and beauty; courtesy, consistency, service to elders, and gratitude.
Having a retinue that is not mean-spirited, intelligence, having the gods as allies,
being free from enemies among neighboring vassals, power, dexterity, and swiftness of action.
Valor, fortitude, forgiveness, magnanimity, purity, pleasant speech, diligence,
lack of despondency, and the constant practice of dharma.
Popularity with the people, good fortune, proficiency in the sciences, weapons, and missiles, discernment, firmness of mind, skill in the arts, and wealth.
Inflicting punishment proportionate to the offense, the desire for the welfare of all beings,
compassion, graciousness, and showing kindness toward one's dependents.
A king who is upright, a seer of reality, ever-energetic, skilled in policy, and observant of auspicious customs— one endowed with these qualities is a worthy suitor.
Truthfulness, heroism, forgiveness, generosity, and fifthly, the recognition of merit—
these five qualities are inevitable for rulers of the earth.
If a king would constantly maintain these qualities— prosperity, fame, righteousness, victory, happiness, and glory— then he shall succeed.
Thus end the qualities of a king.
One who eats [only] on the path should always practice this; from that, he becomes free from disease.
A king, being exempt from illnesses, becomes capable of performing his royal duties.
Endowed with wrinkles and grey hair, one becomes devoid of beauty;
even a king is held in contempt by women and his circle of servants.
Therefore, a king should diligently employ these formulations of elixirs;
by means of them, he shall possess firm limbs and be free from wrinkles and grey hair.
May the king live for a very long time, free from disease;
therefore, out of a desire for the welfare of kings, I shall describe the elixir (rasāyana).
The practice of rejuvenation (rasāyanakriyā) has been described by the ancient sages as twofold:
one involving entry into a sealed chamber (kuṭīpraveśana), and the other being endurance of wind and sun (vātātapasaha).
Those intent on protecting the world should avoid entering the harem;
instead, they should employ those who can endure wind and heat, who do not neglect royal duties, and who are capable of withstanding the elements.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, at twilight, having performed the worship of Bali and other rites, one should encircle a Śālmalī tree with a red thread.
"Oṃ hrāṃ, O Amṛtasyandinī, flow with nectar, svāhā!
Having consecrated a śālmalī tree seven times with this mantra,
the wise man should strike it many times with an axe.
Having taken its exudate at dawn when the sun has risen,
[he should mix it] separately with the fresh juices of dhātrī, śatāvarī, and guḍūcī.
One should perform the meditation upon each juice seven times;
having ground it in a mortar, one should make pills equal in size to jujube fruits.
One should place a single pill in the mouth every day;
when fourteen days have passed, new teeth and nails will appear.
From that, hair arises, possessing the luster of a bee's wings;
he appears with the form of a sixteen-year-old, endowed with strength and valor.
One shall live for a thousand years; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The five constituent parts are the root, bark, leaf, flower, and fruit.
Having gathered [the substance] from the silk-cotton tree (śālmali), one should have it made into a fine powder;
mixed with honey and clarified butter, in a quantity the size of a cat's paw.
Having risen early in the morning and eating wholesome food for one month,
by that practice one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair within a month.
By practicing this for two months, one becomes as beloved as a rutting elephant;
radiant and youthful in form, he lives for thousands of years.
Free from disease and endowed with vigor— of this there is no doubt—
one should gather the Hastikarṇī plant on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism.
One should dry it in the shade, then grind it together with its roots into a fine powder.
Having strained it through a cloth and mixed it with honey and clarified butter,
one should place it in a greased vessel and bury it within a heap of grain.
When twenty-one days have passed,
one should extract that medicine and consume it day by day, one pala at a time, without weariness.
As long as one hundred days pass, one should avoid sour things;
one should eat what is sweet and light, combined with mung bean soup.
A man sixteen years of age, intelligent and possessing the voice of a cuckoo,
can travel a hundred yojanas in a single day.
Endowed with the strength of nine elephants, one shall live for a thousand years;
this is the certain result of the application of *hastikarṇī*, as spoken by Bhava.
One should worship the fourfold Muṇḍī— white, red, yellow, and black—
on the fifth day of the bright fortnight or on the night of the full moon.
One should collect the five parts under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Puṣya, or Revatī, and dry them thoroughly in the shade.
One should consume this powder, measuring the size of a cat's paw, together with ghee and honey,
while subsisting on a diet of milk and ṣaṣṭika rice.
When twenty-one days have passed, a man becomes possessed of a divine body;
by practicing this for three months, a person attains invisibility.
By practicing for five months, one rejoices with the gods;
by practicing for six months, one becomes long-lived and a wanderer in the sky.
One should take the leaf, flower, and fruit of the white Brahmavṛkṣa tree;
having dried them, one should consume that powder with honey and clarified butter.
By practicing this for seven nights, a mortal becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair;
having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, he shall live for three hundred years.
Having dried the Amarī plant, together with its roots and sprouts, under the Puṣya constellation,
one who is diligent in purifying the body should reduce it to powder.
One should consume one karṣa of this together with clarified butter and honey,
combined with cow’s milk, and eat a meal of śāli rice;
by this, all fevers, diseases of the mouth, and hydrophobia are destroyed.
The disease arising in the eyes and ears, as well as all piercing pains, are pacified.
Itching, scabies, burning sensation, leprosy, spiders, fistula-in-ano,
urinary disorder, abdominal enlargement, abdominal tumor, consumption, and epilepsy as well.
When the first week has passed, these ailments clearly perish;
when the second week arrives, the man becomes possessed of a divine body.
In the third [stage], he also sees treasures situated beneath the earth;
in the fourth, his hair becomes curled and blue.
Endowed with youthfulness, he shall live for three thousand years;
in the fifth [month], his body will fully bear the fragrance of the gandhanīraja lotus.
In the sixth [month], a man is born endowed with wisdom like that of Vācaspati;
in the seventh, he becomes radiant as the full moon, bringing delight to all.
In the eighth [week], he distributes nectar to all sentient beings;
and in the ninth week, he shall attain sovereignty over the seven continents.
In the tenth stage, a person knows the past, the present, and the future;
in the eleventh, he understands even those scriptures not previously heard.
When his twelfth year was reached, like a second god of love,
he brought under his sway the hearts of all men and women alike.
By using it for one year, he will live happily for three thousand years, his body freed from old age and grey hair; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has this elixir been proclaimed by King Someśvara, out of a desire for the welfare of kings, as that which prevents disease in men.
Thus concludes the section on elixirs. Thus concludes the chapter on the master. ||1||
They were of noble birth, endowed with sacred learning, pure, and full of devotion;
they were brave, steadfast, free from disease, and experts in the treatises on political ethics.
Ministers who are eloquent, wise, free from passion and hatred, and who do not seek to avenge past enmities, lead to prosperity.
Truthful in their resolve, high-souled, firm-minded, and free from blemish— such ministers,
esteemed by the people and skilled in their duties, lead to the prosperity of a king.
Ministers who are united in royal affairs, free from passion and hatred,
and skilled in income and expenditure, lead to the increase of the treasury.
For a king who persists on an improper path, ministers who act contrary to his inclinations yet seek his royal prosperity should admonish him with pleasing words.
A wise king should appoint seven or eight ministers who have come down through hereditary lineage, who are pure, and who have been tested by means of secret trials.
Born in their own country, possessed of true wisdom, skilled in reasoning and refutation,
knowing place and time, steadfast, and capable of distinguishing between what is achievable and what is unachievable.
Ministers who understand the gestures of others, who are wise, who conceal their own facial expressions,
and who are trustworthy guardians of counsel, should serve as the advisors of a king.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of a minister.
One who is proficient in the three Vedas, in the science of government, in rites for pacification and prosperity,
and in the Atharvaveda, should be the royal domestic priest.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristics of a domestic priest.
Sixty multiplied by sixteen, combined with the elapsed years beginning from Prabhava,
and further joined with the [lunar] days, are the years elapsed since the Śaka king.
When one thousand fifty-one years had elapsed [of the Śaka era],
while Somabhūpāla, the ornament of the Cālukyas, was ruling as Śaka.
While he who has crushed his enemies rules the earth,
he who is born from the pitcher— the ocean of the entire essence of the meaning of all the scriptures— [governs].
In the Saumya year, on a Friday at the beginning of the month of Caitra,
these fixed points (dhruvakas) shall be those obtained from the refined Siddhānta.
Edward [is] seven ghaṭikās and twenty padas;
Bhāni [is] twenty-six and forty-one nāḍikās.
Every month, one should cast [the following] upon the lunar day (tithi):
thirty-two hours (nāḍikās), two asterisms (nakṣatras), two quarters (padas), and eleven further hours.
Those [units] to be added and those to be subtracted should again be applied to the weekday, the nāḍīs, the piṇḍaka, and the lunar mansion;
by this much, the tithi is completed.
When the lunar day is combined with the weekday and divided by seven, the remainder shall be the weekday; such is the determination of the weekday.
One should divide the portion corresponding to the lunar day (tithi) by fourteen when applied to the position;
that which remains up to fourteen is to be known as wealth (dhana), while the remainder becomes debt (ṛṇa).
In the first [day] and the thirteenth, fifteen nāḍīs are prescribed; in the second and the twelfth, ten;
and in the third and the eleventh, fifteen nāḍīs are recorded.
In the fourth and tenth [houses], however, those [nāḍīs] would be nineteen;
in the fifth and ninth, twenty-two nāḍīs are declared.
In the sixth and eighth [periods], twenty-four ghaṭikās are declared;
in the seventh, the ghaṭikās should be known by the number twenty-five.
In Capricorn, one should cause the six and three ghaṭikās of the sun to enter;
in Cancer, it should be exactly the same, but one should cause them to depart.
In the pitcher (Kumbha), twelve [units] are to be known as the "sun-destroyers" (ravināṣikā) to be added;
so many ghaṭikās are to be exhaled by the wise in Leo (Siṃha).
In Pisces, eleven Rudras (eleven) and eleven Rudras (eleven) should be applied as the nāḍīs of the Sun;
exactly that many should be subtracted by the wise in Virgo.
In Aries, the Rudras (eleven), the directions (ten), and the channels (sixty) are to be added, being designated as wealth;
in Libra, those same values are to be subtracted, being designated as debt.
In Taurus, eight and six nāḍīs should be mixed by the wise;
however, those nāḍīs are declared to be excluded in Scorpio.
The best of astrologers should combine three and zero in the pair;
the wise one should likewise place that same [zero] in the sign called Kodaṇḍa (the Bow).
Having added these together, one should multiply the lunar day (tithi) by four;
then, take one-third of that lunar day as well as the ghaṭikās of the asterism (nakṣatra).
In this case, the solar nāḍīs known as "wealth" (dhanākhyā) are to be added; those that are negative, divided by eight, are to be subtracted.
Having added them together, one should divide by sixty and then add half a lunar mansion (ṛkṣa).
I shall explain the lunar mansion of the moon; one should join it with the lunar mansion of the sun. One should multiply the lunar day by six and add the nāḍīs of the lunar day.
That [remainder] is to be subtracted from the solar nadīs; from that, the lunar portion is obtained.
The yoga is found in the sum of the moon and sun; its nadīs are in the sum of their nadīs.
One should eliminate the external lunar day there;
then, one should subtract one ghaṭī from that, and divide the remainder of the day by seven.
The remaining portion is produced as the Karaṇa; enjoyment [of the Karaṇa] occurs prior to sunrise.
A Karaṇa consists of thirty Ghaṭikās; such is the determination of the five limbs [of the calendar].
Thus concludes the determination of the five limbs.
Having brought [the date] according to this method, including the lunar day (tithi) and the day of the week (vāra),
as well as the asterism (nakṣatra), the yoga, and the karaṇa, the best of astrologers [should proceed].
During consecrations, the binding of the turban, marriages, birth ceremonies and the like,
entering a new home, journeys, the commencement of a house, and in battle;
In the bright fortnight, the strength of the moon is primary; in the dark fortnight, the strength or weakness of the stars is primary.
A wise man certainly destroys five hundred defects.
Venus certainly destroys five thousand faults,
while the preceptor of the gods (Jupiter) dispels one hundred thousand faults.
Thus, he who can correctly describe the strength and weakness of the planets as well as the ascendant for sinful men should be appointed as an astrologer by kings.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of an astrologer and calculator.
Of noble birth, virtuous, steadfast, and proficient in the four languages;
skilled in riding elephants and horses, and expert in both weaponry and the treatises on statecraft.
He was a knower of omens, signs, and medical treatment;
he understood the different methods of training horses and discerned the distinction between what was essential and what was not.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of a commander-in-chief.
Those who are experts in the meaning of the Smṛti scriptures, free from passion and hatred,
devoid of greed and fear, should be appointed as judges over matters of dharma.
Having deliberated with those learned in the Smṛtis, the king should inflict the prescribed punishment;
he should appoint a twice-born man who is capable and knowledgeable in judicial inquiry as the wielder of the rod of punishment.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristics of the presiding officer of the court of justice.

He was a knower of the distinctions between iron, cloth, skins, and other such items as well as gems; he was skilled in their expenditure, possessed specialized knowledge of their particular qualities, and was expert and pure in their preservation.
One who is incorruptible, well-contented, trustworthy, with a large family, and diligent—
one who is skilled in calculation— should be appointed to the treasury.
The nine numerical digits, beginning with one and ending with nine, exist by their own nature;
these increase in the order of tens and so forth when augmented by the addition of a zero.
There is one drop at ten; there would be two drops at a hundred;
there would be three drops at a thousand; and at ten thousand, there are four of them.
There are five dots in a lakh, six dots in a million (prayuta),
seven dots in ten million (koṭi), and eight dots in a hundred million (arbuda).
There should be nine dots in a *padma*; there should be ten dots in a *kharva*;
eleven in a *nikharva*; and twelve in a *mahāmbuja*.
In the Śaṅkha [system], thirteen are declared; in the Samudra [system], they are the "manu-bindus"; in that designated as Antya, the bindus are said to be equal in number to the lunar days (tithis).
Twice eight bindus in the middle, and ten and seven in the highest place;
thus is the eighteen-place calculation for common practice.
If there is a single dot in the first position, that is proclaimed as ten;
if there is a dot before the second position, the number is considered to be twenty.
Thus, if there is a dot (bindu) preceding the third and subsequent digits,
then that number is proclaimed to range from thirty up to ninety.
Whatever number of dots (bindus) are situated before a numeral at the end of a hundred times a parārdha,
that numeral shall have that many zeros [at its end].
A few digits should be set down as the multiplicand;
beneath the first digit, one should write the multiplier.
One should multiply each [number] by all those situated above it;
one should place the quotient there and write it above its own digit.
The wise should apply the digits in reverse order by multiplying them starting from one;
however, the quotient situated in the tens place should be added to the preceding digit.
First, one should place several digits according to the sequence of the forms of the qualities (guṇas);
beneath them, the wise person should arrange the divisors in a perfectly even manner.
Having placed the lower mark upon the heart, one should infer the upper mark;
by that means through which the division is obtained, one should determine the portion.
By this sequential method, one should divide that which is to be divided;
one should place the quotient in one location and likewise the remainder in another.
Furthermore, having divided the remainder according to the respective shares, one should add that to what has been obtained; such is this method of division.
One should desire the measure and the result; thus the triad of heaps is described.
One should divide the object multiplied by the desired quantity by the measure.
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is declared to be substance (dravya), and the result (phala) is held to be wealth (draviṇa);
the wise maintain that desire arises from the differentiation of the classes of substances.
This calculation known as *trairāśika* (the rule of three) has been proclaimed by those skilled in mathematics;
herein also are the *pañcarāśika* (rule of five) and the *saptarāśika* (rule of seven).
In this method of the three proportions (trairāśika), the nine-proportion rule (navarāśika) should also be understood;
thus, the entirety of calculation has been explained in brief according to the six flavors (rasa).
I shall explain the distinct calculation that was indeed interrupted in the introductory section;
namely, the integer (rūpa), the fraction (aṃśa), and the denominator (cheda)—this is the practical arithmetic.
The form [of the divisor] above and below is its part; the portion below that is intended as the subtraction.
Two heaps must be made: the multiplicand and the multiplier itself.
The complete form is said to be the whole; that which remains when a part is extracted is the "part" (aṃśa), and the division of that part is proclaimed as the "fraction" (cheda).
The wise one should multiply the numerator by the numerator and the denominator by the denominator;
then the knower of the subject should divide the resulting numerator by the denominator derived from that multiplication.
Multiplication is declared to be distinct, and division is likewise described as distinct;
the dividend is established by means of the numerator, denominator, and divisor.
Likewise, another wise person should write down the divisor;
one should multiply the numerator by that divisor and add the result to the obtained quotient.
One should multiply the numerator by the denominator in the pair of quantities due to inversion;
then one should divide the dividend by the divisor—such is this method for fractional parts.
Thus ends the calculation.
He who knows with certainty, according to reality, such multipliers, divisors, and the method of the three proportions (trairāśika).
One who is free from greed, vigilant, and devoid of attachment and aversion,
who grasps the minds of all, is praised as a gatekeeper.
Thus ends the definition of the *pratīhāra*.
He was bold, wise, and skillful, proficient in all languages;
he understood the principles of peace and war, was knowledgeable in scripts, and could read and pronounce every syllable.
He was exceedingly skillful in the invocation, dismissal, and installation of the lords of the surrounding regions who were worthy of honor.
He who knows the true principles of the sixfold policy, who understands the distinctions of place and time,
and who knows income and expenditure, the world, and the resources produced by the country;

The king should appoint as his minister for peace and war one who is devoted to the protection of wealth, who knows how to distinguish between what ought and ought not to be done, and who is expert in state affairs.
Thus ends the definition of the minister for peace and war.
One who knows the scripts of all countries, is skilled and dexterous in writing,
learned, eloquent, and wise— that scribe should be appointed by the king.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of a scribe.
He was a knower of Ayurveda, an expert in omens such as signs and portents,
a master of the training of horses, and proficient in the characteristics of various terrains.
He is an expert in the strengths and weaknesses of chariots, pleasant of speech, and pleasing to behold;
he is learned, heroic, and a charioteer worthy of a king.
Thus ends the definition of a charioteer.
One who is incorruptible, pure, skillful, an examiner of prepared food,
and a connoisseur of cooks is appointed as the superintendent of the kitchen.
Those who have come down through the lineage, who are contented, beloved, and imitative;
those with trimmed hair and nails, self-controlled, invincible, and devoted to the king.
They were connoisseurs of various foods and drinks, experts in the preparation of meats,
skilled in the art of cooking vegetables, and wise in the making of cooked dishes.

The king should employ as cooks those who know the true nature of drinks and side dishes, who are experts in the preparation of sugar-based sweets, and who understand the various varieties of milk preparations.
Thus ends the definition of the cook.
And those who know the medical treatment for humans, elephants, horses, cattle, wild animals, and birds;
They had correctly reached the further shore of the eightfold medical science,
were skilled in the techniques of surgical procedures, and were experts in both mantra and tantra.
Physicians are skilled in eight fields: the body, the head, the hair, poison, foreign bodies, planetary afflictions, aphrodisiacs, and rejuvenation therapies.
However, the best of physicians truly understand the cause of a disease by its name,
and they know the remedy through both its form and its name.

Physicians who are thoroughly proficient in the five therapeutic procedures (pañcakarma) are highly recommended for emesis, purgation, nasal therapy (nasya), enema (basti), and even surgical operations.
Those physicians who correctly understand whatever is beneficial or harmful to the body, and what can be accomplished through medicinal treatments, are fit for a king.
They know in truth whether a disease is curable with difficulty, incurable, or easily curable,
taking into account the place, the time, the age, the stage of the disease, as well as the patient's constitution and suitability.

Physicians who are devoted to the welfare of their own selves and masters, who know the Dharma, and whose minds are firm, should be appointed by the king; they are not to be treated as mere subordinates.
Thus ends the definition of a physician.
One who is handsome, free from greed, attentive, and has conquered his senses;
who is skilled in interpreting gestures and facial expressions—such a person is desired as the superintendent of the inner apartments.
Men who resemble those whose desires are dormant, who are pure, resolute,
and of noble birth, should be appointed by the king as supervisors of the inner apartments.
They were knowers of the Dharma, pure, steadfast, devoted to their lord, and masters of their senses.
The king should appoint supervisors for his princes who have been thoroughly tested.
They were skilled and pure in all other duties as well,
being brave, intelligent, and proficient in the arts of weaponry, treatises, and crafts.
For the sake of security and well-being, for the restraint of the wicked,
and for his own diversion, the king should employ [officials] according to their merit.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the harem guards and the young attendants.
Thus ends the chapter on ministers. ||2||
A country prospers through the qualities of its land; the prosperity of a country leads to the prosperity of the king.
Therefore, for his own welfare, a monarch should settle in a land endowed with such qualities.
It should be served as a land abundant in all crops, containing mines of wealth,
favorable for cattle, rich in water, and inhabited by meritorious people.
A land endowed with forests of elephants, possessing many beautiful gardens, and sustained by rivers,
is always praised for those who rule the earth.
A king who protects a kingdom endowed with such a stage and illuminated by great cities shall cause it to prosper for the sake of increasing his own treasury.
In his own kingdom, the king should protect his subjects like his own legitimate sons,
[guarding them] from thieves, from his ministers, and likewise from those in positions of financial authority.
The king should protect his subjects who are oppressed by thieves, violent men, flatterers, those of wicked conduct, and others— especially by scribes (kāyasthas).
That king who, out of delusion, oppresses his own kingdom through neglect shall quickly fall from his sovereignty, along with his life and his kinsmen.
Just as the life-force of living beings is diminished by the oppression of the body,
so too the life-force of kings is diminished by the oppression of the realm.
One should appoint a lord over one village, and likewise a lord over ten villages;
one should appoint a lord over twenty villages, and lords over a hundred and a thousand villages.
If one is unable to restrain a fault that has arisen in a village, one should report it to the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten should report it to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all that to the lord of a hundred;
the master of a hundred villages should tell everything to the master of a thousand.
But once those faults have arisen and been quickly reported from the village,
all those stationed there, having learned of them, shall provide a remedy for them.
Thus concludes the investigation into the Rāṣṭrapāla Sūtra.
Kings may take as a tax one-fiftieth part of cattle and gold,
or even one-eighth, one-twelfth, or one-sixth of grain.
The king should collect taxes from the subjects in proportion to their fields;
