furthermore, he should take a sixth part of honey and clarified butter as commercial goods.
Of juices, fragrances, and medicinal herbs; of roots, flowers, and fruits; of grasses, vegetables, and leaves; and even of ritual acts and hides.
Even when facing distress, a king shall not collect a tax from a Śrotriya for earthenware vessels or for those made of stone.
Thus concludes the investigation into the imposition of taxes.
The king should designate uncultivated land for the grazing of cattle,
and he should bestow well-established divine gardens upon the sages.
He should protect a forest situated on the outskirts of the city, rich in herds of deer and devoid of cruel creatures, for the purpose of his own recreation.
The king shall assign forests situated in border regions and endowed with mountain caves for the purpose of providing household goods for all.
The king should take a tenth part from those men who subsist there upon fruits, roots, grass, wood,
and vegetables growing in that place.
The excellent elephant-forest of Dvipijana, where elephants currently dwell,
must be protected by the king from those people who roam the wilderness.
Thus ends the protection of the country and its people.
The region situated between the Gaṅgā, the ocean, the Golden Mountain (Hemādri),
and Prayāga is declared to be the Eastern Forest (Pūrvavana), with the Red Sea (Lohitābdhi) to the west.
In Tripurī, Kosala, and other regions, there is the forest known as Vedikārūpaka;
Śrīkṣetra, Gauḍa, Vaṅga, and Āla are remembered as the forest of Māṅgireya.
The forest named Kāliṅgaka, situated between the Vindhya and Citrakūṭa mountains and extending through Kaliṅga and Draviḍa as far as the ocean, is thus celebrated.
On Śrīśaila, Vedaśaila, and likewise on Malaya mountain,
there is a forest named Dāśārṇaka, which is the source of birth for elephants.
The forest of Aparānta is known to extend from the Sahya mountains to Bhṛgukaccha;
and the forest of Saurāṣṭra is said to lie between Dvāravatī and Avantī.
From Kālañjara and Kurukṣetra to the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean,
the region bounded by the Himalayas is declared to be the Pañcanada forest.
The Kalinga region is like a sacrificial altar, while the Dasharna country is an excellent forest;
likewise, the Angireya and Prachya regions are considered the middle forest.
Aparānta, Pāñcanada, and Saurāṣṭra are the inferior forests;
thus they speak of eight forests as the birthplaces of elephants.
Thus ends the description of the divisions of the elephant forest.
The king should cause those wicked elephants that kill others to be slain;
when the elephants have died by chance, he should collect their tusks.
One should recognize a herd of wild elephants by forest-dwellers whose limbs are smeared with the urine and dung of elephants and who are covered with the leaves of the *aruṣkara* tree.
One should recognize elephants by their footprints, their dung, the trees they have destroyed by trampling,
their resting places, and even by their trumpeting.
Equipped with defensive armor and provided with foot-rope nets,
he was surrounded by many attendants mounted on female elephants and horses.
Commanded by the lord of the earth, one who is skilled in discerning the marks of elephants should maintain, during the summer, well-trained elephants endowed with auspicious characteristics.
One should restrain elephants by means of the three types of bonds, such as the adhipa and others;
this should be carried out by men who are experts in the art of binding.
The binding by means of a cow, the binding by means of water, and the subsequent binding—
this threefold binding of elephants is considered the best.
The two bindings known as *āpāta* and *avapāta* are considered censurable, for by them elephants perish; therefore, one should avoid those two.
Having observed the place where it grazes, one should then scatter pleasant fodder,
such as sallakī stalks, plantain stems, and sugarcane joints, which are like nectar.
Purified lotus stalks, fresh sprouts of the Pippala tree,
a green bamboo leaf, and likewise other items dear to the elephant.
A herd of leopards, greedy for raw meat, would assemble there;
every day it was seen that the path was then blocked by them.
One should surround a piece of ground one krośa in length and equal in width with trees or even with iron enclosures on all sides.
One skilled in the construction of waterworks should provide a gate there, measuring the area required for the turning of elephants, for the purpose of their entry.
Having clearly observed the elephants that have entered there,
the wise man should block the water-gate with large trees placed across it.
One should bind the serpents residing within, endowed with all auspicious characteristics;
such a binding as this is called the "water-binding" (vāribandha).
Seven or eight female elephants, large-bodied and swift,
were mounted by elephant-drivers who were covered with leaf-shields and held nooses in their hands.
The wise man should cause nooses for binding elephants to be placed on the trunks of female elephants;
then, moving slowly below the wind, he should approach the vicinity of the elephants.
Having yoked the female elephants with the male elephants, one should bind the tuskers there;
this is declared to be the captivating "female-elephant" (vaśā) binding.
Thus ends the binding of the barren cow.

Having observed with effort that the herd of elephants was asleep, he was surrounded by many men bearing nooses in their hands and beards in their hands— those who subsist on the ill-gotten wealth of hunting.
The elephant-keeper should go along with some holding spears in their hands, others holding iron bars, and various musicians playing diverse instruments.
Accompanied by wise men mounted on horses, mules, and elephants,
he should proceed when appointed by the king for the purpose of capturing elephants.
At all the water-stations and among the nearby trees,
he should station many clever attendants holding musical instruments in their hands.
When the heat of summer has arrived, one should proceed slowly in the morning to the place where the herd is stationed, having fallen under the power of sleep.
Having silenced the noise of the people below the Sadāgati,
one should suddenly cause musical instruments to be played together with the blaring sound of the kāhala trumpet.
Rising up suddenly and with speed, the sleeping herd of elephants would become agitated in mind,
terrified, and intent on flight; then,
those experts in constructing waterworks should follow after them.
By which path the terrified herd had gone into the interior of the forest.
If one should depart from the herd with a mind terrified by fear,
the elephant-keepers, carrying nooses and brushes, shall pursue him.
Thirsty and exhausted, having approached the edge of a body of water,
one flees in another direction upon hearing the sound of musical instruments.
When the water and parched grain had been completely consumed by the elephant, he became utterly sluggish;
his trunk and tail grew limp, and his ear-fans became motionless.
Then, urged by their drivers, swift and obedient elephants,
having approached the exhausted elephant, surrounded it on all sides.
Then those heroic men, skilled wielders of nooses, concealing themselves within the bodies of submissive female elephants, bound that elephant by its hind limbs.
And with leather-made chains around his flanks and neck,
they bind the elephant to the trunk of a nearby tree.
The method of binding an elephant performed according to this procedure is to be known as the "Anugata" (following) bond by those skilled in the science of binding.
Thus ends the section on pervasive bondage.
A noose fashioned from the fibers produced by the inner bark of the coconut and *añjana* trees,
sixty cubits in length and equal in thickness to the forearm.
One should place half of it against its body and firmly fill it with earth;
the remaining half should be made like a noose to restrain the elephant's neck and legs.
One who is bound by that snare will suffer great torment;
yet, due to some lapse of care, the elephant might survive here or there.
This bond, known as the *āpāta*, is described by elephant-trainers;
it is always censured and considered as dangerous as a lion.
(216) A pit measuring four cubits in depth and two cubits in width [is prepared].
A wise person should make it long with a measurement of five cubits.
One should conceal it with effort using sticks, grass, and twigs;
for if an elephant were to fall upon it, an obstacle would surely arise even for him.
He is born lame in his feet, or his chest is shattered;
he is deprived of his teeth, or perhaps he barely survives at all.
This bond is called "the fall" (avapāta) and is therefore exceedingly censured;
since by it even the Nāgas perish, the wise man should avoid it in this way.
Thus ends the section on the downward-falling bond (avapātabandha).
Having captured elephants, the king should thoroughly examine their excellent characteristics, their lineage, their physical proportions, their temperament, and their breed.
A male elephant that is seven cubits in height, nine cubits in length,
and ten cubits in circumference is auspicious according to the measurement of his proportions.
An *arāla* is proclaimed by an excess of one *aratni*;
an *atyarāla* by an excess of two. These two, being excessive in measurement, are censurable.
A elephant that is deficient by one *aratni* in measurement is considered middling;
one deficient by two *aratnis*, however, is proclaimed to be the smallest.
He who is inferior even to the youngest is called a dwarf (vāmana);
he who is inferior even to a dwarf is a hunchback (kubja)—both of these are contemptible like elephants and sheep.
His two canine teeth are very glossy and rounded, his right eye is prominent,
his palate is unscarred and copper-colored, and his eight nails are auspicious.
A penis that is not pale is praised, as is a tail joined with hair;
the ears should be large and without holes, and the eyes honey-brown.
His voice was amplified, deep as a thundercloud, and his excellent lotus-like palms were red;
his fingers were rounded and long, and the complexion of his body was fair-dark.
This auspicious mark of a hundred thousand elephants brings victory;
therefore, kings should accept only those elephants endowed with such characteristics.
Thus ends the section on the auspicious characteristics of elephants.
Therefore, whatever else is different from that— whatever is deformed or distorted,
and whatever form is deficient or excessive— all that they know to be inauspicious.
Elephants endowed with inferior characteristics should be abandoned by the king;
they bring about famine, grief, and fear, and cause agitation to the eyes.
That which imitates the gait, movement, and voice of a particular being should be known as *anūka* by those skilled in the behavior of elephants.
Indeed, the conduct of virtuous beings is known as auspicious and excellent;
likewise, they know the conduct of the censurable to be censurable.
His drops are clearly visible, his complexion is fair and captivating,
the corners of his eyes are red, and his teeth are smooth and strong.
An elephant thus endowed with these characteristics is considered a portion of Brahmā;
it is worthy of worship by kings and increases their victory and health.
He whose armpits and neck are symmetrical and broad-shouldered,
whose face has the luster of a red lotus, and who is adorned with two rows of hair;
This hero, who has long been intoxicated with pride, rejoices at the roar of the clouds;
for this Naga is a portion of Prajapati and is indeed the increaser of progeny.
On whose body moles or wrinkles are seen, resembling svastikas, vardhamānas, lotuses, and nandyāvartas; |||
He whose eyes resemble red lotuses is an Indra-like elephant;
he shall grant victory in battle and the wealth of rival kings.
His lips are copper-colored, and his tongue has the luster of the dhātrī fruit;
his eyes and teeth resemble water infused with flowers.
Born from a portion of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), this best of elephants, who brings about an abundance of riches and jewels,
dwells in the palaces of kings, being held in high honor.
In color he resembles a dark cloud; his head is like solidified ghee;
he is beautiful upon his seat; and from his head issues a deep, thunderous roar.
Born from a portion of Varuṇa, this gem bestows abundant gifts;
it destroys enemies in battle and grants victory to its own master.
His neck was adorned with three folds, his eyes were tawny like honey, his teeth possessed the luster of ketaka flowers, and the tips of his lips were broad and red like young shoots.
Marked with a dot, pale in color, and originating from the moon-like Śaśāṅkāsaka,
this elephant bestows victory upon kings on the field of battle.
His body hair resembles flames of fire;
he is tawny-haired, with tawny eyes, a tawny palate, and is adorned by tawny ears.
Born from a portion of Agni, he is like fire itself in battle;
he always reduces the entire army of his enemies to ashes.
The shadow of his body is black, while his eyes and ears are fair;
his nails have the luster of the flame of a firefly, and his body is firm and fleshy.
Born from a portion of Agni and Maruta, he is irascible and swift;
his sole flaw is that he does not regard the goad as a restraint.
When the festival of battle has arisen, his very faults appear as virtues;
because of his ferocity, this elephant instills fear in the enemy armies.
Starting from the middle of the teeth, the hand gradually diminishes in size;
its fingers are well-proportioned and long, extending as far as the copper-colored palms.
The spray of his breath was fragrant, the succession of his sighs was long,
the sound of his bellowing was like that of a thundercloud, and his firm body was free from wrinkles.
Her body hair was soft, fine, and dark like collyrium, covering all her limbs;
and a luster like that of a lotus containing the essence of beauty clung to every part of her body.
The two teeth should be like the luster of a golden ketaka flower, round and firm;
the cymbal-bowl (vādakumbhaka) should be elongated, elevated in the middle, and depressed at the base.
His lips were hairless and his chin was firm, symmetrical, and auspicious;
the circle of his face was exceedingly beautiful and pleasing to the eye.
Her eyes were like the essence of flowers, with long lashes and reddish corners;

Twenty, or ten, or eight [lines] are proclaimed to be auspicious;
the chest is broad and firm, the belly is bound [in], and the breasts are slender.
A non-protruding penis is praised, and the hindquarters of a boar are excellent;
the backbone resembles a strung bow, and the tail is long and slender.
If a serpent is seen with drops or coils shaped like a conch, a discus, or a mace,
it has originated from a portion of Viṣṇu.
Worthy of consecration and worship, the bestower of jewels accomplishes all undertakings;
he purifies the kingdom and brings about an abundance of wealth and grain.
A noble elephant is one who always delights in pure food, is free from wrinkles and lines on the forehead,
is healthy, steadfast, brave, and possesses a divine nature.
An elephant born with the temperament of a Gandharva is praised for its intelligence, skill in action, passion, agility, and sharpness; it is excellent at standing still and watching.
Addicted to plunging into water, irascible,
and exceedingly cowardly, yet constantly greedy for food— such is the elephant born from the nature of a brahmin.
A well-trained elephant should possess the character of a Kṣatriya: it should be self-controlled, brave, ever-energetic, powerful, skilled in combat, fearless in battle, and steadfast.
An elephant that is controllable by force, base, foolish, a consumer of impurities,
devoted to combat, and brave, would possess the nature of a Śūdra.
A treacherous, cruel elephant, whose gait is crooked when moving and who does not eat excessively during rut, is considered to possess the nature of a serpent.
Indeed, these three qualities belong to one of a rajasic nature;

Lacking discernment, he constantly travels by the wrong path;
like one possessed, his conduct is that of an elephant born of a demonic nature.
At night, the swift and powerful elephant-like Rākṣasa, born of a demonic nature, roams at will, delighting in the slaughter of men.
These two are the tamasic qualities of sattva; the tamasic elephant is exceedingly windy, appears parched with wind, is drowsy, and is fickle.
He who is born with a pale-white color on his hair, body hair, tail,

Capable in battle, resembling a crane, wrathful, and skilled in combat—

Dark-complexioned, with a beautiful body, black hair, and a slender waist;

Pracaṇḍa, Kumudacchāya, Kapotanayana,

Resembling a white water-lily, with a stout body and smooth, reddish eyes,
his broad black trunk-tip was like that of an elephant of the *kumuda* lineage.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the different breeds of elephants.
Having thus examined with effort the elephants of superior characteristics,
the protector of the earth should accept them and reject those that are the opposite.

foot-hooks, and blows, whether for the purpose of sparing them or killing them.
On an auspicious day and in an auspicious field, having positioned the elephant facing the northern direction in the morning,

The king should properly worship the elephant for four days with curds, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, flowers, sandalwood, saffron, and other such offerings.
Then that elephant, born of a noble breed, would remember his former birth,
rejecting the happiness found in the wilderness while longing for the life of his home.
On the final day, one should further bind the nāgas with fetters made of leather,
making them firm and tight as is appropriate.

Three [spokes] should be placed at the front, two men at the region of the ears, and likewise two at the rear; thus, in sequence, there are seven spokes. On both sides, two highly trained female elephants should be stationed.
Then, that elephant was restrained by all of them using their arms as goads.
Then, the elephant keeper should daily train the elephant in speech for the sake of performing tasks,
through diligence and persistence, without laziness.

One should cause the removal from both sides and apply it;

however, when it strikes against a pillar or similar object, the instructors should say "hijja-hijje."
When the limbs are being lifted, "Bhale! Bhale! is what should be uttered by the drivers;
when they are being bent back, what should be said by the wise? "Kiḥ! Kiḥ! [is the answer].
For the purpose of requesting [alms], the Mahāmātra should utter these words:

In the act of swallowing morsels, the word "curu" (swallow) should be uttered twice for each morsel until it is swallowed;
in the act of spitting out, the word "cudu" should be employed.
Those skilled in the training of elephants should not say "mā mā" (do not, do not) as a prohibition;
rather, when it strikes its tusks against the ground, they should say "higa higa."
When [the elephant] strikes with its trunk from the outside, one should awaken it with the word "hū hū.
When moving slowly, the elephant should be addressed with the sound "ghe ghe.
One should train the elephant in this manner as the first language.
Once an elephant has become proficient in speech, one should subsequently employ it in its work.
Standing before him, one should slowly draw back the trunk;
out of fear of that, the elephant remains with its trunk withdrawn.
Seizing the two sides of his face and pricking him with their tusks, the two elephants raise his head; out of fear of them, the serpent remains still.
Then, standing near Karṇa,
the elephant, out of fear of the goad being applied to the root of his ear, stood with its ears drawn back.
If an elephant, terrified by the fear of being struck with a goad, should retreat backward,
two attendants standing at its sides apply the prodding with their goads.
Then, having mastered the postures, the elephant attains grace;
thereafter, one should train the restrained elephant in all its tasks.
Then a skillful servant, holding a leather bag in his two hands,
entered before the elephant while it was standing in its place.
Having first beaten the pair of bellows together, he should display a single bellows;
with cries of "hūhū," the driver should urge the elephant toward the striking of the bellows.
The elephant, having extended its trunk coiled like a basket and holding a leather bag,
should strike with its outer hand when urged by the rider.
Raising his hand, the driver should cause the lord of elephants to strike firmly with his trunk against the interior of the bellows, using well-trained commands.
Then, on both sides,
two workmen with bellows in their hands drew the serpent toward themselves.
There, the elephant should strike one bellows with its outer trunk,
or likewise strike another repeatedly with its inner trunk.
In this sequence, three,
four, or five skillful men stand with bellows in their hands, displaying their own bellows.
Mounted upon them, he should strike one with his inner hand and the other with his outer hand, using those bellows in their proper sequence.
Then the elephant among men becomes skilled in striking;
thereafter, he strikes the limbs of men, camels, elephants, and horses.
Then, the elephant should be trained by experts in the art of training who are skilled in its handling,
using his preferred fodder, molasses, rice, or even sugarcane stalks.
Having displayed himself and enticed the elephant by stretching out his trunk,
he should coil his own body around him and manifest a desire for fodder.
Firmly encircled by the trunk, it should take the morsel held in the hand;
then, having struck the elephant's trunk and pulled it away for itself, it departs.
When holding [the breath], one should hold it without hesitation even without the eyes;
and the internal fire, being held with effort, should be deceived by means of rotations.
Then, restrained by the hook and tormented by the goad, he was firmly held by a servant while being repeatedly addressed with the cry, "Hika! Hika!"
Pressing his face against the ground and repeatedly contracting his trunk,
the elephant of the ritualist should encircle its limb with its hand.
Thereafter, having fashioned a protective armor, he should cast a likeness— a formless image—
into the trunk of that elephant seeking his death.
Then, by the striking of his trunk, by the piercing with the tips of his tusks,
by the crushing with his two hind legs, and by grinding, [he destroyed them].
Trained in the art of slaughter, he grinds them to powder;
then, like Death himself well-trained, he slays living beings.
A square, fashioned for ritual action, slightly filled with sand,
and fixed upon the tip of a staff— this is what is called *lākṣā*.
One should show the target at the tip of the staff and cause it to tremble with a sound;
then the elephant, urged by the driver, strikes it down with its tusks.
One trained in the art of striking with the tusks should strike the lac using various blows— whether high, low, heavy, or delivered from the side.
Having first released the binding and returned to his former position,
he should then cause the elephant to move along the path, nudging it with both thumbs.
Having displayed the *kavala* (the "mouthful" maneuver), one should cause the pursuing [opponent] to run after;
then, from the flanks with circular movements, one should subsequently lead him through *maṇḍalas*.
Thus thoroughly trained in the deeds of both slaying and non-slaying,
he, though alone, conquers many men, horses, and elephants in battle.
Elephants of the Bhadra breed, endowed with auspicious marks and trained in all tasks, should be employed for service by the king in times of need.
Thus concludes the exposition on the training of elephants.
The king should protect the mines of silver, gold, and gems;
he should collect taxes on all things produced from them.
A king should recognize treasure hidden in the earth by various signs;
I shall now describe those signs for the purpose of identifying such treasures.
In that spot where a lizard, a scorpion, or a snake dwells continuously during the rainy season and the cold season, there shall be a treasure in the earth.
Wherever on the surface of the earth the mating of wagtails is seen,
there surely a treasure lies, even if the fire should burn without fuel.
Wherever a whirlpool is seen in a body of water without an apparent cause,
or where lotuses with two heads appear in that water, there a treasure-trove shall be found.
Where sprouting is seen on a tree that does not normally sprout,
or where a thorny plantain tree grows upon the ground, there a treasure-trove shall be found.
Where a palm tree is seen joined with two crests,
or where flower upon flower appears upon the ground, there a treasure shall be found.
Where steam rises to a height of two cubits without any apparent cause,
or where there is a common worldly tradition [of its existence], there the king should dig for treasure.
In all the treatises on mining, it is defined by its characteristics;
therein, too, the treasure is identified by those who know it through the methods prescribed in the sciences.

When a substance has been indicated by its characteristics, the wick is said to be mentioned for the purpose of determining its location and for the cessation of doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist.
One should prepare collyrium using a wick made from these: owl fat, *aṅkola* oil, and lotus fibers.
A man who, being purified, applies collyrium to his eyes with that [substance] will certainly see a treasure situated on the ground as if it were in the palm of his hand.
When collyrium is produced from even cotton-wool soaked in sesame oil, wrapped in lotus fiber,
and processed seven times with the fat of a boar,
ignited by the clarified butter of a tawny cow;
With eyes smeared with that soot, one shall see the treasure situated upon the earth.
Having taken the heart and the tongue of a black crow, one should grind them together;
having anointed the eyes with this along with honey, one shall then behold the treasure.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should light a wick made from lotus fibers and smeared with owl fat for the purpose of producing collyrium.
With his pair of eyes thus anointed, he should look with the gaze of a vulture;
at night, he will clearly behold a treasure situated beneath the surface of the earth.
One should prepare a wick from realgar, sulphur, orpiment, and the dung of a hare,
together with lotus fibers and cotton from the sun-plant (Arka).
A wick ignited with tawny cow's ghee, when brought near a treasure,
will leap up if the object is clearly manifest and fall upon that great treasure.
One should wrap the crest of the peacock with threads made from the fibers of the arka, śālmali, and kārpāsa cotton,
as well as with strips of cloth and lotus fibers.
That great blue blazing flame, when displayed at the location of a treasure,
instantly becomes three-tongued or falls down upon the spot where the treasure lies.
Having thus ascertained the location of the treasure, one should worship the deities of the three heavens with flowers, incense, unbroken grains, fruits,
and offerings as is appropriate.
A wise person should worship Śrīdhara together with Śrī, Maheśvara with Umā,
and Brahmā accompanied by Sarasvatī.
One should worship Gaṇeśa together with his attendants (gaṇas), as well as the presiding deity of that place,
and Kṣetrapāla accompanied by bhūtas and vetālas.
One should especially worship Dhaneśa, accompanied by his retinue of hosts of Yakṣas, and Varuṇa at a place situated near water.
By three, or five, or seven, or nine,
or even by more uneven numbers of practitioners intent on digging.
Having fasted, become pure, and being capable and free from fear,
one should proceed according to the science of mining while protecting one's own limbs from injury.
The king should extract the treasure-trove in the presence of his own superintendent;
in this way, all treasures are successfully recovered, without a doubt.
The King was ordained by Brahmā as the lord of riches,
especially those found upon the earth, since he is the sovereign of the gods.
Thus ends the section on treasures.
The origin of pearls occurs in various places within the ocean;
one should protect those locations and extract wealth from them.
It has a core of various jewels, it is the abode for the multitudes of diverse beings,
and it shines with the play of waves resembling autumn clouds.
By the nectar-essences that rendered the hosts of gods immortal,
and by the waters from the crests of the submarine fire that concealed the jewels on the hoods of serpents;
The body of the Lord of Indirā, who is the abode of trustful sleep, is embraced by lofty waves resembling sapphires.
It stood upon the horizons of the great mountain ranges, terrified by the fear of the falling thunderbolt,
spreading far and wide with foam mingled with the brilliance of a mass of jewels.
By bestowing the art of producing nectar, he rendered Śiva’s purpose fulfilled;
and by bearing waters that reached as far as the very base of Pātāla.
With the luster of the submarine fire, they were mistaken for fresh coral creepers;
and with their conch shells, they spread the illusion of the ashes of the Vaḍavā fire.
With the shimmering herds of water-elephants, brilliant with fragments of foam,
it appeared like Mount Maināka, its silver peaks agitated by them.
Because of its infinity and vastness, it bears a resemblance to the sky;
yet, with its wildly surging, lofty waves, it inspires terror.
They bore a direct likeness to King Someśvara himself, who provided protection for the mountains that had come seeking refuge out of fear of having their wings clipped.
Of Hari’s couch, which was born from Airāvata, the nectar, and Lakṣmī,
and which pervaded the sky and the quarters with its lofty undulations.
Having bestowed the Pārijāta tree, the nectar of immortality, Lakṣmī, Vāruṇī, and the cool-rayed moon— the very essence of the three worlds— he attained the reputation of being most generous.
In all the coastal cities situated near the ocean,
protection must be diligently provided by the king who desires prosperity.
The king shall take a tenth part from those who engage in the business of transporting goods by ship while stationed on their own shore, once the vessel has returned from that voyage.
The king may, at his own discretion, take possession of all the goods of ships driven by contrary winds, and the lord of the earth should give a small portion thereof.
Thus ends the chapter on the kingdom. ||3||
And by means of various alchemical applications, he should increase his wealth;
he should produce gold from copper and purify silver with tin.
Having dried the flower of the *puṣpapalāśa* when its leaves have withered, one should grind it into powder;
that powder should then be infused three times with goat’s milk.
One should smear this with a paste made from the powder of one-sixth part of tin;
when burnt by means of *puṭapāka*, it becomes beautiful silver.
One should visualize the flower of the white Brahma-tree with its own essence;
with that [essence], one should smear the tin thirty-two times while reciting the *tāla* mantra.
When that tin is burnt by means of *puṭapāka* (herbal-enclosure roasting), it attains the state of silver;
it certainly abandons its softness, blackness, and odor.
One should saturate sulphur seven times with the seed-oil of the white Brahmataru tree, and then [saturate] copper leaves with that [oil].
Copper placed within that crucible and heated becomes gold;
it then becomes fit for the application of processes such as heating, cutting, and rubbing.
One should grind cinnabar, sulfur, and mercury with that oil on a small stone until it reaches the state of a paste.
The wise man should smear the leaves of vaṅga with that paste on all sides;
having burned them again and again, he should apply it thirty-two times.
Then that vaṅga becomes gold, colored by means of darada and other substances;
it becomes pure, fit for commerce, and suitable for ritual application.
One should strain the resin of the Śākavṛkṣa tree through a fine cloth,
together with the powder of the root of Āsrigru and the resin itself.
Having repeatedly incinerated copper leaves all around and then applying [the medicinal paste],
this [base metal] becomes auspicious gold through five burnings.
One should take the ripe fruits of the śākavṛkṣa tree and process them;
with that juice, one should also [process] it together with mañjiṣṭhā.
One should smear the silver leaves with that paste and burn them by means of *puṭapāka* until they become gold.
Having pulverized the bark of the *śākī* plant and infused it with its own juice, one should mix it with the juice of the *karavīra*; with this, the leaf should be smeared.
Copper, when heated in a closed crucible (puṭapāka), becomes silver;
it becomes as bright as gold and is perfectly fit for use in commercial transactions.
By means of these and other methods for composing treatises on debate,
the lord of men should cause gold and silver to be produced for the increase of his wealth.
The treasury of the king must always be filled with gold, silver, gems, garments, and ornaments, and maintained in such a way that it can sustain expenditure.
Thus ends the alchemy of the elixir of the elements.
Gold that has been heated in fire while enclosed in a crucible and remains without depletion shall be known as sixteen-carat; indeed, that alone should be kept in the treasury.
Resembling the radiance of the rising sun and possessing a luster equal to the flash of lightning,
it is pure, worthy of ornaments, and fit for the gods and kings of the earth.
Whether it be fashioned in the form of a coin or as a solid mass,
or established as an ornament, one should keep pure gold in the treasury.
This work, which accomplishes virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and delights all people, is pure; contained within a golden casket, it bestows long life and prosperity.
One should never wear an impure [metal] alloyed with other elements;
it is incapable of serving the purpose of gold and brings about the destruction of domestic prosperity.
Silver mixed with naga and purified by fire,
resembling the orb of the moon, should be placed in the treasury by the ruler of the earth.
Silver that is kept in the home produces fame and good fortune and bestows excellent sons; however, when it is tarnished, it brings unhappiness.
One should keep in the treasury jewels that are pure and possessed of excellent qualities,
having examined their origin, their species, and their specific attributes.
In the Kṛta Yuga, he was born from a thunderbolt among the Kaliṅgas and the Kosalas;
in the Tretā Yuga, he was born from a thunderbolt on Mount Mataṅga in the Himalayas.
In Pauṇḍraka and Surāṣṭra there was the lineage of Dvāpara;
in Vairāgara and Sopāra, in the Kali age, the origin was Hīraka.
Five qualities have been fully described and five defects have been proclaimed;
these four types of luster are to be recognized by those expert in gems regarding diamonds.
Hexagonality, lightness, as well as having eight equal petals,
sharpness of the tips, and purity— these are remembered as the five qualities.
A stain, a dot, a line, a crack, and a crow’s foot—
these five defects are declared by the learned to exist in diamonds.
The fourfold complexion— white, red, yellow, and black—
belongs respectively to the Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra castes.
Whatever one attains through sacrifices, gifts, and austerities,
that one shall obtain by wearing a diamond of excellent quality belonging to the Brahmin class.
Victory, prowess, and the destruction of enemies arise for him;
for in his war-chamber dwells the virtuous thunderbolt of the kṣatriya caste.
Skill in the arts, wealth, wisdom, security,
and great fame belong to the virtuous one who possesses pure jewels by virtue of belonging to the Vaiśya caste.
Benefiting others, skillfulness, and abundance of wealth and grain belong to one endowed with virtue,
because he maintains the diamond-like nature of the Śūdra caste.
Impurity is declared for the east; from its retention, there is fear of fanged creatures.
In the southeast corner, the fear of disease is proclaimed; in the center, there shall be fear of fire.
The drop (bindu), the whirlpool (āvarta), the revolution (parivarta), and the barley-shaped (yavākṛti)—
thus are the four drops resting upon the vajra fully described.
In this context, the *vartula* is a red dot; the *āvarta* is a clockwise turning;
the *parivarta* is red as well; and the *apasavyaka* is indeed red and turns counter-clockwise.
The *bindu* destroys longevity and wealth; the *āvarta* indicates danger;
in the *parivarta* there will be disease; and in the *bhava*, the fruit is said to be [as follows].
And that [dust] is considered to be of three kinds: red, yellow, and white.
When barley is known to be red in color, it portends the destruction of elephants and horses.
If barley is drunk when the moon is in the dark fortnight (kula), it brings an end to the family; if it is white (the bright fortnight), it results in wealth and long life.
Thus have the defects and virtues of one who knows barley been described in their entirety.
A curved line on the right side brings auspiciousness; one curved on the left is terrifying.
A broken or wavering line causes distress, while a severed line portends fear of weapons.
That line which is visible on both sides and goes toward a break is proclaimed [as such];
when it rests upon a thunderbolt (vajra), it arises for the destruction of one's kinsmen.
A parrot-shaped mark resembling a crow's foot that appears on the surface of the pulse portends imminent death, or it may carry away one's entire wealth.
A diamond that is broken at the tip, broken in the middle, lacking facets, round,
or devoid of luster leads to misfortune and not to virtue.
Fear that causes the delusion of a fracture will clearly produce terror;
thus have the defects and qualities of diamonds been described by King Soma.
Thus are the defects and qualities of the vajra.
The production of pearls occurs on the heads of the kolāhi, kari, and matsya fish;
the production of pearls occurs within the interior of bamboo, oyster shells, and conch shells.
In the continuous streams [of waterfalls], pearls may be produced from drops of water;
that rare great jewel is carried away from the sky by the gods.
In the Kali age, pearls produced from elephants and other sources— which are difficult to obtain without ascetic penance—
can be obtained by men from pearl-oyster beds.
A pearl that is round like a hen’s egg, dense, heavy,
produced from a thick [oyster], resembling the sun, and superhuman, is fit for the gods.
Produced from a jar in Kamboja, resembling the dhātrī fruit in appearance,
with a coppery-yellow luster, the pearl possesses a soft radiance.
Those devoid of merit do not behold the hood of Vāsuki, which is circular, beautiful, blue-hued, and of great splendor, born from his lineage.
Born from the kola fruit and possessing a luster like its teeth,
that pearl— a jewel unattainable by men devoid of merit— is difficult for humans to obtain.
A pearl from a fish is light despite being as large as a guñjā fruit;
one that resembles the pāṭalī flower is of inferior quality, though it may be perfectly round.
Born from the bamboo, resembling the moon, and the size of a kaṅkolī fruit—
this is obtained through great merits and must be protected by means of Vedic mantras.
Resembling a rain-stone in its brilliance, born from the lineage of Pañcajanya,
the size of a pigeon’s egg, it is beautiful and the supreme remover of sins.
Auspicious pearls are produced from pearl-oysters in the midst of the ocean, in Siṃhala, Āravāṭaka, Pārasīka, and Barbara.
When the sun is situated in Svāti, the drops of water released by the clouds are swallowed by oyster shells and emerge as pearls of pure luster.
They are large, medium, and small according to the measurement of the *bindu*;
their value depends upon that measurement and their form.
The oyster shell is named Rukmiṇī;
the excellent pearl born within it is stainless, the color of saffron, and as beautiful as a nutmeg.
That has been declared by those who know the characteristics of jewels to be priceless;
it is difficult to obtain and fit for kings, and is not acquired by those of meager fortune.
The pearl produced in Siṃhala is very glossy and has a sweet luster;
that originating from Āravāṭa is very pure and has a yellowish hue.
Pearls originating from Persia are clear, white, and auspicious;
those originating from Barbara are slightly dark and rough.
There are four great defects and six middling ones have been proclaimed;
thus ten have been fully described, and I shall state their characteristics.
Where a fragment of mother-of-pearl is perceived adhering to one part [of the stone],
that defect is declared to be "adhering to mother-of-pearl" (śuktilagna), and it causes leprosy.
That pearl which resembles the eye of a fish is known as the "fish" defect; it certainly causes the destruction of one's sons.
The wise know that belly to be devoid of luster and lacking in radiance;
since it generates poverty, one should therefore avoid it.
Experts in coral recognize a pearl that has the luster of coral as being excessively red;
if such a one is worn, death ensues—of this there is no doubt.
Where rows of pearls stand one above the other, it is known by the name Trivṛtta; it brings about misfortune.
That which is turned back and bent is called the *carpaṭa*;
by wearing such a pearl, one shall possess eternal fame.
A triangle is said to be a three-cornered figure that causes the destruction of good fortune;
that which is elongated is declared to be thin and brings about the ruin of wisdom.
That pearl which is bent to one side and has a thin flank is said to be defective;
it is always inauspicious and brings about a lack of effort.
A pearl that is irregular, covered in spots, broken, disfigured,
unattractive, devoid of quality, and small in size is indeed of very low value.
That which resembles the luster of a star is called *sutāra*;
that pearl which is perfectly round and possesses excellent qualities is proclaimed as *guṇavat*.
A pearl is considered clear when it is free from defects and stainless;
that which possesses weight when weighed is considered a dense pearl.
A pearl that resembles the orb of the moon is said to be smooth;
that which is free from pitted lines and is uncracked is auspicious.
The life of one who wears such a pearl, endowed with all these qualities, increases; his prosperity flourishes, and all his sins are destroyed.
The luster of pearls is declared by experts in the examination of gems to be of four kinds: yellow, sweet-white, white, and blue.
Yellow [chāyā] should be known as bestowing prosperity; sweet [taste] increases the intellect;
white [chāyā] brings fame; and blue [chāyā] destroys good fortune.
Thus ends the examination of pearls.
Three *guñjās* are called a *māñjalī*, and three of those constitute a *rūpaka*. Ten *rūpakas* are said to be by name a *kalañja*.
Two bell-metal vessels, circular and identical in appearance and name,
each provided with four holes and secured by cords.
The staff shall be made of bell-metal, smooth, twelve finger-breadths in length,
symmetrical at both ends, and provided with a seal at its extremities.
In its center, one should fashion a thorn made of bell-metal;
it should be five finger-breadths long, and one should make a hole at its base.
Having inserted a probe one finger-breadth long into its opening,
one should fix two probes at its two ends in the shape of an archway.
In the middle of the top of the gateway, a small ring should be made;
there one should fasten a cord, and holding it, the wise man should weigh [the object].
One should place a substance weighing one *kalañja* in one part,
and on the other side, one should drop a drop of water for the purpose of weighing.
When the two ends of the beam are level and the center of the architrave is even,
then the expert should recognize that the weighing is indeed balanced.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the balance.
Four, three, two, or likewise one [grain] placed on the scale,
measured by the standard of a *kalañja*, is respectively the highest, very high, and so forth [in quality].
When the pearl is equal in size to a *kalañja* bean, ranging from nine down to five,
it is to be known by those who know gems as the highest quality in that sequence.
Starting from fourteen and proceeding in sequence down to ten,
the pearl is considered of medium quality because it is equal in size to a *kalañja* bean.
Beginning from twenty and decreasing in sequence down to fifteen, these are called "light" pearls; their value follows that same order.
Beyond this, pearls are said to be subtle;
this sequence applies both to their weighing and to the determination of their value.
For subtle things, the price is very small; for light things, the price is low;
for middling things, the price is middling; and for heavy things, there is a high value.
If even a single pearl should be of the measure of two *kalañjas*, it must not be worn by lords of men; it is unsurpassed and fit only for the gods.
The origin, the source, the appearance, the merits and defects, the auspicious and inauspicious,
the weighing, and the determination of value— these have been described by King Soma.
Thus concludes the determination of the weight and value of pearls.
His birth is celebrated in Sindh, on the Rāvaṇagaṅgā, and in Siṃhala;
the wise declare that there are four sacred fields for the Māṇikya jewel in those places.
Siṃhala is the first field; there, Kālapura is supreme.
Andhra is declared the third, and Tumbara is remembered as the fourth.
In Siṃhala, however, there is the unsurpassed red ruby (padmarāga);
that which originates from Kālapura is yellow and is known as kuruvinda.
They know the *saugandhika* to be [found] in the shade of the *aśoka* sprouts;
that which has the shade of the *tumburu* is proclaimed as being blue and having a blue fragrance.
The ruby originating from Siṃhala is the best, that from Tumbura is the lowest,
and that from the middle regions is to be known as mediocre, according to the distinction of their provenance.
The lords of sages have declared eight defects of the ruby;
four qualities have been proclaimed, and sixteen lusters have been celebrated.
Connected with two shadows, it has two shadows and destroys kinsmen;
having two forms and two feet, one suffers defeat because of that ruby.
That which is broken with fissures is said to bring about injury from weapons;
that which is gravelly and mixed with pebbles causes the destruction of one's cattle and kinsmen.
And that which is smeared with milk is called a "garlic-cloth" (laśunāpaṭa);
it is declared to be inauspicious by those expert in gems.
That which is described as being delicate and having a luster like a drop of honey destroys longevity, fortune, and victory; one should never wear such a gem, for it is defective.
A smoke-colored [fire] that resembles smoke is said to be dull and devoid of luster; it causes loss of wealth and brings about censure. A fire with the appearance of lightning portends fear.
Jewels possessed of such defects are contemptible and devoid of value;
even if obtained, they should not be worn in the home by one who desires beauty.
The four qualities of ruby have been proclaimed by the preeminent sages:
a glossy luster, heaviness, purity, and an intense redness.
If a ruby endowed with all auspicious characteristics is kept at home,
one shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, as well as wealth, long life, and victory.
The luster of a ruby would be like the radiance of a red lotus;
the fire of khadira wood would resemble the eyes of a cakora bird or the eyes of a cuckoo.
The eyes of a crane, the gaze of a cakora bird, and the sevenfold contact—
these are the qualities, the fruit, and the luster found in a great gem originating from Siṃhala.
Resembling vermilion and lodhra flowers, and similar to gunja berries and kimshuka blossoms—
these four types of shadows of the kuruvinda gem are thus proclaimed.
Because of its transparency, this shadow of the saugandhika gem resembles the luster of milk and is like water infused with saffron;
it appears as if slightly tinted.
Experts in gems have declared that there are two shadows of the nīlagandhimaṇi: one resembling the petal of a blue lotus, and the other possessing a luster like molten iron or fire.
Thus concludes the examination of rubies.
The origin of indranīla is known to be from the midst of Siṃhaladvīpa,
on the bank of the river Rāvaṇagaṅgā at a lotus pond.
A Brahmin has a white complexion; one of Kṣatriya birth is copper-colored;
one of Vaiśya birth is yellow; and a Śūdra has a dark luster.
I shall declare its six defects by name and by their characteristics;
I shall also describe its five qualities and its eightfold complexion.
That which has a layer like a cloud is known as *abhra* (mica);
by wearing it, one's prosperity and even one's life are destroyed.
That which is mixed with sugar should be known as "with sugar" (saśarkara);
when that is worn, poverty and exile from one's country arise.
Fear arises from the suspicion of division; through that, there may be danger from fanged beasts.
One should recognize that "divided, divided" is the destruction of wife and sons.
That stone in whose interior earth is perceived by experts in gems is called *mṛttikāgarbhaka*;
it causes skin diseases.
That stone whose interior is perceived by experts to contain blue [sapphire] is called *aśmagarbha* (emerald); one who wears it is overcome by misfortune.
Heaviness, glossiness and luster, beautiful color, darkening of the sides,
and the ability to catch blades of grass— these are proclaimed as the five qualities.
Resembling the juice of indigo, similar to the *vaiṇavī* flower,
like the *lavaṇī* flower, and possessing the luster of the blue lotus.
Resembling the flax flower and possessing a luster like the wings of a blue jay,
she bears a radiance equal to that of the black mountain and the karṇikāra flower.
It has the luster of a peacock's neck and is likewise like the throat of Śambhu;
it possesses a brilliance equal to that of Lord Viṣṇu and a radiance like the wings of a bumblebee.
Free from defects and endowed with all virtues, the great sapphire (indranīla) brings wealth,
longevity, strength, and fame to the one who holds it in his hand.
If one throws a blue stone into the midst of milk and the milk turns blue,
it should be known as an indranīla, beloved by the son of the Sun (Yama).
When an indranīla gem is worn, the Sun becomes perpetually propitious;
he bestows long life, great fortune, and health.
Thus ends the examination of indranīla gems.
In the land of the Turuṣkas, near the ocean on rugged terrain, there may be the marakata gem; its quality and defect are now described.
It has seven defects and its qualities are said to be fivefold;
indeed, the luster of the emerald gem is eightfold.
That which is ununctuous is said to be dry; if it is worn, disease will arise. There will be eruptions accompanied by pustules, and if it is worn, there will be injury from weapons.
If an emerald containing a stone fragment is worn, there will be the loss of kinsmen;
they say that one which is lusterless and dull brings about deafness.
A stone that is rough and covered with gravel, when worn, brings grief for a son;
a belly-shaped stone causes loss of luster and brings fear of fanged beasts and fire.
If it is of a variegated color, speckled with black, then there will be fear of death;
thus have the defects been fully described, and now the virtues are being set forth.
It is said to be stainless when it is clear; it is heavy when it possesses weightiness;
it is smooth when it is free from roughness; and it is dustless when it is devoid of particles.
A deep red color and an abundance of luster—these are remembered as the five qualities;
an emerald endowed with these removes all sins and fears.
Some resemble the feathers of a peacock, others are like the wings of a blue jay;
another has the appearance of green gold, and yet another resembles moss.
Resembling the back of a firefly, like the wing of a young parrot,
with the luster of fresh green grass, and comparable to a śirīṣa flower.
Thus, eight types of luster resting upon emeralds have been described;
an emerald endowed with these lusters is considered the most excellent.
They call that emerald of priceless value "all-purifying," which possesses the luster of a row of moss, is brilliantly colored, free from flaws, and removes all sins.
Thus ends the examination of emeralds.
In the Himalayas, in Siṃhala, in the Vindhya mountains, and likewise on the banks of the Tāpī,
the crystal gem is produced in various beautiful forms.
On the Himalaya mountain, there shall be one [stone] resembling the moon, transparent and endowed with luster;
and therein, one shall be sun-crystal (sūryakānta) and another likewise moon-crystal (candrakānta).
By the mere touch of the sun's rays, it vomits fire at that very moment;
therefore, it is called *sūryakānta* (sun-loved) by those who know gems, though it is a crystal (*sphaṭika*).
Upon contact with the rays of the full moon, it instantly distills nectar;
that is called *candrakānta*, and it is difficult to find in the Kali age.
Having the hue of an Ashoka sprout and a luster like that of a pomegranate seed,
it grows with dull brilliance in the region on the banks of the Tāpī in the Vindhya mountains.
In Siṃhala, at Kṛṣṇamākara and Nīlagandhika,
and in the place where rubies originate, various kinds of crystal are found.
Thus ends the examination of crystal.
Slightly yellow, with the luster of a lotus leaf, transparent and captivating in its brilliance—
this is known as the *puṣparāga* gem by those who examine jewels.
Thus concludes the examination of the ruby.
That which is white, resembling smoke, slightly black, or white,
and which resembles the eye of a cat, is called vaidūrya.
Thus ends the examination of lapis lazuli.
That gem which has a luster like a drop of honey or like cow's urine and so forth is called gomedaka by King Soma.
Thus ends the examination of the *gomedaka* gem.
In the middle of the ocean, at Setu, there grows a creeper known as coral;
it is intensely red, difficult to obtain, and possesses the nature of a jewel.
When this [substance] is boiled with effort, it attains the state of stone;
that gem, known as coral (pravāla), is rich in color but possesses dull luster.
Thus concludes the examination of coral.
Whatever defects have been proclaimed for rubies and sapphires,
a gemstone vitiated by those very same flaws should be rejected by kings, even if it be crystal.
Weight, translucence, luster, and hardness are the qualities born of jewels;
apart from the diamond (vajra), lightness in other gems would not be auspicious.
Scoundrels exert great effort to make jewels appear identical in form;
I shall now describe their examination, which distinguishes between genuine gems and those that are not.
If artificial [pearl] is pierced with a diamond, it will break;
artificial pearl is destroyed when washed with salt water.
A wise connoisseur of gems should purify rubies and other precious stones by means of rubbing and boiling, thereby distinguishing between the artificial and the pure.
One who abandons passion when provoked is said to possess artificial softness;
that which is seen upon being rubbed should be known as artificial by the wise.
Having reflected thus, the king should collect jewels in his treasury;
from the accumulation of jewels, he obtains long life, prosperity, victory, and fame.
Thus ends the examination of gems.
Ponds are filled drop by drop with water-drops;
for it is from the accumulation of particles of clay that an anthill grows.
Honey and royal wealth increase little by little;
therefore, a king should make a diligent effort to accumulate treasure in his treasury.
The king should set aside one-fourth of the wealth acquired from the kingdom;
he should employ three parts for the accomplishment of dharma, artha, and kāma.
One must certainly accumulate a treasury with even a single portion [of revenue];
for one who possesses a treasury attains happiness, while one devoid of a treasury perishes.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the Treasury.
A water-fortress, a mountain-fortress, a fortress constructed of stone,
one made of bricks, and a fortress consisting of earth— each of these is a type of fortress.
I shall describe the characteristics of the forest-fortress, the wind-fortress, the fortress constructed of wood, and the ninth, the human-fortress.
Then, there may be a lotus-pond surrounded by unfathomable water,
and a mountain peak that is difficult to climb and filled with water.
That which is declared by those expert in the science of policy to be a mountain-fortress (giridurga) is called a stone-fortress (aśmadurga) when it is constructed of stone and difficult to access.
Constructed properly with bricks, well-smeared with lime, and brilliantly radiant,
that great fortress made of bricks is known as Īṣṭikādurga and is surrounded by a moat.
That which is constructed from clay is a fortress made of earth;
that which is surrounded by dense thorny trees is known as a forest fortress (vanadurga).
Water accumulated within is difficult for those situated outside to obtain;
therefore, it is known as a "wind-fortress" (marud-durga), as it is similar to a desert region (maru-deśa).
A fort constructed with wood and bamboo is known as a wooden fort (dārumaya-durga);
one built by great warriors with weapons in hand is called a human fort (naradurga).
Among these, they say that a mountain fort and a water fort are the best;
those other than these are middling, while a wooden fort is the lowest.
Thus ends the description of the nine kinds of difficult terrain.
The king should cause various mechanical devices and diverse weapons to be made for the fort,
and he should also ensure that the gates of the fort are well-guarded.
And here, a store of all kinds of weapons is prescribed,
as well as an abundance of stones, both dry and wet.
A storehouse for spades, ropes, canes, baskets, and likewise for all kinds of artisanal implements is desired there.
There was also a collection of all kinds of medicinal herbs, as well as musical instruments,
abundant fodder, and fuel.
Of molasses, of all oils, of ghee, and likewise of honey,
as well as of all grains, and even of cattle and cow dung.
The king should keep venomous serpents in jars, tigers and lions in cages,
and collect all other necessary provisions within his fortress.
Thus ends the chapter on fortresses. 5.
The hereditary force, the hired force, the friendly force, the guild-based force, and the forest-dweller force;
the sixth is the enemy's force, and a seventh is not found.
An ancestral servant inherited through family lineage, a servant won by the granting of wealth, and a friend won by the cultivation of friendship— this triad of forces is the most excellent.
That strength which is connected with one's birth and actions, and determined by conventions, is called hereditary (śraiṇa); and that is considered to be middling.
That force consisting of Niṣādas and Mlecchas dwelling on the slopes of mountains is declared by the wise to be the lowest type of forest-dwelling army (āṭavika).
But when enemies have been completely overcome and reduced to the state of servants,
their strength should be understood by the wise as the strength born of foes.
That task must not be performed in his presence, nor should one ever place trust in him;
it should be carried out in battles by kings who are experts in warfare, positioned at the front.
Armor should always be made very firm, whether fashioned from iron or leather, crafted from cotton, or constructed from scales.
The army would be covered with arm-guards, helmet-guards, and body-armor,
and it would shine with banners, standards, and pillars.
For the protection of the army, circular armors should be constructed from cane, bamboo, wood,
and leather with firm bindings.
He should always cause variegated shields, some covered with tiger skins and others made of gold, to be fashioned for his own army.
But those who are the leaders among the principal forces,
one should honor them with jewels, ornaments, garments, and pleasing, heart-captivating words.
One should provide them with a full livelihood as is appropriate,
whether by means of a single village, two villages, several villages, or through accumulations of gold.
A king, being unwearied, should give wages to his servants at the proper time—
whether daily, monthly, every three months,
or even for a period of a year— according to the requirements of the work.
Every day, he should have inspections conducted by his own men who are free from greed;
every fortnight, he himself should personally inspect the soldiers maintained on wages.
The lord of men [honored] those heroes who had exerted themselves, who were ever full of zeal, who held weapons suited for battle,
who had conquered fatigue, and who were equipped with arms.
The lord of the earth should bestow favors upon his servants so that they become full of enthusiasm;
he should punish those who are lazy with weapons.
Thus ends the description of foot soldiers.
That supreme force was joined by many well-trained horses, including those from Sindh, born among the Yavanas, and originating from Kamboja.
Even enemies situated at a great distance are overcome by horses alone;
fame is attained through horses, and for him who possesses horses, the earth is secure.
Horses that have been properly broken in and nourished should be employed by the king;
those that have not been broken in are unfit for the path of battle.
One should nourish horses with dūrvā grass, barley, and chickpeas for food;
and with unctuous substances such as ghee, and flavorful broths for their meals.
One should diligently exercise the horses every day during the morning hours;
for through the hardships of cold and heat, diseases arise in horses.
Their medical treatment must be performed by those skilled in the science of veterinary medicine;
medicine should be administered without delay for the pacification of the disease.
Rising again and again, he enters [the bed] and even contracts his limbs;
distended and overwhelmed, he finds his head heavy to bear.
When one voids feces spontaneously and with sound due to the upward-moving wind (jaṭharānila),
this is proclaimed as the symptom of the disease known as Subhikṣavarta.
Having applied powdered ginger to the nine apertures, the horse should be made to move slowly; by that means, the vital air returns to its natural state.
Nevertheless, if he is not well,
one should then apply an oil massage for the horse using oil mixed with white mustard, salt, and the three pungents (vyoṣa).
The diligent physician should repeatedly foment the sides, the abdomen,
and the back with a heated stone wrapped in a moist blanket.
Nevertheless, if it should not subside,
one should then administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) consisting of a paste made from tamarind fruit mixed with sour gruel (kāñjika).
Combined with rock salt and *siddhārtha*, joined with the fruit of *kandarpa*,
mixed with the liquor of *śatapuṣpā* and blended with sesame oil.
One should employ a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa); by that, the Vāyu is pacified, and the person becomes healthy and vigorous, even if not [otherwise] through this [other] treatment.
Then, many drops of heated iron needles should be applied to both his sides, arranged in two rows.
At that moment, the horse becomes healthy, its belly becomes relaxed, and it attains mental tranquility; of this there is no doubt.
On another day, one should administer a drink that is digestive and stimulates the digestive fire:
cardamom, long pepper, ginger, neem, and the five salts.
A powder prepared from these— vacā, ativiṣā, and hiṅgu—
in the measure of half a pala, combined with half an āḍhaka of wine, [is used] along with that wine.
This sequence is proclaimed for the pacification of all types of colic;
one should administer ginger either combined with jaggery or alone.
Triphalā, pippalīmūla, tryūṣaṇa, the two types of jīraka, rāmaṭha, tintiḍīka, yavānī, the two types of jīraka,
rāmaṭha, tintiḍīka, yavānī, and gaurasarṣapa.
Ajamoda, aśvagandhā, paṭola,
amlavetasa, trivṛt, nimba, mustā, parpaṭa, and kaṭurohiṇī.
One should grind together in one place pomegranate, black salt, rock salt, biḍa salt, sea salt, and mountain salt.
One should administer one pala mixed with ghee in diseases caused by Vata;
in diseases arising from Pitta, it should be mixed with honey and sugar.
In diseases born of phlegm (kapha), one should administer it together with wine;
when given combined with fermented gruel (āranāla), it is a supreme remedy for colic and flatulence.
This [mixture], when combined with meat broth, increases the nourishment of horses;
or, when given with warm water, it is the supreme remedy for all diseases.
If phlegm becomes aggravated and flows from the nostrils of dogs, then that is the disease known as siṃhāṇaka; I shall now describe its treatment.
Oil produced from white mustard seeds,
mixed with goat's urine and the juice of *siṃhī* fruits, used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), removes catarrh (*siṃhāṇaka*).
Dry ginger, duralabhā, mustā, karcūra, the two types of bṛhatī,
bhārṅgī, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, vacā, and puṣkara-pippalī.
When indigestion of food-essence (rasājīrṇa) arises, all the limbs become numb;
I shall now describe the remedy for that horse which moves with difficulty due to distress.
For one suffering from the loss of bodily fluids (rasa), fasting should be administered until lightness is achieved;
one should smear all the limbs with lukewarm black clay.
Venesection should be performed when there is excessive heaviness of the limbs;
it should be done on the anterior part of the chest or on the posterior part in cases arising from *pāṇḍu* (anemia).
When there is excessive heaviness in the front or back part of the body,
all the veins located even in the region of the spine and the temples should be opened.
Diseases arise in elephants;
their treatment must be performed with medicines produced in the forest as well as those brought from the marketplace.
One should give ten palas of powder for each cubit-length of horned animals;
the paste should be double that amount, and one āḍhaka of decoction is prescribed.
For a solid substance, the root; for a liquid, water—both remaining in equal proportions;
at the time of awakening, [the urine]; and at the proper time, the urine of an elephant.
One should make the animal, afflicted by the pain of the nine-fold binding, drink water from its horns;
when half a watch and one *nālikā* of the day remain, one should release it from the water.
Then the wise man should tether the elephant and sprinkle all its limbs with clarified butter purified a hundred times, both at day and at night.
Thereafter, after two days have passed, one should sprinkle [the patient] with ghee alone;
however, if the naga is afflicted by cold, the expert should sprinkle it with oil alone.
One should gradually decrease the time spent immersed in water,
while consuming sugarcane, lotus stalks, lotus fibers, and sweet trees.
The roots of plantain, lotus-root, water-chestnut,
kaseruka, madhuka, akola, vāraṇa, and āragvadha;
One should give that which brings joy to the mind for the sake of pacifying distress;
now I shall describe the medical treatment for a serpent afflicted by disease.
First, I shall describe the Lord of Disease, who resides in both the stationary and the moving,
who is endowed with many names, and who manifests at the beginning and at the end of birth.
He is known as Jvara among humans, Pālaka among those born from mares,
Abhitāpa among horses, and Vāraka among donkeys.
Alasaka is said to be among camels, and likewise Īśvara among cows;
Akṣaka is among biting insects, and Hāridra is also among buffaloes.
There may be bleating among goats and sheep, disease among deer,
falling from heights among birds, and that which is called Indra-mada among fish.
Jyotis is declared for shrubs and for knots; Vanaspati for medicinal herbs;
Parvata for flowers; and Rūpaka for lotus ponds.
Among grains he is known as Cūrṇaka; among kodrava grains he is remembered as Lala;
among vegetables he is Madhuka; on the earth he is Ūṣara, and in the waters he is Nīlikā.
By these names, fever alone is proclaimed in the world;
apart from humans, others are unable to endure it.
Therefore, no medical treatment is prescribed for this protector;
having first pervaded the internal elements, it subsequently manifests externally.
Furthermore, that Pālaka is difficult to treat and takes the form of death;
therefore, treatment for him has not been described by many teachers.
Suvahā, surasā, dāru, mustā, kuṣṭha, rasonaka,
madhuśīrṣa, viḍaṅga, bhārṅgī, and the two types of siddhārthaka.
Radish, the five spices (pañcakola), the two types of karañja,
and the great five roots (mahā-pañcamūla) serve to pacify phlegm and wind.
Guḍūcī, the two types of Parṇikā, the two types of Medā,
Jīvaka, Ṛṣabha, Kākoli, Aśvagandhā, Vidārī, and Śatāvarī.
This formulation— whether as a powder, a paste, or a decoction— certainly destroys all diseases arising from wind and bile in those born of Soma.
Patola, patha, kustha, nimba, dhatri, amrita, visha, dhanyaka,
parpata, tikta, and vatsaka conquer kapha and pitta.
Asafoetida, black salt, dry ginger, and jaggery [are used] for the pacification of colic;
likewise, an ointment made with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) applied to the eyes, or even with dry ginger alone, [is beneficial].
Aśvagandhā, kaṇā, rātri, kṛmighna, and the five juices—
eight palas each of these, with one muṣṭi of variṣṭha.
This formulation, combined with the five salts, destroys wind disorders;
it also removes dysuria, flatulence, and colic.
Kuṭaja, śṛṅgavera, yavakṣāra, citraka,
the two types of pūti, siddhārtha, viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, and ghana.
Long pepper, long pepper root, turmeric, drumstick, costus, rock salt, vacā, and asafoetida— these, powdered and mixed with cow dung, [are used as an ointment].
This *yoga* is the supreme stimulant for the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) of elephants;
it quickly destroys *sāmavāta* and the ailments arising from *sāmavāta*.
[It consists of] rock salt (*saindhava*), cumin (*jīraka*), *dantī*, ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), and the three fruits (*phalatraya*).
Two types of karañja, black paṭola, and nimba sprouts.
A bolus made from the well-powdered mixture of jyotiṣmatī, guḍūcī,
and vāsā destroys the craving for clay and quickly stimulates the digestive fire.
Trivṛt, arka, snuhī, dantī, nīlī, the five salts,
and brāhmī are purgatives that destroy colic, worms, and flatulence.
Pāṭhā, paṭola, kuṣṭha, nimba, bhūnimba, parpaṭa,
jyotiṣmatī, snuhī, vāsaka, cavya, granthika, and śigru.
Vacā, kaṭphala, rodhra, citraka, the two types of bṛhatī fruit,
tiktā, durālabhā, rātri, karañja, and likewise triphalā.
This powder, consisting of the three pungents (trikaṭu), trāyamāṇā, pauṣkara, gajapippalī, and dhātakī,
when taken with honey, cures diseases of the throat.
Rock salt, ginger, kuṣṭha, vacā, drumstick tree, the two types of turmeric,
white mustard, and barley alkali— all these ground together into a powder.
Curd stirred with curdled milk and served lukewarm conquers swelling born of phlegm and wind;
one should also apply fomentation to the swelling, or perform scarification as appropriate.
When an abscess has suppurated and been incised,
a mixture of honey and rock salt (saindhava) should be diligently injected into the interior of the wound to pacify the pus.
In a case of fresh wound, the blood and bile become excessively aggravated;
therefore, for three days, that area should be filled with ghee and honey.
Sesame seeds, nimba leaves, and turmeric,
ground together and mixed with honey, constitute an excellent cleanser and healer for wounds.
The fruit of *kataka*, *rodhra*, *madhuka*, *candana*, *ghana*,
*prapauṇḍarīka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, as well as *vālaka* and *uśīraka*.
A wick, powder, or eye-drop prepared from these is recommended for all eye diseases arising from the vitiation of the humors.
One should subsequently add trivṛt,
triphalā, rocanā, lac, vermilion, rodhra, and guggulu to a decoction of milk-yielding trees.
Bhallātaka, turmeric, the fruit of ghoṇṭā, kāsīsa, rock salt,
sourāṣṭrika, añjana, and the resin derived from the sarja tree.
Having powdered śrīveṣṭa as well,
the physician, knowing the procedure, should then mix it into the decoction, stirring it gently with a ladle over a mild fire.
When it has become solidified like molasses and viscous like adamantine glue,
a wise man should prepare it for the purpose of binding the feet of elephants.
Thus ends the treatment of elephants.
*Parṇikā*, *mudgaparṇī*, and *māṣaparṇī*; *ugragandhā*, *vacā*, and *rasona*; the five juices (*rasapañcaka*); the two types of putrid plants; *kṛṣṇā* (black) *pippalī*;
*vāsā* (also known as *āṭarūṣaka*); and *granthika* (the root of *pippalī*).
Kaṭphala is the fruit of *kāśmarya*. Saurāṣṭrikā is ferruginous clay (*tuvara-mṛttikā*). Trivṛtta consists of the three unctuous substances (*tri-sneha*). Śrīveṣṭa is the resin of the *sarala* tree.
Thus ends the Gajauṣadhinighaṇṭu.
The strength of elephants is the primary force for kings desiring victory in battle;
therefore, kings should maintain many elephants within their own armies.
The king should perform the ceremonial honors for the sake of gifting the elephants;
[these vehicles] should be crowded with various weapons, resplendent with banners and standards,
yoked to four horses, sturdy, and urged on by charioteers.
Many chariots should be occupied by great car-warriors and kings in a fourfold army during battle by those desiring victory.
Some were bearing swords and shields, while others had spears in their hands;
some carried javelins and discs, and some held mallets in their hands.
Some were archers, some carried axes in their hands;
some bore spears and tridents, and others carried short swords.
Some had weapons already released from their machines, some likewise had weapons already released;
some held weapons in their hands that were not yet released, and others likewise had weapons released from their hands.
A king who understands these four powers, who has conquered fatigue,
and who is intent on destroying his enemies, should act with vigilance for the sake of battle.
Thus ends the chapter on strength.
One who is of noble birth, possessed of good character, esteemed in both happiness and sorrow,
free from deceit, firm of mind, and one who does not betray you even with his wealth or life.

A king should make one who knows policy, who is endowed with purity, and who does not turn away in times of calamity, his friend for the sake of dharma and wealth, and for the attainment of happiness.
Thus ends the chapter on friends.
Those who know the science of polity understand that a king is best when dependent on himself, middling when dependent on both himself and others, and inferior when dependent on his ministers.
This kingdom is under my control, and the king is subject to my will;
whatever task is performed by me, who can possibly thwart that task?
Where a minister, puffed up with self-conceit, speaks thus,
that kingdom is called "inferior" and is said to be dependent upon the minister.

When a minister speaks while equating himself with the two [the king and the people], saying, "Whatever task I have proposed, the Lord surely considers it necessary," he thus provides both pleasure and displeasure,
for the success of the undertaking depends on both.
A kingdom dependent on both [the conqueror and the enemy] is proclaimed as "intermediate" (madhyama).
"Without my lord's command, I am not capable of accomplishing this task"—
wherein a minister speaks thus to the king out of both fear and devotion.
But that kingdom which is free from fear, bestows happiness, grants all success, is excellent,
exceedingly stable, and is rightly said to be dependent upon oneself— [that is the true kingdom].
In favoring and in restraining, in giving and in the act of not taking,
in engagement and in withdrawal, and likewise in seizing and in releasing.
That king who is himself capable, whose own command is unimpeded,
and who is endowed with his own power— he is a lord, and he is called a true master.
That power which exists in the form of a command upon the heads of all should be known as the power of sovereignty; it is radiant and the source of greatness.
Thus ends the chapter on the power of the lord.
The means for accomplishing the task, assistants capable of performing it,
consideration of place and time, and the counteraction of obstacles.
"The accomplishment of the task and happiness"— this is held to be the five-limbed counsel,
according to the opinion of Guru and Śukra, as well as that of Cāṇakya and others.
A distinguished counsel is desired that is free from regret, brings about continuous and rising happiness, is agreeable, and is without delay.
A secret counsel is betrayed by many, but a counsel shared by two does not perish;
a counsel devised by oneself is not betrayed even by Brahmā.

The undertakings of one who always guards his speech and constantly conceals his gestures and facial expressions are to be known by their fruits, just as previously acquired merit is known by its results.
The deaf, the blind, the dull-witted, the mute, the diseased, the elderly, and children;
even beloved women, barbarians, and even animals such as parrots and the like.
At that time, O Lord of Men, the ruler of men should diligently preserve [the teaching] from being lost, whether it be within the range of hearing, within the range of sight, or through others.
Having ascended to a high place or a secluded palace,
or even in a lonely forest, one should perform the mantra-consultation unobserved.
At midday, having eaten and being free from fatigue, one should recite the mantra;
or during the latter part of the night, having risen comfortably and being free from sleep.
Dharma, wealth, and pleasure; what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; the weak and the strong; enemies and even friends; and the sequence of actions for protecting the country.
The means for subduing enemies, the exertion for acquiring wealth,
the maintenance of dependents, and the counteraction of obstacles.
The honoring of friends, the instruction of sons in statesmanship,
the protection of the women of the inner apartments, and the training of elephants and horses.
The wicked counsel of ministers, the conduct of evil-minded men,
the protection of princes, and the subduing of neighboring vassals.
The attachment and aversion of people, the virtues and vices of oneself,
the income and expenditure of wealth, and the replenishment of the treasury.
The subduing of the wicked, the protection of the virtuous,
the honoring of gods and brahmins, and the supervision of the social classes and stages of life.
The proper protection of fortresses, the activities of enemy kings,
the execution of thieves and others, and the sequential method for the protection of oneself.
He should also ascertain the condition of the constituent elements, the market prices of grains and other goods,
and perform rites for pacification and nourishment, both regularly and on specific occasions.
