The lord of the earth should show honor to those advanced in wisdom, deliberate upon the considerations of place and time, and reflect together with his ministers or by himself.
Having summoned all his ministers, he should consult with them individually;
having ascertained their opinions, he should deliberate upon their merits and defects.
Having deliberated with his ministers and having weighed the merits and defects of the counsel,
the lord of the earth should personally determine one course and carry out the task.
"What has been done? What remains to be done? What is currently being done by me?
What has been accomplished? And what is yet to be achieved?"—thus one should reflect again and again.
A king desiring his own welfare should, after due deliberation, undertake an action that yields great profit, is easily accomplished, is righteous, and increases his fame.
Where both acquisition and expenditure are equal, or where expenditure is greater,
and which cannot be accomplished by any means despite a hundred stratagems— that one should not deliberate upon.
One should not deliberate upon that which is unrighteous, disgraceful, and productive of remorse; that which is difficult to achieve, fraught with much suffering, and based on bad counsel.
One who is not deluded when tempted by desire, anger, fear, or other forms of greed—
endowed with which power one succeeds in action— that is known as the power of counsel (mantra-śakti).
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the Power of Mantras.
The king, augmented by his prowess, was intent on seizing the land, wealth, elephants, horses, jewels, and likewise the victory of his enemies.
If an undertaking that one has begun oneself does not succeed due to fate,
the energetic person does not desist from performing it, but tries again and again.
That king who always possesses a mind endowed with enthusiasm in his exertion—
his power of enthusiasm should be known as the source of prosperity for those kings who desire well-being.
Thus ends the chapter on the power of energy (utsāha-śakti).
A king skilled in statecraft should enter into a treaty with anyone who cannot be subdued by force, taking into account considerations of place, time, and other such factors.
One who is skilled in the science of policy should make peace even with one who has conquered a powerful enemy, or with one who is superior to him.
Being oppressed by one who is more powerful and unable to fight him,
one should nevertheless make peace, recognizing that as the supreme policy.
Alliance is said to be of four kinds: that based on friendship, that arising from kinship, that known as mutual assistance, and likewise that consisting of a gift.
Knowing "this person is a virtuous man," one who is himself a kinsman of good qualities forms an alliance out of disinterestedness;
that is called an alliance with a friend.
When a king, for the sake of accomplishing a specific purpose, effects an alliance through the giving of a daughter in marriage,
that alliance should be known by those who deliberate on treaties as one born of kinship.
When a king enters into an alliance for the purpose of mutual assistance,
that treaty is called "reciprocal benefit" by the wise.
When peace is made by giving elephants, horses, jewels, gold, and even land,
that is called "upahāra" (an offering).
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the Twilight Meditation.
A king should wage war with one who possesses great effort, allies, capability, and strength, even if that opponent is devoid of secret counsel.
That born of desire, that born of greed, that born of the earth, that born of the mind,
that known as fearlessness, that born of affection, and that arising from intoxication— these are fully described.
In the Arthaśāstra, the supreme [type] is known as one who desires a single object;
thus eight types of conflict have been declared, and a ninth is not found.
For the conflict that arises on account of women is known to be born of desire;
likewise, the conflict produced by the seizure of property is born of greed.
That great conflict arising from the earth which has arisen for the sake of land,
and that conflict born of pride which has been undertaken for the sake of a flower garland;
That great conflict which occurs for the sake of protecting those who have sought refuge is called by those learned in political science "the war of granting safety" (abhaya-vigraha).
A conflict that one should undertake for the sake of a friend, for the sake of kinsmen, or for the sake of dependents,
is designated as "born of affection" by those who perceive the clear meaning of political ethics.
Whatever conflict arises among men due to intoxication from liquor, the pride of knowledge and wealth, or the intoxication of youth;
Arising from these intoxications, there occurs a great derangement of the intellect;
that which arises from a lack of discernment is born of intoxication.
That conflict which arises between two parties for the sake of a single object is declared by those who know the truth of the scriptures to be one that covets a single substance.
Thus ends the chapter on the analysis of compounds.
Or one whose treasury is struck down by fate, or who is afflicted by disease,
or whose mind is addicted to vice, or who is oppressed by an enemy.
A king desiring victory should march against one who is deprived of his army and treasury, or one who has been separated from his allies, for the sake of achieving success.
In autumn or in spring, when no enemy is present,
a king should set out on a military expedition after having obtained an auspicious omen.
The Sandhānajā, the Pārṣṇirodhā, the Mitravighaṭanī,
the Dvandvanirvyājajā, the Kulyā, and the seventh is the Āśīghragā.
Having made peace with the rear-attacker, the king should then set out;
this is known as the "expedition after making peace," which brings security to kings.
Having deployed his own great army for the purpose of blocking the rear-enemy (pārṣṇigrāha),
that expedition undertaken by him will be auspicious as it secures the flanks.
Having caused a well-constructed conflict between the enemy and one's own ally,
that expedition undertaken by those two shall be the supreme "alliance through war" (mitravigrahaṇī).
That expedition upon which one sets out oneself, or causes an enemy to be brought, is called a "pair-born" (dvandvaja) march; it brings about the destruction of the foe.
That expedition of a king which is undertaken when he is entirely composed in mind, powerful, and capable of destroying his enemies, is proclaimed as the "Nirvyāja" (the guileless).

That expedition which one undertakes together with a member of the enemy's lineage for the destruction of the foe shall be a family-expedition (kulyā), striking fear into the hearts of the adversaries.
That expedition which is undertaken suddenly, aiming at the destruction of the enemy and setting aside all other negligence, shall proceed with great speed.
Thus end the varieties of journeys.
For one who always acts after deliberating upon the place, the time, the ally, the cause, and one's own strength, an expedition becomes a giver of success.
Mūla, Ārdrā, Śravaṇa, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Kṛttikā are joined with Mercury;
while Jupiter is conjoined with Punarvasu.
Venus in Bhāgya and Saturn in Svāti bestow all accomplishments;
therefore, these have been declared as Siddhi-yogas by the wise.
The thousand-rayed sun was in his hand, the moon in his head (Mṛgaśīrṣa),
Mars in Aśvinī, and the son of the Moon (Mercury) in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
The preceptor of the gods [Jupiter] in Puṣya, the descendant of Bhṛgu [Venus] in Revatī,
and Saturn on a Saturday in Rohiṇī— these are proclaimed as the Sudhā-yogas.

When the Sun is in the *Riktā* tithis and the Son of the Sun (Saturn) is present; when the Son of Bhṛgu (Venus) is in the *Nandā* tithis; when the Son of the Earth (Mars) is in the *Jayā* tithis; and when Mercury and the Moon are in the *Bhadrā* tithis.
When the preceptor of the thirty-three gods (Jupiter) is situated in the full lunar mansions, the lunar day becomes "perfected" (siddha);
it accomplishes all undertakings for men, especially during a journey.
The first lunar day (pratipad) is praised for setting out on a journey; the second bestows safety;
the third leads to the acquisition of wealth; and the fourth is always censured.
The fifth lunar day is to be known as bringing prosperity; the sixth is most contemptible for a journey;
the seventh is for the sake of obtaining cattle; and the eighth lunar day is contemptible.
The ninth day is always to be censured, while the tenth becomes the giver of land;
the twelfth, which is eternally Vaiṣṇavī and bestows victory, is to be avoided.
What need is there for much speaking? All the *siddhis* are found on the thirteenth day; however, the fourteenth day must be avoided in both the dark and the bright fortnights.
The full moon is excellent for traveling when it has abandoned its eastern quarter;
the new moon, however, is especially to be avoided when it is devoid of the moon's light.
The three Uttaras and Puṣya on Sunday bestow auspiciousness;
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, and Citrā on Monday bring happiness.
The *ahirbudhnya* and *pauṣṇa* [nakṣatras] are recommended on Tuesday;
*punarvasu* on Thursday; and *bhāgya* when the moon is situated in *śravaṇa*.
The asterisms presided over by Hari (Śravaṇa), by the two (Punarvasu),
and by Vahni (Kṛttikā) are always recommended for these days, specifically on Saturday.
Hasta, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Revatī, Mṛgaśīrṣa,
Anurādhā, Aśvinī, and Śravaṇa are the asterisms recommended for the journeys of men.
If the ascendant is a movable sign or a dual sign, one may set out on a journey with kings;
however, those who desire safety on their expedition should not travel when the ascendant is a fixed sign.
Avoiding the eighth and twelfth signs from birth,
and having obtained the strength of the planets, a king may go forth if he desires victory.
Mercury is in the ascendant, Venus is in the fourth, Jupiter is in the fifth,
Mars and Saturn are in the sixth, and the Sun is in the third house.
He for whom the Moon is the tenth house shall be successful on his journey;
he travels with safety and returns in safety.
If even a single planet among Mercury, Jupiter, or Venus should occupy a quadrant or a trine, the journey of that person will bestow happiness.
If two [planets] are situated in a Kendra and a Trikona, that is called Ati-yoga;
therein, the journey of kings brings security and destroys enemies.
When [the lords of the ascendant and the seventh house] occupy three angles or trines, it is called *yogādhiyoga*;
therein, the traveler shall experience safety, gain of land, and the destruction of enemies.
If, at the time of departure, the benefics are situated in the ascendant, the trines, and the malefics are in the sixth, third, and eleventh houses,
that person shall experience gain and victory.
For kings desiring prosperity, a journey undertaken under the auspices of yoga is recommended;
for the twice-born, it depends on the qualities of the stars, and for others, on omens and the like.
When traveling under the asterisms of Uttarās, Viśākhā, or Rohiṇī, O King,
the monarch should avoid the first third of the day.
Indeed, during the days of the asterisms of Āśleṣā, Mūla, and Ārdrā, or on the day of Jyeṣṭhā,
a lord of the earth should avoid the middle portion of the day when setting out on a journey.
A king desiring victory should avoid the latter part of the day when setting out on a journey during the asterisms of Svāti, Aśvinī, Puṣya, and Hasta.
A king who always desires victory should avoid the first portion of the night for sacrifices dedicated to Mitra, Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Pūṣan.
In the southern direction, in the three eastern asterisms, and in Anurādhā, one should avoid the middle of the night;
for traveling at such times, a king becomes skillful, a slayer of enemies, and eager for victory.
During the three asterisms beginning with Śravaṇā,
and specifically under the asterism presided over by Diti (Pūrvabhādrapadā), the final portion of the night should be avoided for the departure of a ruler of the earth.
Travel is always recommended for kings who desire success during the asterisms of Śravaṇa, Hasta, Puṣya, and Mṛgaśīrṣa.
Maitra (Anurādhā), Aśvinī, Puṣya, and Hasta bring auspiciousness in all directions;
they are highly recommended for a journey and are known as the "gatekeepers" of all quarters.
One should travel toward the east or the north during the seven asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā;
during the seven beginning with Maghā, one should travel toward the south or the west.
During the seven asterisms beginning with Maitra (Anurādhā), one should travel toward the western and southern directions;
during the constellations beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā, one may go toward the directions of the lord of Yakṣas (the north) and the south.
If one should proceed in the opposite manner, the *parigha* (obstructive yoga) becomes transgressed;
when the *parigha* is transgressed, it destroys all the undertakings of those who march forth.
Occupying the northwestern direction between Vāyu and Anala, he stands there like a staff; therefore, one should avoid setting out on a journey when he is there.
Some maintain that traveling during the seven asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā toward the southeast or the east incurs no fault arising from the Parigha obstacle.
Likewise, when starting from Maghā and the following asterisms, one does not incur fault by traveling toward the southeast or the east;
when starting from Anurādhā and the following, one may travel toward the direction of Vāyu or the direction of Kubera.
As you proceed toward the northern quarter through the constellations beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā, reaching as far as Vāyavyā and Vāruṇī,
the Parigha obstacle shall not be transgressed.

Jyeṣṭhā destroys the eastern direction; Rohiṇī [destroys] the southern and the western directions; and Pūrvābhādrapadā [destroys] the northern direction for those who travel, resulting in the fruit of their desires.
Likewise, during the asterism Uttaraphalgunī, the northern quarter will always be afflicted;
there shall be suffering for travelers and a return [home] with uncertainty.
Thus are the asterisms for all directions.
On the day of Venus or the Sun, one who intends to travel should avoid the western direction;
on the days of Mercury and Mars, one should likewise avoid the northern quarter.
On a Saturday, one should avoid the eastern direction;
on a Thursday, one must not travel toward the southern quarter.
This is indeed called Vāraśūla by some teachers;
therefore, the wise should not travel during this Vāraśūla.
Thus ends the section on the "Spear of the Days" (vāraśūla).
On a Sunday, the wise should avoid Dhaniṣṭhā, Kṛttikā, Maghā,
Anurādhā, Āśleṣā, and Bharaṇī for travel.
The two Āṣāḍhas and Viśākhā should be avoided on Monday;
Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, and Śatabhiṣaj are to be shunned on Tuesday.
Those who desire auspiciousness should avoid Kṛttikā, Revatī, Mūla, Anurādhā, Aśvinī,
and Śatabhiṣak on Wednesday.
One should avoid the asterisms Mṛgaśiras, Śatabhiṣaj, and Revatī on a Thursday;
one should avoid Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī when traveling on a Friday.
Thus end the remedies for warding off the defects of the constellations.
On the Bahulā days, one should consume curd; on the Brāhmī day, ghee and milk-rice;
on the Aindava day, bean-cakes; and on the Raudra day, sweet curd.
In Punarvasu, one should eat patola; in Puṣya, ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa);
in Āśleṣā, sesame seeds as food; and in Maghā, kṛsara and boiled rice.
One should offer milk-rice to Aryaman under Pūrvaphalgunī; a meal of vegetables under Pāṇi;
and a meal of variegated foods under Citrā.
Under Svāti, one should eat the fruit of the dhātrī; under Dvidaiva (Punarvasu), jaggery with boiled rice;
under Mitrana (Anurādhā), kulattha beans; and under Śakradaivata (Jyeṣṭhā), barley gruel.
In Mūla, one should taste radish; in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, wealth and curd;
in Uttarāṣāḍhā, cold water; and in Śravaṇa, fine flour-meal.
One should eat boiled rice under Dhaniṣṭhā, cakes under the constellation of Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj),
honey under Pūrvābhādrapadā, and likewise citron under Uttarābhādrapadā.
If one sets out after consuming cooked mung beans under Revatī, sweet food under Aśvinī,
or water mixed with sesame seeds under Bharaṇī, one will travel happily.
Thus ends the Nakṣatradohada.
When the great queen Puṣpavatī saw an untimely rain,
and when a dispute arose among the clansmen, as well as a conflict between cats and deer;
During a period of ritual impurity, during a house fire, during an earthquake, during a violent wind,
during a preternatural glow of the quarters, or during a thunderous roar from the earth, one who desires victory should not set out on a journey.
Upon sneezing, whether by oneself or by others, or when obstructed anywhere; or upon seeing smoke without a flame, or the sight of chaff and wood.
One who desires happiness should not go near ink, ashes, oil, dried cow dung, a rabbit, or one who is naked.
Mounted upon donkeys, camels, and buffaloes, these renunciants, disciples, and outcastes were deprived of ears, noses, and other limbs;
they had disheveled hair and wore black garments.
A woman with disheveled hair, one with excessively dark limbs, one smeared with oil, one in her menses,
a pregnant woman, a widow, and men who are insane, impotent, blind, or deaf [should not be touched].
When these are seen, one must never proceed;
likewise, when one is in a state of mental distress, a journey will not grant success.
Thus end the inauspicious omens.
Likewise, [one should gaze] upon a full water-jar, a mirror, curd, wine,
meat, a fish, a conch, a banner, an umbrella, a chowrie, or a beautiful woman.
In a blue jay, a deer, a bharadvāja bird, or even in fruits, flowers, and unhusked grain; in a bull, an elephant in rut, a white horse, or an excellent brahmin.
When gold, divine gems, a lute, a drum,
or even a bound animal is seen, the journey will be fruitful and grant success.
A king, a brahmin, a friend, a courtesan, and a maiden dressed in white garments;
bulls and elephants, as well as men and women mounted upon them—these bring auspiciousness.
"Go" is an auspicious word when spoken from behind; "Come" is auspicious when spoken from the front;
blessings are praised from all sides, as is a powerful contentment of mind.
Expressions such as "cut," "shatter," and "slay" are clearly suitable even for those intent on destroying an enemy or engaging in the sport of hunting. They are always auspicious in such contexts.
Thus end the auspicious omens regarding a journey.
If, at the time of departure, a dog should go to the left or from the right,
or touch the left ear, then there will be success in the journey.
If, upon entering, she moves toward the right, yawns, or becomes intent on sexual pleasure, she brings about supreme happiness; however, the contrary behavior belongs to the Kukkurī.
When a mongoose travels two krośas along with a traveler,
or urinates while moving to the left, it then indicates auspiciousness.
The elephant-stable, the horse-stable, the threshing floor, the bedchamber,
the mortar, the banner, the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the fruit-bearing tree.
A dog passing by a heap of bricks, a water-jar, a pack-saddle, a mound of earth,
or a place adorned with flowers and fruit, brings good fortune.
When the son of Saramā goes ahead after having voided his urine,
then the desired undertaking of the traveler will certainly succeed.
If a dog urinates on wet cow dung while moving to the left, it indicates a delicious meal;
if it urinates on dry dung, it indicates a meal devoid of flavor.
If a dog goes along after placing in its mouth impure rice, meat, or some other fresh substance, it indicates gain for the traveler.
If a dog approaches with wet bones, a garment, or footwear in its mouth,
and then releases them, it brings good fortune.
Thus end the omens concerning dogs.
The directions should be known in their proper sequence by the wise, through the distinction between calm and radiant aspects,
for the purpose of discerning knowledge regarding auspicious and inauspicious results.
First there is a flame in the sun, then smoke, followed by the emergence of embers;
thereafter, in the western quarter, the place of ashes is proclaimed.
The directions toward ash, charcoal, flame, and smoke are designated as "blazing";
the remaining four directions are declared by the ancient sages to be "pacified."
The place of the ashes is fruitless; the charcoal brings fear;
in the flame, death occurs; and in the place of smoke, suffering is certain.
The sun dwells for only one watch (yāma) in each of the cardinal and intermediate directions as it moves clockwise;
there are likewise four watches in a day in Yāmavatī.
In the first watch of the night, the sun shall become filled with flames in the direction of Mahendra;
in the second, in the region of Agni; and in the third, in the quarter of the Pitṛs.
In the fourth region, that of Nairṛta, the sun remains at night;
in the third region, that of Dhanada, it stays at dawn in the direction of the wielder of the trident.
If jackals howl while the fires are blazing, it brings about the fruit that has been described; if they howl "Śiva" while the fires are burning calmly, it certainly foretells auspiciousness.
Crying out in a direction that is peaceful, she should predict these results in sequence: gain, victory, happiness, and the meeting with friends.
In this very manner, one should predict the outcome for the village bird;
a crow crying in a position that is "blazing" (dīpta) shall predict an auspicious result.
When a crow with a flaming mouth utters a harsh sound in a blazing fire,
it indicates the success of an undertaking but will certainly bring about destruction.
Having begun with the Dipta [mudrā] facing forward, one should again rest in the Śānta [mudrā];
having made the task appear doubtful, one should then declare its accomplishment.
When the fire is blazing, a crow with a peaceful face, uttering a sweet sound,
indicates the attainment of desired objects, the destruction of enemies, and the gain of a jewel among women.
Whether in the air or upon a tree, the crow, uttering a sweet sound,
always speaks auspiciously when it is at one's head.
Thus end the omens concerning the crows of Śivāpallī.
Having observed the location of the *potakī*, one should construct the arches (*toraṇas*);
from one arch to the next, the distance should be forty-eight steps.
They know that two trees standing on either side at a distance of eight *dhanus* apart,
or a pair of stone fragments, constitute a constructed *toraṇa*.
The wise man, having fashioned a pair of quails out of flour in his house,
should worship them with flowers, incense, and other offerings, and he should also feed a young girl.
Having arrived at the site of the gateway, he should consecrate the two young girls;
then, being self-restrained, he should go home and sleep upon a cotton mattress while remembering [the deity].
Rising at sunrise, he should go forth accompanied by his companions,
remaining self-restrained and intent upon observing the omens near the gateway.
Having become one whose face is turned toward the peaceful quarters of the sky, praising the goddess Potakī by her names,
one should recite the ten names of the middle son of Pāṇḍu:
Pāṇḍavī, Potakī, Durgā, Śyāmā, Umā, and she who is called Caṭakā.
She is known by the names Vārāhī, Śakunī, Kṛṣṇā, and Śvetapakṣā.
Having invoked him with these, one should scatter unbroken rice grains along with flowers;
and one should meditate upon the heroic Phālguna, the bearer of the burden of all warriors.
Kirīṭin, Vijaya, Kṛṣṇa, Bībhatsu, Phālguna, Arjuna,
Savyasācin, Pārtha, Śvetāśva, and Dhanañjaya.
Oṃ, O auspicious Jvālāmukhī, accept this offering; svāhā!
Oṃ! O Śivā, O Śivadūtī, O Blessed Caṇḍā! Accept, accept this arghya offered by me with playfulness.
"Come with the speed of the wind; perform, perform [the auspicious rite], svāhā!
With this mantra, one should offer an oblation (bali) and water for honor (arghya) to Śivā at a triple-path or a quadruple-path.
At the archways, one should proclaim these names.
The Goddess, who rendered assistance to the sons of Pāṇḍu, becomes the bestower of success.
If the black crow passes to the right of the archway as one goes, being either silent or making faint sounds, it is then considered auspicious by the knower of omens.
For one who has turned back from the gateway, a female owl passing on the left is auspicious;
likewise, a crow in front on the right, or a man on the left in front, is favorable.
One star, Tārā, should be known as the giver of fearlessness; the second shall be the bestower of desires;
and the third, moving toward the southern direction, leads to the attainment of sovereignty.
If, having first gone to the left, she then goes to the right,
Kṛṣṇā will undoubtedly destroy the undertaking and bring it to completion.
When the remaining [strategies] are employed in reverse order, they yield reverse results;
those that do not proceed according to the sequence of leadership portend mixed outcomes.
Whether auspicious or inauspicious, that very [omen] at its conclusion yields the fruit;
thus has the knowledge of the *potakī* bird been proclaimed by King Soma.
Thus ends the section on the Potakī bird.
A milky tree, rich with fruits, flowers, and foliage,
joined with sacred objects and accompanied by a pair of tawny-colored parrots.
The wise man, being composed, having bathed and dressed in white garments, accompanied by his assistants, should perform worship at evening for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
Having smeared the ground with fresh cow dung and fashioned it into the shape of a cowhide,
the learned practitioner should draw an eight-petaled lotus with moistened flour.
Having fashioned there an auspicious pair of Piṅgalas made of flour,
one should install Caṇḍī there as well, fashioned from flour and equipped with her weapons.
There, one should meditate upon the eight world-protectors on the eight petals of the lotus,
with Brahmā above the lotus and Acyuta situated below it.

One should worship with fruits, flowers, and so forth, along with incense, food offerings, and lamps, using mantras consisting of the respective names preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with "namaḥ."
"Salutation to the one who resides in the tree"—this is the mantra for the seat.
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Cāmuṇḍe huṃ, salutation; descend into this tree, svāhā.
Meditating while reciting this mantra, one should cause Caṇḍī to descend into the tree.
Now this mantra is also declared for the pair of Piṅgalās.

Oṃ piṅgale mekhale revati rātricāriṇi brahmaputri, speak this to me yourself, svāhā! This is the invocation mantra (āvāhana-mantra). Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ cali vauṣaṭ! This is the root mantra (mūla-mantra). Oṃ siddhacāmuṇḍe kṛṣṇapiṅgale svāhā!

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Kālarātri, you whose form is mantra, Maheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, protector of progeny, Mistress of Yoga! Come, come hither! Stay, stay! Oṃ hrīṃ cili cili, for the sake of sound, svāhā! This is the mantra for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
One should perform worship, recitation, and fire-offerings with the root mantra;
having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should perform the fire-offering consisting of a tenth part of that number.
Recalling Caṇḍikā, one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks from the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Āmra, Dūrvā, and Brahma trees, mixed with honey and clarified butter.
Seated upon a corpse, emaciated, smeared with ashes, and carrying a skull-cup;
having an owl as her emblem, holding a trident in her hand, drinking blood, and wearing a garland of severed heads.
Having performed his worship, he should meditate upon Caṇḍī— black, smeared with fat and blood, clad in the skins of elephants and lions,
seated upon the axle-tree, and terrifying.
Having thus worshipped the tree, one should encircle it with white threads;
then, one should offer everything—the fire oblations, worship, recitations, and so forth—to the preceptor.
Having informed the Goddess of his purpose, he should then go home at the onset of night;
and in the house, he should feed the maidens and eat himself together with his kinsmen.
Then, having risen at dawn and performed the worship of the gods and other rites,
he went to the consecrated place and knelt upon the ground.
Having joined his palms in the añjali gesture, he should recite the collection of mantras;
he should speak with a loud voice, preceded by an oath regarding the task at hand.
"Tell the truth, O Goddess, daughter of Brahmā! Speak of what is auspicious and inauspicious.
Having said this, the wise one turned his back toward the blazing quarter of the sky.
One who is intent on observing the omens should, with a one-pointed mind, listen to its cry and likewise observe its movements.
The earth-born is the horse, the water-born is the elephant, and the fire-born is the peacock;
the wind-born is the deer, while the space-born is the crow, like a *kiṃśuka* flower in the sky.
These five notes are known to belong to the bird named Piṅgala;
their distinction in terms of duration (mātrā) will now be explained according to the differentiation of the notes.
That which consists of one [unit] is said to have one measure (ekamātra); with two of those it has two measures (dvimātrika);
with three it would have three measures (trimātra), and with four it has four measures (caturmātra).
This [vowel] consisting of five [mātrās] is to be understood by the wise as having five parts;
I shall describe its essential nature according to the imitation of the vowels.
Cil is one mātrā (1); cili is two mātrās (2); cilili is three mātrās (3);
cilicili is four mātrās (4); cilicilili is five mātrās (5)—this is the Pārthiva.

Kic 1, kici 2, kcici 3, kici kici 4, kici kicici 5—these are the watery [mantras]. Kug 1, kuku 2, kukuku 3, kukukuku 4, kukukukuku 5—these are the fiery [mantras]. Cīc 1, cīcu 2, cīcucu 3, cīcucīcu 4, cīcucīcucu 5—these are the airy [mantras]. Sṛk 1.
Cica 2, kusuru 3, kīḥ kīsaru 4, curucuru curu 5—this is space (ākāśa).
The five distinct *mātrās* have been described in the sequence beginning with the earth element;
whichever among them is uttered three times is desired as a short vowel (*laghu-svara*).
The Guru is said to be sixfold when uttered, and ninefold when protracted (pluta);
in a short (laghu) syllable the result is slight, in a long (guru) it is middling, and in a protracted (pluta) it is full.
When joyful, one produces the earthy (pārthiva) tone; when conversing, the watery (jalaja) tone;
and when overcome by passion, the fiery (taijasa) tone—thus these are the three tranquil tones.
When one is enraged, one produces the Vāyavya tone; when afflicted by grief, the Nābhasa tone.
These two tones are proclaimed by the wise as being called "blazing" (pradīpta).
In the southeastern direction, the earth-born sound is powerful;
and in the western and northern directions, the water-born sound is strong.
In the northwestern (vāyavya) and southeastern (taijasa) corners, the taijasa vowel is most powerful;
in the northeastern (aiśāna) and southwestern (nairṛta) corners, the nābhasa vowel is more powerful.
There is friendship between the watery and the earthy elements; of these two, the watery is superior in strength.
There is enmity between the watery and the fiery elements; of these two, the watery possesses great power.
There is enmity between water and wind; of these two, wind is the stronger.
Between earth and fire, earth is the stronger; however, the ether is stronger than both of them.
Neither the enemies nor the friends, nor even the neutral elements, are mutually so powerful;
nevertheless, the aerial sound (nābhasa-nāda) is proclaimed to be the most powerful of all.
There is friendship between the earthly and the fiery elements, and in that case, the sound is for the most part powerful;
there is friendship between fire and wind, and of those two, the wind is the stronger.

The two sounds produced by water and wind were previously described as enemies of the earth-born sound; yet those same two, when arising subsequently, are declared by him to be friends of the earth-born sound.
Among all four types of sounds, the celestial (nābhasa) is not considered an enemy;
thus has been declared the relative strength and weakness of vowels as friends and foes.
In its own direction, the fruit is full; half of that in the house of a friend;
there is an absence of fruit in the field of an enemy, or else the opposite.
The water element, which follows immediately after the earth element, bestows all accomplishments;
however, the two vowels [the earth and water signs] in reverse order cause the destruction of results.
First there is an earthy sound, and immediately after that, a fiery one;
these two grant the desired object, whereas otherwise they are the reverse.
If the sound is first produced by the earth and subsequently by the wind, then there is loss preceded by gain;
from the reverse, there is gain preceded by loss.

If the first sound arises from the earth and the second from the ether, suffering will follow happiness; from suffering, happiness follows by the reverse process. If the fiery sound occurs after the watery one, it will bring about destruction after having produced its fruit.
Arising through inversion, they produce inverted results.
If the first sound is that of water-born creatures and the subsequent one arises from the wind, there is fear for the destruction of wealth; the same applies if the order is reversed.
If the sky-born [planet] follows the water-born [planet], death results from a battle with three enemies;
if they arise in the reverse order, they indicate death by the enemy.
The sounds of fire and wind, arising in their proper sequence, are destroyers of wealth;
when they arise in the reverse order, they should be known as indicators of death.
Whether in regular or reverse order, the fiery and the ethereal notes at the beginning cause fierce quarrels and very great fear.
Whether by inversion or in regular order, these two sounds— the Vāyavya and the Nābhasa—
certainly bring about the loss of wealth or death in battle for a man.
A roar of the earth uttered by others causes the obstruction of the accomplishment of one's purpose;
however, a roar of the earth uttered by the king himself bestows the fruit of all desires.
Whether three, four, or five [notes] are heard,
the earthy (pārthiva) sound, which is heard last, is the most excellent and superior.
When the Piṅgala bird, rising upward from its own place upon a tree, produces an earthy sound like water,
it portends gain, happiness, fame, and victory.
Descending from its own place and uttering auspicious sounds,
the bird indicates a minor result and gain through some effort.
Crying out from the top of the tree, the bird foretells that the king will obtain abundant water-born fruit; it is middling in the middle and small at the bottom.
Having placed food in its mouth or having eaten it, that bird,
perched in a pleasant place and making auspicious sounds, shall indicate good fortune.
When the Piṅga bird, having abandoned the food held in its beak, utters auspicious sounds,
it then foretells the loss of prosperity.
Having abandoned a well-honored tree and taken refuge in another tree,
one who produces a beautiful sound may find happiness in another land.
If a tawny-colored bird makes an auspicious sound in the sky, upon a dry tree, on a broken branch, or in a hollow, it foretells fierce danger.
Whether stationed in an auspicious place or having gone there, if it circumambulates from left to right,
then, while in a state of peace, it portends something other than auspicious— an inauspicious sound.
If Piṅgala, remaining in the northwestern direction (Śānta), produces an auspicious sound from the left side,
it indicates a favorable result after a long period of time.
When the Piṅgalā bird, situated in an auspicious place, utters sounds produced by earth,
water, or fire, it announces joy, happiness, gain, victory, and fame.
Thus ends the omen of Piṅgalā.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, the destroyer of all obstacles,
three women, together with a young girl, [remained] while all the people were asleep.
Having offered salutations to Caṇḍikā, one should fill those vessels— whether they be a kuḍava or any other measure— with unbroken grains, consecrating them seven times with mantras.
Having performed the purification rites, they should install Guṇādhipa;
then, taking him with them, they should go to the house of the washerman.
They should scatter white parched grains in front of that house,
and with well-composed minds, they should listen while keeping the intended person in their thoughts.
A certain statement was heard within the precincts of a washerman’s house,
spoken by a woman, a man, a child, or some other person.
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
the fruit arising from their casual conversation should be understood by those who hear it through reflection upon the meaning of their words.
Even in the dwelling of a Caṇḍāla, this is the procedure for hearing and explaining;
whatever word they may speak therein, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
Having examined the science of omens (*śākuna-śāstra*), which reveals future events,
King Someśvara has correctly described the nature of omens.
Thus ends the section on omens from whispered voices. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the expedition.
One should never, under any circumstances, go to a region that is parched by drought, afflicted by famine, beset by pestilence, or where others are in a state of distress.
While the enemies are wasting away through mutual conflict,
let the wise king remain as long as their destruction may be achieved.
The posture called "remaining in one's own place" (svasthāsana), known as equanimity (upekṣā), the "obstructing the path" posture (mārgarodhāsana),
the "difficult-to-conquer" posture (durgasādhyāsana), and the "appropriating the kingdom" posture (rāṣṭrasvīkaraṇāsana).
There is another called the pleasant seat (ramaṇīyāsana), as well as the nearby seat (nikaṭāsana),
the seat for the long journey (dūramārgāsana), and likewise that known as the alluring (pralobha).
This tenth posture, known as *parādhīnāsana*, is highly extolled;
no other posture superior to this is seen by those who are experts in policy.
When the kingdom is free of thorns and the circle of enemies has been subdued,
the state of kings remaining in their own place is known as "seated on one's own throne" (svasthāsana).
Whatever is to be performed by us is indeed brought about by destiny,
due to the application of severe punishment, calamity, and the lack of a means of livelihood.
"He will certainly meet his destruction through famine, pestilence, or invasion"—thinking thus, the king neglects his royal station; this is called the posture of indifference.
If the flow of a river is obstructed by its full current,
that place where the path is blocked due to that defect is known as *mārgarodhāsana*.
One who is intent on capturing a fort should station himself near it, obstructing its supplies of fodder and the like; for that is indeed the siege of a fort.
That place where one remains for the sake of subduing a kingdom acquired by force is called by kings the "throne of the acquisition of a realm."
A king desiring victory, having gone forth and slain his enemy on the field of battle,
beholds a delightful dwelling where he may reside with his followers.
That location which abounds in fodder and fuel, and is well-supplied with water and grain,
is declared by those who know the principles of policy to be a pleasant seat of government.
When a king is intent on the destruction of a distant enemy,
his remaining nearby would constitute "sitting too close."
Having gone to a distant land and completed his business in its entirety,
the king realized that his own city was far away, where he remained undisturbed.
From the change of the rainy season until the arrival of autumn,
whatever place is appropriate is indeed a distant journey on foot.
"Elephants, horses, wealth, jewels, as well as fortresses and the kingdom—let there be a temporary stay; once I have slain the enemy, I shall give these to you."
When a ruler of the earth remains where he is while being enticed by another in this manner,
that is called "the seat of enticement" (pralobhāsana) by those who know political science.
"Whether in a month, a fortnight, ten days, six days, or five nights, I shall give you a gift"— having enticed him with such words, one should keep the king under one's control.
But when one remains there for a long time, supported by one's underlying intention (āśaya),
that is described by the wise as the "seat of enticement" (pralobhāsana).
When one is unable to go to one's own country, whether due to affection or enmity,
that place where one remains is known as a state of subservience to others.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter on postures (āsana).
A king who is himself weak in strength does not perceive the cause of victory— that is,
one who, being oppressed by a stronger power, should seek refuge in a secure place.
Resorting to the virtuous, avoiding association with others, and likewise taking refuge in a stronghold—these three methods have been declared; a fourth is not found.
A wise king who, possessing little strength, is oppressed by a great enemy,
recognizes him as one true to his word and seeks refuge with him alone.

Indeed, those who know the principles of policy declare that when one takes refuge with an enemy after observing many of his excellent qualities, that very quality is called "resorting to the virtuous."
For one who is being oppressed by an enemy, or who himself lacks the necessary means,
should recognize his own adversary as lacking in merit and seek refuge with another who possesses superior qualities.
He who takes refuge in one who is powerful, endowed with capability, knowledgeable in dharma, and truthful,
is said to have "resorted to another.
For he is oppressed by an enemy possessed of strength, being himself an unequal foe.
But when one takes refuge in a fortress, that is considered "taking refuge in a fortress."
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter on the Basis.
Placing himself between two powerful enemies by means of words,
he should conduct himself with a policy of double-dealing, remaining unobserved like the eye of a crow.
Whether out of gain or even out of fear, one who is intent on securing his well-being should spend a long time between the two parties by means of a policy of double-dealing.

By those who know the essence of the meaning of the treatises on ethics, he was designated with the names "Mithyācitta" (False-minded) and "Mithyāvacana" (False-speaker) through their diligent effort to distinguish the various meanings of names.
"False action," "the other [party]," "one who employs both," and "the one who offers gifts to both"— thus, the policy of double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*) is fivefold in this context.
One harbors hostility in the mind while speaking pleasant words;
this is called "duplicity" by those skilled in the meaning of the deceitful mind.
One speaks pleasant words with the voice but acts otherwise in deed;
this other form of duplicity is called "false speech."
At first, for the sake of gaining confidence, such a person of corrupt disposition performs some small task little by little; yet he will ultimately destroy a great undertaking.
Thus, when a king employs such false measures for the destruction of an enemy,
this is proclaimed as the double-dealing known as "false action" (mithyākaraṇa).
A deceitful man, desiring the welfare of the bandits, takes secret wages in one place and openly displays them in another while acting as a spy.
Remaining unobserved, he should penetrate the enemy's counsel and deliver it to his own master;
because he dwells in a state of duplicity, such a person is known as a "double-agent" (ubhayavetana).
"Subdue my enemy"—with these words, a great gift was presented;
likewise, horses, elephants, and other such things were offered by another person intended for him as well.
"I shall send a messenger; I will overcome your enemy"—speaking thus, one should accomplish one's purpose by means of two contradictory [strategies].
When the king proceeds while his true form remains unknown to those two,
the wise call that state "double-dealing" (dvaidhībhāva), characterized by the simultaneous presentation of gifts to both sides.
The king who, being skilled in the protection of his counsel, conducts himself by adopting a double policy, seizes the fortune of his adversaries.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, on the Double Policy.
He who knows how to employ peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge,
and duplicity within the circle of enemies;
Strong, endowed with a treasury, skilled in the performance of the six qualities,
and knowing the proper place, time, and allies— he enjoys the entire earth.
Among the means of policy, conciliation is considered the best; sowing dissension is regarded as middling; bribery is the lowest; and punishment is remembered as the most difficult to employ.
Furthermore, because it is free from misfortune and because there is no loss of wealth, undertakings reach completion;
therefore, conciliation is considered the best [of the four means].
Those who are contemptible fall into dissension; they are not grounds for trust.
Therefore, because it is characterized by doubt, this type of dissension is known as "mediocre."
The depletion of wealth comes first, while success is established in destiny;
therefore, the wise have declared that giving away one's possessions is the lowest course.
War is waged for the sake of gain, yet victory in battle is uncertain;
both kingdom and life itself are at stake, and from that arises the misery of punishment.
When one is angry, pleasant speech only serves to increase that anger,
just as drops of water upon heated clarified butter only serve to increase its flame.
A wise person should first employ conciliation toward those who are of noble birth, grateful, compassionate in heart, virtuous, and intent on accomplishing their tasks.
The first is said to be pleasant to the ear; the second is likewise divine;
the third is declared to be traditional; and the fourth is remembered as born of greed.
In the same way, the fifth means is known as *nijārpaṇa* (self-surrender);
it is said to be the supreme among the means (*upāyas*), free from all affliction.
Through sweet and pleasant conversation, as well as other heart-pleasing words—
such conciliation through speech is remembered as being "charming to the ear."
That which is practiced by those skilled in policy through means of generating trust, such as oaths preceded by [invocations to] the gods, is known as divine conciliation (sāma).
When one is reminded, "That which was formerly a kinsman has now been forgotten by you," that Sāman by which such a reminder is provided is known as Smāraṇa.
The conciliation that says, "I shall give you a village, a city, a kingdom, horses, elephants,
or wealth," is known here as being born of greed.
"In your service, my own body has been offered by me"—
thus, when the Sāman had been offered through speech, that offering of oneself was declared.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter on Conciliation.
Those enemies who are intoxicated by pride and cannot be subdued by the means of conciliation (sāma) should be won over by the king seeking victory through the means of sowing dissension (bheda).
Just as a swan separates milk and water when they are mixed together,
so too should one separate well-united enemies by means of creating dissension among them.
Through his own secret agents stationed among the enemy, as well as through double-agents,
he should cause dissension among those men who are afraid, humiliated, or enraged.
The taking of life, the shattering of pride, the loss of wealth, imprisonment,
the longing for another's wife, and the breaking of limbs— such is the sixfold classification here.
I have understood the secret plan correctly: the king is intent on killing you today or tomorrow with his most cruel weapons; yet even now you do not realize it.
When fear arises through slander, even by means of causes that should not be disclosed and which consist of mere conjectures, that is known as "breach," which destroys life.
"Prompted by your enemy, the king will take away your honor.
Thus has been described the breach caused by enmity, which is the destruction of one's honor.
"This man is indeed very wealthy, yet he does not wish to give you anything;
therefore, it is right that you should take his wealth by some means or other."
Having deliberated thus with the king, he said to the creditor:
"This king is greedy for wealth; he will surely seize your property."
When one who receives wages from both sides causes a division by means of such slander,
this breach is declared by those learned in policy to be a loss of wealth.
Your master will never place any trust in you;
having bound you with fetters, he will cast you into prison.
Having thus created confidence, one who, intent on the welfare of his own master,
divides another through his intellect— that is known as "sowing dissension," which is considered a form of bondage.
A man of luxury, fickle, indulgent, handsome, young, and a libertine,
gazes upon my wife in the inner apartments with sidelong glances.
"He is to be executed"—thus the king consulted with me;
he who creates such a division [between us] would be one who covets my wife.
Describing your wife, who is endowed with beauty and graced with fresh youth,
before me, the king was observed to be full of longing.
"Because he will not obtain you while you are alive, he will commit an offense against you;
this is what is proclaimed as the 'distinction of desire for a wife,' or it is described in this way."
Born in this family, he might at some time desire the kingdom;
likewise, his fingers, eyes, and all his means are constantly [at his disposal].
"The king has resolved to cut [us down]; he will certainly do it by all means"—this dissension thus created is proclaimed as *aṅgabhaṅga* (the breaking of limbs).
He who, through the correct application of sowing dissension, shatters the subjects of his enemies—
that heart of the rival king is split asunder by the thunderbolt of division.
Thus ends the chapter on differentiation, [chapter] 18.
By the withholding of the burden of wealth, by the family [of officials] exceeding their own jurisdiction,
by the non-payment of wages, and by the seizure of property.
And those ministers who have become alienated from their enemies for these reasons—
including counselors, assistants, and likewise vassals and men of high standing— [should be won over].
He should bestow gifts upon his servants, kinsmen, those who live within his domain,
and those who assist him with their counsel for battle.
Even to those who are intent on greed and whose minds are attached to calamities,
the king should extend gifts with the desire to destroy his enemies.
Likewise, one should bestow gifts even upon those ministers and others who are free from passion, for the sake of the prosperity of the kingdom.
The desired [tribute] consists of the annual tax, that which is local, produced from hands, born of elephants and horses,
village-born, royal edicts, ornaments, clothing, what is obtained through service,
mines, gold, maidens, the Vaiśya, and likewise the harbor-tax.
Thus, bribery has been described by the wise as being of sixteen kinds.
Whatever object is pleasing to someone, when it is given to that person according to their fitness,
that is declared to be the highest gift, known as abhīṣṭa-dāna.
Whatever is given by someone for as long as one year, being sufficient to maintain his family,
that gift is known as *hāyana*.
That which is given as a kingdom is called a gift of territory (deśya);
that which consists of the taxes arising from a kingdom is known by the wise as a gift born of taxes (karaja).
The gift of an elephant is known as the "gift of the tusker," while the gift of a horse is declared by those skilled in policy to be the "gift of the steed."
Whether the hands are folded in supplication or held out in offering,
that which is given as a village is considered a gift born of a village.
Whatever is given by one's sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons shall never be subverted;
that gift which is characterized by its immovability is known as a *śāsana* (an edict).
That gift which is bestowed as a beautiful ornament fashioned from gems and gold is declared to be known as "ornament-giving" (bhūṣā-dāna).
Variegated with many colors, made of various threads,
originating from many lands, and both fine and thick.
When garments that are exceedingly beautiful and abundant are given out of grace,
that gift is proclaimed as "vasana" (clothing).
A seat, a fly-whisk, an umbrella, a vehicle,
or anything else worthy of honor that is given as if to a human being— that gift is called *pratipattika*.
That earth from which silver, gold, and gems are produced,
when it is given away, is called an "ākara" (mine).
When numerous excellent gold coins (niṣkas) are given,
that gift is called "gold-born" (rukmaja) by those expert in the treatises on statecraft (arthaśāstra).
When a maiden, adorned with ornaments and endowed with auspicious marks,
is given according to the prescribed rite, that they know as the gift of a daughter (kanyādāna).
When a courtesan endowed with beauty and youth, and skilled in dance and song,
is given away, that gift is called Vaiśya-dāna.
There, on the shore of the ocean, dwell many wealthy men who subsist by means of ships and trade extensively in various commodities.
That gift which is bestowed as a city endowed with unprecedented resources and yielding many articles is known as a *vailākara*.
For that which is indeed unattainable through division is accomplished by means of giving;
by the gift of one's own cattle in this world, one becomes a conqueror of both worlds.
There is no one in this world who is not subject to the power of destiny;
even the gods here become subject to the will of all embodied beings.
Giving is the most excellent means to prosperity; giving accomplishes all goals.
A king who is habitually generous is worshipped by the people in this world like a god.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter on giving.
If a king is powerful, he should employ punishment against an enemy who cannot be overcome even by the threefold means.
Enemies consider one who employs conciliation and the other means to be powerless;
therefore, one should employ punishment, for punishment brings men under control.
Likewise, twelve types of punishments are to be administered by one who is powerful;
three are to be administered by one who is incapable. Thus, fifteen are traditionally recorded.
Furthermore, a king who abides in righteousness must impose other punishments—
such as execution, affliction, or confiscation of wealth— to protect the livelihood of his subjects.
The destroyer of countries, as well as the severer of people's limbs;
the seizer of cattle, the stealer of grain, and another who is a captor of prisoners;
the plunderer of regions, the taker of wealth, and another who is the robber of all one's possessions.
The destruction of fortresses, the burning of dwellings, and likewise banishment from the country.
The great rod of punishment, which brings about war and effects the destruction of enemies,
has been described by King Soma as the fourth among the strategic means (upāyas).
Where forests are cut down and reservoirs are breached,
and where villages are burned— that is the punishment that destroys the country.
Where the noses and pairs of ears of the local inhabitants are cut off,
that punishment is considered the "mutilation of the limbs."
All the cattle born in that land are seized suddenly by force;
this is known as the "seizure of cattle" (gograha), a punishment inflicted upon foreign territories.
Grain hidden within its husks, that which has been struck by the sickle in the field,
that which is heaped up in the marketplace, and that which is gathered into a heap on the threshing floor.
All that which is situated in the enemy kingdoms is seized;
this punishment, consisting of the plundering of grain, causes famine in the country.
Those householders, family men, wealthy men,
or merchants who are led away bound by him are said to be his captives.

Having granted security to the people and remaining there, he likewise brings other born beings under his own control; that kingdom is thus made his own—this is the "seizer of the country" form of punishment.
Having forcibly occupied villages with his soldiers and having formed a firm alliance, he should collect gold; this is called the fine consisting of the seizure of wealth by force.
Where a city or town, famous for its wealth, is surrounded by a great army and plundered of its riches, grain, cattle, and other possessions.
Iron vessels, clothes, and household utensils—
since everything is seized from him, he is indeed called "the taker of all possessions."
The knower of that [system] should draw a radiant four-cornered Koṭacakra;
there, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the lunar mansions in their proper order.
The wise practitioner should draw the four stars beginning with Kṛttikā within each of the northeastern corners of that Koṭicakra.
Likewise, the triad beginning with Revatī and Punarvasu, while emerging,
and the triad beginning with Āśleṣā, while entering within from the southeast (Āgneya) corner toward the eastern direction.
One should write the four [asterisms] beginning with Maghā according to the traditional teaching;
one should write the triad beginning with Citrā in the south, entering within the southwest.
One should draw the four beginning with Maitrī while exiting toward the west;
likewise, one should draw the three beginning with the north from the corner toward the direction of the wind (the northwest).
The four stars beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā should again be drawn extending toward the north;
the three stars beginning with Revatī should be drawn—this is the rule for the asterisms.
Those squares situated within the interior, located in the middle of the lines,
are designated as "pillar-stars" (stambhatārā) by those proficient in the science of astrology.
The eight stars situated on its exterior are joined to the enclosure wall;
furthermore, the other stars situated even further outside are proclaimed as the outermost stars.
A wise person should recognize that those other constellations which lie along the pillars and walls are indeed external.
If a malefic planet is situated within [the camp], the destruction of the army occurs;
if a benefic planet is outside, victory belongs to those stationed on the outside.
In whichever direction the Moon may be, in that direction the division shall break out.
Having fully ascertained the location of the weak point, one should engage in battle there.
One should have water situated in a moat drained away by digging,
or one should cause a dam to be built there, or fill it with earth and other materials.
If one should cross a great, unfathomable body of water by means of boats and the like,
having thus ferried across the troops, one shall conquer the fortress consisting of water.
Having surrounded the mountain-born fortress, which was difficult to ascend, with his army,
[he ensured] that grain could not enter and those stationed within the fort could not depart.
By means of such strategies as the depletion of food supplies, the cessation of reinforcements, persistent pressure, and sowing dissension, the king should conquer a mountain fortress.
Whatever fort is constructed of stone, brick, or earth,
one should cause it to fall by means of mechanical engines, stones, and excavations.
With pavilions covered in skins, with moving wheeled-machines,
and with warriors stationed there shouting and rushing forth in every direction;
With arrows having fire and oil for their tips, propelled by the wind,
the heroic divisions of soldiers ascended using provided ladders.
One should acquire the three types of forts by means of firm blows from elephant tusks, by volleys of arrows discharged by warriors,
and by the construction of counter-forts.
A king may conquer a forest stronghold by cutting down its branches with hundreds of thousands of axes,
or even by burning it with a forest fire.
Water-jars were filled with waters brought from afar by many buffaloes,
camels, oxen, and even more.
Having brought his own forces and having gratified them on all four sides,
he should surround the area and dig deep wells everywhere.
Then one should commence the battle with machines, stones, and fire;
and one should cause the fire to blaze up by means of a favorable wind.
Therefore, one should milk fire consisting of fire-oil from every side;
scorched by the absence of water, those dwelling in the fortresses will meet their destruction.
The king should satisfy his own forces with water for drinking;
by such means and others, he should secure a fortification situated in the desert.
One should overcome a wooden fort by means of pulverization, elephant-ramming,
stone-throwing machines, or by setting it on fire with flames.
A king, joined by the strength of elephants and horses, shall conquer a fortress protected by men;
thus is described the punishment known as the "breaking of the fort."
O King, that city in which an enemy dwells together with his sons, army, and vehicles— let that city, along with its palaces, walls, and gateways, be your abode.
Within the inner apartments were the delightful palaces of the ladies,
as well as the dwellings of the sons and the houses of the ministers.
And there were the residences of the ministers, the palaces of the counselors,
and many other dwellings belonging to various men.
That which reduces stables, elephant-sheds, and various marketplaces to ashes is the punishment known as "burning the site."
Banished from his country and fallen from his enjoyments,
he took refuge in mountain caves, wildernesses, and forest bowers as his dwelling.
Separated from his wife, sons, kinsmen, and ministers,
he was overcome by hunger and thirst, and filled with anxiety and grief.
Deprived of vehicles and seats, and stripped of elephants and horses—
such a punishment for an enemy is known as banishment from the country.
Having understood the strength of his own voice as well as the strength of the earth,
a king should perform all his duties, and especially engage in battle.
Therefore, I shall describe the strength of the vowels (svarabala), divided into ten types:
it is fivefold—namely, mātrā, varṇa, graha, jīva, and rāśi.
The infant, the boy, the youth, the aged, and the one whose voice has ceased—
this second group of five varieties is thus remembered as tenfold.
The letter *a* was first, followed by *i*;
then *u*, *e*, and *o*—such was the Mātṛkā in the beginning.
One should place five letters each, in sequence, within thirty-five cells— starting from the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ha*, excluding *ṅa*, *ña*, and *ṇa*.
Six lines should be drawn upwards and eight horizontal lines;
by their arrangement, there will be exactly thirty-five squares.
There, in the first five squares, one should write the five short vowels in sequence;
beneath them, one should write the consonants beginning with *ka*, excluding *ṅa*, *ña*, and *ṇa*.
Those letters which are arranged one below the other in the row of *a*—
all those letters and vowels possess the same properties as the letter *a*.
Thus, among the vowels beginning with *i*, those which are situated below possess the very same properties; these letters are designated as "vowels" (*svara*).
The letter that occurs at the beginning of a name is proclaimed to be a vowel (svara).
In a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga), the first letter is to be taken [as the initial]; for there is no fixed rule regarding vowels [in such cases].
The vowels of the measures (mātrāsvaras) and likewise the vowels of the letters (varṇasvaras) have been fully explained by me;
now the vowels of the planets (grahasvaras) are being described according to the divisions of the zodiac signs (rāśis).
The letter 'A' shall be the planetary vowel for Aries, Scorpio, and Leo;
thus the planetary vowels have been declared, and now those designated as the life-force (jīva) are described.
In whatever name there are as many syllables endowed with vowels,
one should count those syllables according to the order of the classes of consonants, and likewise the vowels.
Having counted and formed the heap, one should divide it again by five;
the remainder of the heap is declared to be the *jīvasvara*.
The excellent planetary vowels have been fully described, as well as the vowels of the living beings (jīvasvara);
hereafter, I shall explain the vowels of the zodiac signs (rāśisvara) in accordance with the science of vowels (svaraśāstra).
The vowel *a* is declared to be the preeminent sign (*rāśi-vara*) among the seven [asterisms] beginning with Revatī;
likewise, among the others, the vowels beginning with *i* correspond to each group of five.
The lords of the zodiac signs have been fully described; now the rising vowels and so forth will be explained.
The vowel 'a' rises on the day Nandā, while the vowel 'i' always rises on the day Bhadrā.
The syllable *ja* shall always be victorious in all [days] and possess rising power;
the syllable *o* rises on the empty lunar days (*riktā*), and the syllable *au* on the full lunar days (*pūrṇaka*).
On the first day it would be arisen; on the second day, a youth;
on the third, known as a young man; and on the fourth, it would become an elder.
On the fifth day, the tone certainly attains dissolution;
this sequence has been proclaimed for all the vowels beginning with 'a'.
The five vowels beginning with *a* are manifested as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*);
likewise, the differentiation of vowels such as *a* is appropriately joined even within the consonants beginning with *ka*.
Whichever letter is seen at the beginning of the name of anyone whatsoever,
one should determine the result after considering the state of that letter.

One should understand the strength of those planetary sounds which have been proclaimed in connection with the zodiac signs beginning with Aries; having understood them, one should perform the ritual action.
The Sun is the lord of Leo; the Moon is the lord of Cancer;
Mars is the lord of Aries and Scorpio; and Mercury is the lord of Virgo and Gemini.
The Preceptor of the Gods (Jupiter) is proclaimed as the lord of Sagittarius and Pisces; Venus, of Libra and Taurus;
and Saturn, of Aquarius and Capricorn.
The Sun becomes auspicious when [counted] by means of the season, time, direction, and Rudra;
and the Moon is auspicious when [counted] by means of the birth, junction, season, and sun, along with the directions and Īśāna.
Mars brings auspiciousness during the periods of seven, three, eleven, and eleven [years];
Mercury is auspicious during the periods of two, four, six, ten, eight, and eleven [years].
The Jupiter [residing] in the houses of seven,
five, seven, eleven, nine, eight, nine, and twelve is auspicious.
Śukra, the preceptor of the gods, brings auspiciousness when situated in these houses;
likewise, Śanaiścara is a bringer of good fortune when situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses.
Having obtained the strength of one's own planets, one should employ the planetary affliction against enemies;
thus one should wage a tumultuous battle that brings about the destruction of the foe.
Having counted the syllables according to the living vowels, the wise man should engage in battle at that place where there is no superiority for himself.

One should examine those planets that are conjoined with the constellations (dhiṣṇya) beginning with Revatī; if they are auspicious, one should engage in battle while the lord of the zodiacal sign (rāśisvara) is favorable.
If there is one tone, it produces supreme joy for both;
a second produces pride; and a third fosters the accomplishment of the task.
The fourth is equanimity, and the fifth is the destroyer of victory;
having thus understood natural friendship, the king should wage war.
When the Mātrāsvara arises,
one should then perform auspicious rites such as the Garbhādhāna ceremony and the gathering of treasures, grain, and other wealth.
The sowing of all kinds of crops, the entering of cities and houses,
the application of elixirs, and the medical treatment of diseases.
In the Kumāra Lagna, marriage brings about joy;
likewise, the gathering of servants and seeking refuge with a master are recommended.
The king, intent on uprooting his enemies, should undertake a military expedition for the purpose of seizing bribes from them and entering their villages and homes.
When a *yuvan* (short) vowel arises from a *mātrā* (long) vowel, the binding of a turban, consecration,
mounting an elephant or similar vehicle, and union with an excellent woman are recommended.
The king should engage in gambling, acts of combat, military expeditions, the dispatching of letters,
and the slaughter that shatters the lives of his enemies.
When the vowel of the *mātrā* has increased, then the conjunction (*sandhi*) is prescribed;
one should perform rites for pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and the initiation for liberation (*mokṣadīkṣā*).
When the mother has died or when [a son] is born, one should perform the vow of fasting;
beginning from the eastern direction, the wise man should draw a line in a clockwise direction.
One should lead [the breath] from the east to the northwest; from the northwest, one should lead it to the south;
from the south to the northeastern quarter; and from the northeast, one should lead it to the west.
From the western corner one should lead to the south-eastern corner;
from the south-eastern corner one should lead to the north; from the north to the south-western corner; and from the south-western corner one should lead to the eastern direction.
In this manner, the eightfold wheel arises through its arrangement;
therein, the placement of the months beginning with Caitra in the various directions shall now be described.
The month of Caitra shall always consist of the first half of Vaiśākha;
one should cast the second half of the month of Vaiśākha into Jyeṣṭha along with the quarter of Vāyu.
One should arrange the month of Āṣāḍha and half of Śrāvaṇa in the southern quarter;
then one should place the remaining half of Śrāvaṇa and the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada) in the northeast.
One should place the month of Āśvina and half of Kārttika in the western direction (Vāruṇī);
and one should cast half of Kārttika and the month of Mārgaśīrṣa in the southeastern direction (Hutāśanī).
One should place half of Pauṣa and Māgha in the northern direction;
one should assign half of Māgha and Phālguna to the southwestern direction.
In whichever direction a month is situated, its rising occurs there;
it remains for that duration on the earth until four nāḍīs have passed.
The strength of the earth, established in the directions during each half-yāma,
causes the earth to rotate in succession along the path of the arrangement of lines.
From sunrise to sunset, and from sunset to sunrise,
he wandered across the earth through its four watches and in all eight directions.
A seeker of victory should station his forces on the rear or the right;
in this manner, other undertakings will certainly attain success.
One should arrange the eight groups of letters beginning with 'a' starting from the east, proceeding clockwise, by taking recourse to the corners of this very King of Wheels (cakrarāja).
In the *ava* group, Garuḍa is proclaimed; in the *ka* group, the cat;
in the *ca* group, the king of beasts (the lion); and in the *ṭa* group, the son of Saramā (the dog).
In the *tavarga* group, the serpent is proclaimed; likewise, in the *pavarga*, the mouse.
In the *yavarga*, the deer is proclaimed, while in the *śavarga*, the ram is intended.
The eaters are stationed from the east as far as the southwest;
the edible [beings] are stationed from the west as far as the region of the fierce (raudra) direction.
Standing in the fifth position from the devourer, one becomes the object of consumption;
therefore, having reflected with great effort, one should lead an enemy to that fifth state.
Having thus reflected upon the power of names, the lord of the earth should not,
out of a desire for victory, initiate gambling, challenges, or war.
Brahmāṇī is in the eastern quarter on the first and ninth lunar days;
Māheśī is situated in the northern quarter on the second and tenth.
On the eleventh and third lunar days, Kauberī is situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast);
and on the twelfth and fourth lunar days, Vaiṣṇavī is situated in the direction of Nairṛta (the southwest).
On the fifth and the thirteenth days, Vārāhī resides in the south;
likewise, on the fourteenth and the sixth days, Indrāṇī rises in the west.
On the seventh lunar day and on the full moon, Caṇḍikā resides in Vāyavya;
likewise, on the new moon and the eighth lunar day, Mahālakṣmī resides in Īśa.
The seeker of victory should station the Yoginīs behind him on the right;
such is the power of the Yoginīs as described by King Soma.
Thus ends the cycle of the Yoginīs.
On the day before the battle, the king, filled with enthusiasm,
entered the assembly hall along with the princes, the lords of the circles, the vassals, and those worthy of honor.
He should satisfy the soldiers with gold, garments, and ornaments,
and encourage them with words that praise their virtues and honor them.
Relying upon the promise of those warriors, the best of kings [prepared] elephants filled with rut and horses of supreme speed.
Desiring victory in battle, he should bestow gifts upon all as is appropriate;
then, having resolved upon war, he should dismiss them all.
On that night, one should fill the courtyard of the sky with flaming brands,
along with the sounds of great musical instruments and the blare of trumpets and conchs.
With lion-roars, he should terrify the enemy soldiers;
then the king, having consecrated his weapons and his family deities, [should proceed].
Then one should sleep upon the earth, having carefully spread out kusha grass;
then, having risen in the morning and examined both a vessel of ghee and a mirror.
Having bathed in the holy waters of sacred fords and adorned himself with variegated garments,
he propitiated the Lord of the World, who bestows desired fruits upon those who seek them.
Then, having performed various great worship to the family deity,
one should bestow a cow, land, and gold upon the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having accepted their blessings, his horses and elephants were consecrated with the lustration rite (nīrājana);
this was signaled by the scratching of the ground with the tips of the horses' hooves and by their neighing.
One should clearly know victory from the circling of the tip of the right tusk over the left by one's own trunk, and from the trumpeting of elephants.
For men, there is auspiciousness through pure words, the sight of auspicious objects,
and by moving clockwise around the peacocks of Bharadvāja.
And by other auspicious birds that indicate victory and good fortune,
as well as by the throbbing of his right eye and his right arm.
Having thus ascertained victory by these signs— the serenity of his mind and a favorable wind— that warrior, invincible in battle, [proceeded].
All the planets and stars being situated in auspicious positions,
and with a rising tone as well as the strength of the ground for victory;
His enthusiasm kindled by these omens, he departed from his own palace,
having struck the great kettledrum that strikes terror into the enemy soldiers.
Having gone two hundred bows' distance and stationed himself there, that best of kings assembled his entire force and then caused this proclamation to be made:
To him who slays the king in battle, I shall give a hundred thousand;
to those who slay the princes, I shall give three million.
A reward of one million was given for the slayers of the lords of neighboring territories,
and ten thousand for the slayers of ministers and counselors.
I shall provide five thousand for those who slay the principal warriors;
by my grace, I shall give two thousand for those who slay elephants.
I shall give a thousand [pieces of gold] for those who destroy my chariot,
and I shall bestow five hundred for each slayer of my horse-riders.
"I shall bestow a hundred [cows] upon him who brings back the head";
having thus enticed them all, he should advance toward the front of the battle.
[He sent] excellent warriors, endowed with strength, experts in the science of horses,
mounted upon choice steeds, and skilled in the examination of the ground.
The king should again dispatch two hundred, or even one hundred, or half of that number of cavalrymen for the purpose of scouting the battlefield.
Having gone there, they described the virtues of the earth to those who had assembled, at their request.
Having fully understood the military array of his enemies, the lord of the earth...
On a terrain characterized by thickets, large anthills, trees, shrubs, and thorns,
a king skilled in the art of arraying troops should form his battle formation.
Ground that has few trees or stones, free from holes, situated in a cave that is difficult to scale,
devoid of gravel, and free from mud, is recommended for the deployment of cavalry.
It was free from stumps, sand, and mud; devoid of anthills, stones, and unevenness;
and cleared of rice-fields, creepers, pits, trees, and shrubs.
The earth that is exceedingly firm, capable of bearing the tread of razor-sharp wheels,
stable, and level like a chariot wheel is praised for the formation of a battle array.
A terrain with easily accessible hills, uneven ground that does not break under the weight of soft trees,
and excellent mud and reeds is considered the best for an elephant array.
A land free from all defects, provided with water in some places,
vast, abounding in virtues, and suitable for a fourfold army.
Having thus examined the terrain, the king who is skilled in warfare should construct his battle arrays in whatever place and in whatever manner is appropriate.
On ground endowed with all auspicious characteristics, Ripumardana should form the supreme battle array, which shatters the arrays of the enemy.
The face constitutes the eastern division, and immediately following that is the chest;
the region behind the chest is proclaimed as the posterior part of the chest (praurasya).
Likewise, the back of the chest is called the *pratigraha*;
the *kakṣas*, *prakakṣas*, *pakṣas*, and *prapakṣas* are located on the sides in sequence.
The rear portion, devoted to receiving [the enemy], is called the *pṛṣṭha*;
having thus understood the divisions of the battle array, the king [should proceed].
At the front was a rutting elephant, well-trained and mounted by a brave rider,
equipped with armor and accompanied by two warriors.
It was accompanied by a brave warrior mounted on a western seat,
[surrounded] by three hundred, six hundred, or even nine hundred [attendants].
Guarded by excellent warriors divided into three groups and well-positioned in three locations—
on the back and on both flanks— with swords in hand.
And by hundreds of excellent warriors, adorned with fierce bows, who were well-marked and possessed of firm gaits, stationed in the regions of their armpits.
