Likewise, on one side, he was surrounded by thousands or half of that number, or even hundreds, of gods bearing spears and shields.
On the left wing, there were horses equipped with speed, well-protected by body armor, furnished with all types of weapons, and accompanied by charioteers.
One should station in front [the army] surrounded by five hundred horses and brave foot-soldiers stationed on both wings.
One who can repel all armies and ward off the elephants of the enemy—
one endowed with such strength— should be stationed at the front of the battle array.
For the purpose of breaking the enemy's array, the king should form his own array with three faces, two faces, or even a single face.
O protector of the earth, the king should position his core force, consisting of hereditary troops and forest-dwellers,
as well as the weak enemy force, in the center of the battlefield.
In the front, one should lead various war-apparatus and weapons,
as well as abundant water on camels for the complete satisfaction of those afflicted by thirst.
The lord of the earth himself should stand at the place of reception,
[receiving] one born of the lineage of Airāvaṇa, endowed with auspicious marks.
Born from the auspicious lineage of a portion of Viṣṇu, produced in the forests of Kaliṅga,
accustomed to roaming the peaks of mountains, and trained until the point of death.
He had reached the fourth stage of rut, was like a mountain,
a hero of great strength, self-controlled, wise, and one who understood his own true nature;
he was equipped with magnificent wing-armor fashioned of gold.
Equipped with body armor and wielding a firm and powerful bow.
It was adorned with flagstaffs bearing clusters of peacock feathers as their emblems,
its body variegated with many colors, and it was further beautified by banners.
It was filled with warriors stationed within the *ḍheñca* (chariot-fence), formidable with spearmen in its center,
and accompanied by a rear-mounted rider holding a spear and a javelin in his hands.
One who is diligent in discipline, possessing such qualities and being a hero mounted within himself, should mount an elephant equipped with two shields.
He was accompanied by renowned and principal heroes who bore the skin of a Kṛttikā deer on their hands,
were endowed with personal guards, and were proud of those very bodyguards.
Well-protected by ten thousand or five thousand men stationed in the armpits (kakṣa),
and accompanied by a water-jar (ghaṭā) in the side-chambers (prakakṣa), the council chamber (saciva), and the prince's quarters (kumāra);
With allies, servants, and troops on his side bearing bows and arrows,
with spears, javelins, swords, lances, and mallets in their hands,
and with a hundred thousand excellent warriors mounted upon noble elephants;
By the warriors, whose names have been mentioned, who were stationed in their respective positions in due order.
And the lord of the earth was surrounded by twenty thousand brave and well-trained horsemen, bearing various weapons,
who stood at his side.
On the back of the earth, protected by guards and accompanied by throngs of women from the inner apartments seated within beautiful flower-carts mounted on elephants.
Likewise, let him be stationed with a treasury consisting of cows, horses, grain, and bullion;
and for the protection of their rear, he should deploy a force of men and cavalry.
Having thus arranged such a formation of the army, that slayer of enemy heroes—
He shall advance like the agitated ocean, swallowing the enemy's army.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of military array.
With the lion-roars of the heroes, the neighing of the horses, the slapping of the drivers' arms,
and the trumpeting from the throats of the elephants.
He made the quarters of the sky resound with the sounds of drumbeats, the blasts of trumpets and conchs,
and the thunderous noise of great musical instruments foreboding battle.
Therefore, strengthening his own forces, he should first strike down that army which is weak, divided, or commanded by corruptible men.
One should crush the weak with twice its strength and the strong with its own strength;
however, one should break through a compact formation with fierce elephant divisions.
With fierce and preeminent heroes, one should tear apart the weak army;
with horse-formations, one should break the host of foot-soldiers, and with elephants, one should break the array of horses.
With excellent arrows, spears, nooses, sharp-edged spears, and javelins—
arrows consecrated with fire-oil— one should pierce the leaders of the elephant herds.
By the clashing and friction of the masses of vast elephant divisions,
he shattered the multitudes of rutting elephants belonging to his enemies at the forefront of the battle.
Having reflected upon the royal insignia and determined the king's position, he,
eager for victory, should set out there accompanied by his entire army.
Having shattered them with iron arrows, pierced them thoroughly with spears,
split them in two with blows from discuses, and dragged them down with nooses, he should cause them to fall.
Having crushed the soldiers with blows from his mallets and cut them down with his axe,
he then brought his own elephant into contact with the enemy's elephant.
Having struck down that elephant with the fierce blows of his own elephant's tusks,
he should cut off the enemy's head, adorned with earrings, with his sword.
Thus, having slain the wicked enemy who was arrogant with pride in battle,
he gladdened his own brave warriors with the sound of victory-trumpets.
Having struck down the princes, ministers, counselors, vassals, and regional lords who have come against him, he should bestow gifts as prescribed.
Having satiated the earth with the flood of blood of his enemies,
he gratified the Piśācas with flesh and the carnivorous beasts with their strings of entrails.
Having protected according to dharma those who were terrified and intent on fleeing,
he quickly took possession of the excellent elephants that had been freed from their trappings.
Having seized the female cattle, the herds of camels, and the entire treasury without exception, and having likewise scrutinized everything with great effort from all sides;
When a very powerful enemy is thus bound in battle by a strong king, that shall be the punishment known as "killing in war."
A king who has destroyed his enemies but is himself devoid of strength and power should employ three types of punishment: those consisting of poison, sorcery, and malevolent rites.
Hālāhala, Śṛṅgī, the terrifying Kālakūṭa,
and Vatsanābha as the fourth— these are proclaimed as the stationary (sthāvara) poisons.
Poison produced from the fangs of snakes and similar sources is known as mobile (jangama) poison;
that which is produced by the combination of incompatible substances is called artificial (kṛtrima) poison.
Those among the enemies who are disaffected and ready to act— those excellent men—
one should alienate from their faction by means of gifts and then employ them as an agent (rasa).
This should be done at reservoirs, wells, ponds, and likewise at small lakes.
One should administer poison to enemies in bathing water, as well as in oil, in foot-unguents along with sandals, or within a pleasure-pool.
And among the princes, ministers, counselors, and generals,
as well as among the foremost great elephants and the best of horses.
When the destruction of enemies is carried out by one who is impoverished through the application of poison,
that is called the "punishment of poison" (viṣadaṇḍa).
He who is brave, firm in devotion, and has renounced the fear for his life;
he who is heroic, knows the proper timing, and is skilled in the means of slaying.
Having received a large salary provided by his kinsmen and sons,
he should employ lethal means with the desire to slay his negligent enemies.
Among those addicted to song and instrumental music, those devoted to gambling,
those whose minds are intent on hunting, and those occupied with religious processions;
During the diversions of wrestling matches, as well as at other festivals and the like,
during the activities within the inner apartments, and while intent upon the worship of the gods;
When enemies are dejected by their heroic sports, indifferent to food and drink,
or preoccupied with other affairs, one should carry out their slaughter.
The hurling of sharp and excellent mechanical weapons by means of illusion against an enemy is proclaimed as the "Punishment of Slaying" (ghātadaṇḍa).
One should uproot the enemy from afar by means of Brahmins who know the true principles of the Atharva-veda, have conquered their senses, and are experts in the application of mantras and tantras.
By means of homas for malevolent rites and mantras that accomplish the six magical acts (ṣatkarma),
as well as through fierce diagrams (yantra) and drawings, and by means of curses, causing loss of vigor, and so forth, he is a master of these practices.
And with drums and trumpets well-mastered through mantras and tantras,
with banners, lamps, incense, and peacock-feather brooms;
With arrows empowered by mantras and with unbroken grains mixed with white mustard seeds,
one may delude the enemies, paralyze them, and likewise cause them to be driven from their place.
That which causes friends to be alienated, brings enemies under control,
and even takes away life— this is the "abhicāraka" (malevolent) punishment.
Thus end the varieties of punishment.
Free from passion and hatred, the king should examine legal cases together with learned and eminent Brahmins, in accordance with the codes of law (Smṛti).
If a king finds fault with those who are faultless while failing to punish those who are guilty of faults,
he incurs great infamy and falls into a miserable state.
An officiating priest, a family chaplain, a son, a brother, a kinsman, as well as a friend—
none of these are exempt from punishment by the king, nor is there any man who, having deviated from his own duty, remains unpunished.

The king should appoint as members of the assembly those who know the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, who are truthful in their dealings, righteous, and indeed impartial toward friends and enemies alike.
The protector of the earth should deliberate upon virtues and faults in consultation with Brahmins who are steadfast, free from greed, eminent, and skilled in worldly affairs.
Where three, five, or seven Brahmins learned in the Vedas abide in deliberation,
that assembly shall be equal to the sacrifice of Indra.
In that assembly, whoever knows the dharma and is skilled in sacred learning—
whether appointed or unappointed— is worthy to speak the truth.
Those members of the assembly who, having abandoned the path that is right, follow one who has strayed,
must be awakened to the eternal path of dharma.
And even when not specifically questioned, one should speak all that which is true and consistent;
or, having understood it, one should not speak the truth if it would cause harm, for a speaker of falsehood incurs sin.
A few members of the assembly should be appointed from among those who are of noble birth, virtuous, wealthy, advanced in age, and free from envy.
One who is free from greed, true to his word, virtuous in character, pleasant of speech,
skilled in the meaning of the treatises on dharma, and discerning in the conduct of worldly affairs.
He should be a learned and skillful judge, endowed with the capacity for discernment,
one who knows the truth behind gestures and facial expressions, and proficient in the methods of reasoning and refutation.
The lord of the earth should appoint a single Brahmin who is endowed with Vedic learning, proficient in the treatises on Dharma, and worthy of himself as a counterpart.
One who first questions those who have come for the purpose of debate and properly deliberates upon their speech is therefore known as a *pāḍvivāka*.
If the Lord of the people, being himself preoccupied with royal affairs or suffering from physical infirmity, does not personally oversee the case,
the judge shall deliberate upon it.

However, one who is of noble birth, endowed with self-control, fearful of the next world, knower of dharma, brave, tranquil, and free from envy— such a person should be employed when there is a need for deception.
One who is never a cause of agitation to the subjects, who is ever devoted to their welfare,
who is immediately diligent and capable— even such a Kṣatriya may be the lord of the assembly.
Due to the difficulty of finding such a person, even among the Kṣatriyas, the king should appoint a Vaiśya as the presiding officer of the assembly—
one who is superior in virtue, impartial, and esteemed by the people.
The Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas should be made superior, middling, and inferior respectively;
however, under no circumstances whatsoever should a Shudra be made an object of deliberation [in such matters].
Whether out of greed, fear, or passion, those members of the court who destroy the meaning of the Smṛti scriptures shall be punished individually with double the fine imposed on the litigant.
When one who has been oppressed by a more powerful person, having transgressed the path of the virtuous,
makes a representation to the king, that is known as a ground for litigation.
Non-application [of the mind] should be understood as twofold: either through doubt or through conviction.
Doubt arises from association with the wicked; conviction arises from seeing the limbs of another.
The first [title] shall be the non-payment of debt; immediately after that, the deposit;
and the third is proclaimed to be sale without ownership.
The fourth is declared to be collective acquisition;
the fifth is called what is given, and the sixth is the misappropriation of what has been given.
The seventh is non-payment of wages; the eighth is the breach of a compact;
the ninth and tenth are rescission of purchase and sale.
Likewise, the eleventh is declared to be a dispute between an owner and a keeper;
and a dispute between an owner and a servant is proclaimed as the twelfth.
The thirteenth is declared by the wise to be the dispute regarding boundaries;
here, verbal abuse has been defined by the wise as the fourteenth.
The fifteenth [title of law] has been described by the knowers as "Physical Assault" (daṇḍapāruṣya);
"Theft" (steya) is declared as the sixteenth by the seers who perceive the truth.
The seventeenth book is called Sāhasa, proclaimed by the virtuous;
the eighteenth is designated as Strīsaṅgrahaṇa.
The nineteenth is declared by the investigators to be the "Duties of Men and Women," and the twentieth section shall be that titled "Partition of Inheritance."
The twenty-first is gambling (dyūta), and the twenty-second is betting with living creatures (samāhvaya);
King Someśvara has thus declared these titles of legal procedure (vyavahārapada).
Thus end the heads of legal procedure.
A capable lord of the earth should not himself initiate a lawsuit,
nor should a king accept a bribe offered by one seeking redress for his cause.
When one who has come for a dispute stands before the assembly, he should ask:
"What is your business? What is your sorrow? Tell me, casting aside all hesitation."
Once it has been examined, he should ask: "By whom? In what? From where? How?
Therefore, having entered the assembly, speak the truth regarding what was done by you.
Having deliberated with the members of the court so that the course of justice may be right,
he should cause the summoning of the defendant to be carried out by means of written documents and messengers.
If, having been summoned, he does not come because he is diseased,
suffering, imprisoned, in a precarious situation, preoccupied with ritual duties, or afflicted by fever;
Whether he accomplishes the master’s business or is intent on the king’s affairs,
even if he is intoxicated or heedless, he is nevertheless not at fault.
A woman of noble birth, the wife of another, a young woman who has recently given birth, one in her menses, and one lacking a protector— these should not be summoned to the assembly hall.
Having caused the statements of the plaintiff and the defendant to be written down,
he should investigate the case according to the place and time, and by means of various kinds of reasons.
Therefore, the protector of the earth should investigate [a case] by means of these three proofs— documentary evidence, witnesses, and possession— in accordance with the legal treatises (smṛti).
To one who is devoid of these means of proof, the king should administer divine ordeal;
and that should be administered according to the person's age, physical condition, place, and time.
When human evidence is difficult to obtain, then divine evidence should be offered; it should not be offered when human evidence exists.
To those suspected by the king, or accused by thieves,
who seek purification, an ordeal should be administered by him without the requirement of their heads.
Whether the matter has been determined by means of legal proofs or investigated through divine ordeals,
the king shall inflict punishment according to reason and in accordance with the nature of the offense.
The death penalty is proclaimed as the taking of life for evildoers by means of poison, arrows, elephants, serpents, weapons, fire, water, and so forth.
Of the hair, the ears, the eyes, and likewise the nose;
of the tongue, the two hands, as well as the fingers and the generative organ.
The cutting off of the feet or other such limbs,
according to the nature of the offense, is called the punishment of affliction (kleśadaṇḍa).
Binding, beating, and likewise verbal abuse or harsh reprimand—
such forms are proclaimed to be the punishment of affliction (kleśadaṇḍa).
When the fine is five hundred paṇas, it is known as the first amercement;
the middle is to be understood as five [hundred], and the highest is one thousand.
Regarding the dispute, it is said in some places to be equal, in others twice as great;
in some it is declared threefold, and in others it is stated to be fourfold.

A fine may be anywhere from more than one's entire property down to the property itself; such confiscation of wealth is recorded as a punishment according to the nature of the offense and the object involved.
Punishment protects the social order; punishment sets righteousness in motion;
it wards off unrighteousness; therefore, one should employ punishment.
Since the law of the fish prevails in a kingdom where punishment is absent,
therefore a righteous king should inflict punishment upon the wicked.
The world, bound by the fear of the falling rod, stands established in righteousness;
like a victorious elephant, though intoxicated, brought under control by the goad.
Since people in this world are greatly agitated by the fear of severe punishment,
one should therefore protect the subjects through the application of mild measures.
From the application of the punishments as prescribed,
the fame, dharma, kingdom, and treasury of the king who walks the path of righteousness increase.
Thus have been declared the seven limbs of the kingdom, as well as the three powers,
the sixfold policy, and the fourfold means.
The king Somabhūpāla, an expert in political ethics, performed twenty rites for the sake of ensuring the stability of the kingdom once he had attained sovereignty.
Thus ends the chapter on Punishment, the twentieth.

Thus ends the section on the means for stabilizing the kingdom, within the *Mānasollāsa*— the *Abhilashitārthacintāmaṇi*— composed by the illustrious Someśvaradeva, the Bull of the Earth (*Bhūlokamalla*), the ornament of the Cālukyas, the crest-jewel of the lineage of the Great King of Kings, Satyāśraya.
The Second Chapter.
The first part is completed.
